Danil Boparai, a content strategy director at Dazed, thinks "the hype is justified".
"He brings a very raw energy which you see with his reluctance to do much press, no-one knows much about him, it's all about the music for him," he says.
"EsDeeKid has become one of the voices of Gen Z musically, through a unique take on rap due to his Scouse accent and his aesthetic taps into quite medieval-style fashion.
"He had a castle style set [on Sunday] which was quite unique, I haven't see that at All Points East or Outbreak festival before."
It helps that every song on the musician's debut mixtape "became like a TikTok anthem", Boparai says.
![All Points East festival goers Bin and Zari smile at the camera wearing their festival gear. Bin wears a sheer black top and has green and blonde hair with a black furry headband. Zari wears a black slogan t-shirt and has pink and green hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/78f0/live/64c1d0c0-9fb0-11f1-95c3-f94999de983a.jpg)
Guess who?! Fans Bin (left) and Zari say the mystery around the rapper is what makes him interesting
And his appeal has since spread across the pond.
EsDeeKid's tour will begin in North America in September, before ending in December with two hometown shows in Liverpool.
For fan James, the anonymity element is "amazing".
"I work in event promotion, I think giving yourself an aesthetic, something to cling to, something that people can watch is really important in the music industry, it makes you stand out," he says.
Decked out in a bright outfit to see EsDeeKid, fan Zari says the rapper's presence is "very mysterious".
"But that's the good thing about him, it's what brings people towards him, we're all curious."
And for Boparai, the Chalamet rumours may have been big for his brand, but having the music to back it up is crucial.
"EsDeeKid understands the internet," he says.
"It is so important to come across as truly authentic and I think he does because he lets his music do the speaking for him.
"He also doesn't change his accent, he doesn't reveal his face.
"He's just him, take it or leave it."
![A footer logo for BBC Newsbeat. It has the BBC logo and the word Newsbeat in white over a colorful background of violet, purple and orange shapes. At the bottom a black square reading "Listen on Sounds" is visible.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/0d6f/live/397f39f0-d40c-11ef-9fd6-0be88a764111.jpg)
summary: The masked and anonymous British rapper EsDeeKid drew large crowds and positive reactions during his UK festival appearance at All Points East. Although earlier rumors falsely suggested he was actor Timothée Chalamet, the speculation has not slowed the artist's rising popularity. EsDeeKid recently released his debut album, built a large social media following, and announced a 48-date international tour.
key_points: EsDeeKid performed his first UK festival appearance in a while at All Points East.
Early rumors claiming the masked rapper was Timothée Chalamet were dispelled when the actor appeared in a video with him in December.
His debut album Rebel reached number eight on the UK charts and number 23 on the US Billboard 200 chart.
EsDeeKid announced a 48-date tour titled Council House Rat, spanning Europe, the US, and the UK.

title: A new Oasis reunion? Liam Gallagher tells Noel ‘announce the tour’
author: Roisin O'Connor
content:
“Ffs RKID announce the tour we’re all losing our minds.” So said the latest tantalising post from the world’s biggest wind-up merchant Liam Gallagher. Fans might stay sceptical... but could this in fact be the clearest indicator yet that another Oasis reunion is on the cards?
By now, a new tour might seem less of a surprise than those long-awaited 2025 shows. The rock band made history when brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher put an end to their years-long feud and reunited onstage for the first time in almost 16 years to play a record-breaking world tour, including a series of homecoming shows in Manchester.
Even before the 2025 tour concluded, fans predicted that Oasis would be keen to get back out on the road again, given the run of shows were a defining cultural event – as well as a very lucrative one. Oasis Live ‘25 was estimated by Forbes to have generated over $400m (£293m) in revenue, with Noel and Liam each pocketing between $50m-$100m. As a result, the pair cracked the Sunday Times Rich List this year with a combined net worth of $375m.
The Independent’s sources have said they understand that a Knebworth residency is on the cards but have yet to confirm any specific dates. This year marked the 30th anniversary of the band’s legendary Knebworth shows in 1996, where they played to a combined audience of 250,000 (more than four per cent of the population applied for tickets), including the rumoured 7,000-strong guestlist.
![Oasis at Knebworth, August 1996](https://static.the-independent.com/2025/06/25/09/13112940-4ca3860b-788d-4a10-99d9-8e7270096092.jpg)
Sources have also said that Noel has been writing new music – it remains to be seen if this will emerge in the shape of the first Oasis album since 2008’s Dig Out Your Soul, with Liam on vocal duties.
Earlier this month, it was announced that SJM Concerts, the promoter behind the Oasis reunion tour, had secured a licence to host events at Knebworth indefinitely.
The promoter has also worked on shows with Take That and The Prodigy, as well as comedian Peter Kay.
The licence allows events for up to 125,000 people, with live music and dance performances permitted until 3am.
In July, The Sun claimed that Oasis would play six nights at Knebworth over a three-week period in September 2027. Meanwhile, the Manchester Evening News reported that same month that the rock’n’roll stars would headline 12 nights at the Etihad stadium, with an insider telling the paper: “It will be 12 nights at the Etihad Stadium across May and June. They could even add more dates to that as well, there’s talk of up to 20. The wider tour is also going to include a return to Knebworth.”
Before that, there was speculation in 2024 – after the band announced their comeback tour – that they would return to the site. Oasis denied this on X in a statement: “Contrary to reports in some UK tabloid media today, Oasis will not be playing Knebworth Park in the future.”
The Independent has contacted Oasis’s representatives for comment.
![Brothers Liam and Noel Gallagher during their 2025 reunion tour](https://static.the-independent.com/2025/09/24/9/00/SEI263754364.jpeg)
Contrary to tabloid media reports, sources told The Independent that the mood backstage during Oasis’s 2025 reunion was jubilant, with both Noel and Liam in great spirits as their famous friends – from football stars to pop singers, including Manchester City star Jack Grealish and the Happy Mondays’ Shaun Ryder – rubbed elbows.
“It’s been a proper love-in backstage,” one source said. “There’s a friends and family bar which is basically free booze – Guinness on draft (of course) (sic), beer, wine and champagne. It’s like going to a wedding every night.”
They continued: “Cast and Richard Ashcroft [Oasis’s support acts] are having the time of their lives – it’s been so nice to see Noel and Liam’s guests vibing off each other. Everyone’s been making new friends.”
And while it was true that Liam had left early each night – this was nothing to do with animosity towards his older brother and everything to do with him ensuring he was in peak condition for each concert.
“Liam has been completely zen, focusing on his voice and arriving shortly before each show, then getting straight off to avoid temptation,” a source told The Independent.
The 2025 reunion tour is the subject of a forthcoming documentary directed by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, due for release in IMAX cinemas on 9 September and on Disney+. Titled Don’t Look Back In Anger, the film follows Noel and Liam as they undertake the Live ‘25 tour, which kicked off just over a year ago in Cardiff.
A 46-second teaser trailer, released last month, showed cheering fans before cutting to footage of the Gallagher siblings backstage getting ready for their first shows together since their split in 2009.
“Oasis Live ‘25, one of the most anticipated rock ‘n’ roll comebacks of our time,” Disney+ said in a statement. “The film is an unapologetically uplifting account of the biggest musical event of 2025, capturing the experience and emotions of the band and their fans across the world.
“The unique perspective includes rehearsal, backstage, and onstage access as well as the first joint interviews with Noel and Liam in over 20 years.”
When it comes to Glastonbury, Liam insisted over the weekend that an Oasis headline performance is “not happening” next year. Organiser Emily Eavis recently confirmed that all headliners have been booked.
As for a 2027 tour, for now, Oasis fans will just have to roll with it... the band are taking their time.
summary: Following their successful and lucrative 2025 reunion tour, Liam Gallagher has posted a hint on social media urging Noel to announce a new tour. Sources indicate that a Knebworth residency and multiple stadium shows are being discussed, and that Noel has been writing new music. Additionally, a documentary about the 2025 reunion, titled Don't Look Back In Anger, is set for release in September on Disney+ and in IMAX.
key_points: Liam Gallagher posted a message on social media prompting Noel to announce a new Oasis tour.
The 2025 reunion tour generated over $400m in revenue and placed the brothers on the Sunday Times Rich List.
Sources suggest a Knebworth residency and up to 20 nights at the Etihad Stadium could be part of future plans.
A documentary titled Don't Look Back In Anger, directed by Steven Knight, will be released on Disney+ and in IMAX cinemas.
Liam Gallagher stated that an Oasis headline performance at Glastonbury next year is not happening.

title: ‘The Gentlemen’ Officially Renewed for Season 3 as First Season 2 Trailer Drops: ‘I’m Looking Forward to Pushing the Boundaries Further,’ Guy Ritchie Says (EXCLUSIVE)
author: K J Yossman
content:
“The Gentlemen” has officially been greenlit for Season 3, Variety can confirm.
Guy Ritchie’s high-society, high-octane caper starring Theo James and Kaya Scodelario is set to return for a third outing, comprised of eight episodes. Variety understands that while the new season is in pre-production no scripts have yet been finalized, let alone new casting, despite rumors of Meghan Markle joining. The show is due to go into production imminently.
“The ambition of ‘The Gentlemen’ has accelerated, the world has expanded and the consequences carry weight,” says creator, writer, director and executive producer Guy Ritchie. “A third season felt inevitable, and I’m looking forward to pushing the boundaries of it further.”
Popular on Variety
Ritchie will also be returning to direct Season 3, which he co-writes with Matthew Read.
The news of the third season comes amid a host of returning season orders for some of Netflix’s top U.K. shows including “Black Mirror” Season 8, “Legends” Season 2 and “Being Gordon Ramsay” Season 2. Other highly anticipated Netflix U.K. dramas returning for a second season are “Supacell,” “Black Doves” and “House of Guinness.”
The streamer today also released its first full-length trailer for “The Gentlemen” Season 2, ahead of its launch on Sept. 3.
![](https://variety.com/wp-content/themes/pmc-variety-2020/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
Season 2 will see Eddie Horniman (James) and Susie Glass (Scodelario) grow their business internationally as they take to the lakeside villas of Italy where at least one of their crew finds out he’s bitten off more than he can chew.
Meanwhile Eddie’s rise through the criminal underworld is mirrored by his rise through the British establishment, bringing him into the circle of a new oleaginous aristo played by Hugh Bonneville, who is joining the cast.
In the trailer, Eddie hints at his growing ambitions, as he tells Geoff of his stately pile: “Four hundred years ago, this estate spread out as far as the eye could see. I want it all back.”
With American billionaire Stanley Johnston (Giancarlo Esposito) whispering in his hear (“You are destined to rule, forge your own path”) Eddie’s confidence in his ability to play high-stakes games with notorious crime lords soars ever higher — but at what cost?
Season 2 sees Ray Winstone returning as Glass’s kingpin father Bobby while Harry Goodwins returns as her brawny brother Jack.
On the Duke’s side, Joely Richardson is back as Eddie’s mother Lady Sabrina, Daniel Ings as disinherited older brother Freddy, Jasmine Blackborow as sister Charly and Vinnie Jones as Geoff, keeper of the grounds – and family secrets.
![](https://variety.com/wp-content/themes/pmc-variety-2020/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
Also returning for Season 2 are Esposito, Michael Vu, Ruby Sear and Pearce Quigley.
Joining the cast this season are Benjamin Clementine (“Dune”), Benedetta Porcaroli (“The Leopard”), Amra Mallassi (“Dune: Part Two”), Tyler Conti (“Tell Me Everything”), professional boxer Chris Eubank Jr and “Love Island U.K.” host Maya Jama.
“The Gentlemen” is produced by Moonage Pictures for Netflix and Miramax TV. Exec producers are Ritchie, Read, Ivan Atkinson, Will Gould, Simon Crawford, Collins and Frith Tiplady for Moonage Pictures alongside Jonathan Glickman and Marc Helwig for Miramax TV,
Check out the new trailer below:
summary: Netflix has officially renewed Guy Ritchie's series "The Gentlemen" for an eight-episode third season ahead of its season two premiere. Season two, set to launch on September 3, features expanding international operations and new cast members including Hugh Bonneville. Meanwhile, season three is currently in pre-production with no final scripts or casting decisions yet made.
key_points: "The Gentlemen" has been officially greenlit for an eight-episode Season 3.
Season 3 is currently in pre-production with no scripts finalized or new casting confirmed.
Netflix released the first full-length trailer for Season 2, which premieres on September 3.
Season 2 features returning cast members alongside new additions such as Hugh Bonneville.

title: Meghan Markle is reportedly dropped from Netflix series after ‘intense’ backlash
author: Carsen Holaday
content:
Meghan Markle may not be appearing in the third season of Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen after all.
This week, reports that the Duchess of Sussex, 45, was considering a return to acting in the Netflix series sparked waves of backlash in the U.K.
Now, former Vanity Fair and New York Magazine editor-in-chief Tina Brown claims the decision to cast Meghan in the drama has been reversed.
“I learned this morning that the casting of Meghan Markle in season 3 of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series The Gentlemen has been withdrawn,” Brown — who is the author of two books about the Royal Family — wrote on her Substack Saturday.
“The backlash in the UK was so intense, it became untenable to go forward,” she added.
The Independent has reached out to Netflix, Meghan and Ritchie for comment.
According to Variety, Meghan was in discussions to join the third installment of the series, starring Theo James and Kaya Scodelario, which films in the U.K.
The show is a spin-off of Guy Ritchie’s popular 2019 crime comedy movie of the same name, which starred Matthew McConaughey, Charlie Hunnam and Colin Farrell.
The third season of the show has not been officially greenlit. Season two premieres September 3.
The duke and duchess revealed earlier this month that they would be moving from California back to the U.K. with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, who are both enrolled in British schools, six years after they came to the U.S.
![Guy Ritchie’s ‘The Gentlemen’ films in the UK, where Harry and Meghan are returning after six years in the US](https://static.the-independent.com/2023/11/30/12/TG_101_Unit_01121_COMP_NEW_RT.jpg)
Brown reported that the upcoming move across the pond was partly inspired by Meghan’s potential gig in The Gentlemen.
It would have been her first acting role since she quit performing in 2017, when she got engaged to Prince Harry.
However, she recently appeared on screen in a cameo as herself in the upcoming Amazon MGM comedy Close Personal Friends, which stars Lily Collins and Brie Larson.
It marked Meghan’s first performance in nearly a decade after she rose to fame for her role as Rachel Zane in seven seasons of the legal drama Suits. She also appeared in films including Horrible Bosses, A Lot Like Love and Random Encounters.
Powerful leaders in the entertainment industry have spoken out to say that directors and producers will undoubtedly be eager to meet with Meghan if she has officially decided to resume her acting career.
summary: Reports indicate that Meghan Markle's potential casting in the third season of Netflix's 'The Gentlemen' has been withdrawn following intense backlash in the U.K. According to former magazine editor Tina Brown, the negative reaction made moving forward with the role untenable. The third season of the series has not yet been officially greenlit.
key_points: Meghan Markle was reportedly considered for a role in season three of Guy Ritchie's Netflix series The Gentlemen.
Tina Brown stated that the casting decision was reversed due to intense backlash in the U.K.
The third season of the show has not yet received an official greenlight.
Meghan previously quit acting in 2017 upon her engagement to Prince Harry after starring in the legal drama Suits.

title: Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies a year after son
author: Kevin Rawlinson
content:
Tributes have been paid to the Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner, who has died a year after her son and co-star Sam was killed in a car crash.
The physiotherapist from Manchester died after “a long and courageous battle with cancer”, relatives said. She was 61 and is survived by her other son, Charlie.
She and Sam competed in the second series of the BBC’s global travel competition, journeying across South America together in 2020.
Relatives remembered her as “an intrepid adventurer” who was “brave, kind, witty and endlessly loving”.
Her family said: “She had a rare gift for making everyone around her feel more alive. She lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves. She was blessed with countless friends, drawn to her extraordinary magnetism. Somehow, each one felt as though they were among her very best.
“To us, she was more than all of these things. She was our family, our joy, our safe place and our absolute treasure. We know how deeply Jo was loved, and we take comfort in knowing that her laughter, her courage, her kindness and her wonderfully outrageous spirit will live on in the many people whose lives she touched.”
![Jo Gardiner in a PR image for Race Across the World](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/2820b6382c2157febd5aaace20a6ccebcc1e0202/1131_196_2982_2386/master/2982.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The family asked that those who knew and loved her “do exactly what she would have wanted: tell the funny stories, raise a glass, have an adventure, laugh loudly and live life to the full.”
They added: “She was one of a kind. There will never be another her.”
Sam Gardiner died in June 2025 at the age of 24 after his car came off the road, rolled and landed on its side.
The mother and son competed on Race Across the World because Jo wanted to have a travel adventure with Sam, who had ADHD. They competed against four other pairs of contestants racing from Mexico City down to Ushuaia in Argentina.
A spokesperson for the programme said: “On behalf of the Studio Lambert production team, the BBC and the whole Race Across the World cast, we offer our deepest and heartfelt sympathies to Jo’s son Charlie and her wider family and friends.
“Millions of people remembered their transformative journey across Latin America in 2020 and we hold that memory in our hearts as we fondly recall Jo’s passion for life, her kindness, her strength and above all her utter devotion to Sam and her family.”
Jo Gardiner had type 1 diabetes and was an ambassador for Diabetes UK. Her family has set up a JustGiving page in her name and said all donations are to support the charity.
summary: Jo Gardiner, a physiotherapist and star of the BBC show Race Across the World, has died at the age of 61 following a long battle with cancer. Her death comes a year after her son and co-star Sam was killed in a car crash. Gardiner is survived by her other son, Charlie, and was remembered by her family and the show's producers for her adventurous spirit, kindness, and devotion.
key_points: Jo Gardiner passed away at 61 after a long battle with cancer.
She and her son Sam previously competed in the second series of Race Across the World in 2020.
Sam Gardiner had died a year prior in a car crash at the age of 24.
Gardiner was a type 1 diabetes ambassador, and her family set up a JustGiving page to support Diabetes UK in her honor.

title: Jo Gardiner Dead: 'Race Across The World' Star Passes A Year After Son
author: Jake Kanter
content:
![Jo and Sam Gardiner](https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/EastI-Standard-image-2026-08-24T104343.967.jpg?w=681&h=383&crop=1) 
Jo Gardiner, star of the second season of Race Across the World, has died. She was 61.
Gardiner’s family said she died after a “long and courageous battle with cancer.” Her passing comes a year after her son, Sam, lost his life in a car crash in 2025.
Jo and Sam competed together in Race Across the World, traversing Latin America for the BBC reality competition series, produced by Studio Lambert. They became firm favorites among fans of the show, finishing fourth in their race.
“She lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves,” Jo’s family said in a statement, shared with BBC News.
“She was blessed with countless friends, drawn to her extraordinary magnetism. Somehow, each one felt as though they were among her very best. To us, she was more than all of these things. She was our family, our joy, our safe place and our absolute treasure.”
Watch on Deadline
In a statement, Studio Lambert and the BBC said: “We offer our deepest and heartfelt sympathies to Jo’s son Charlie, and her wider family and friends.
“Following the tragic death of Jo’s son Sam last year, we paid tribute to how integral Sam and Jo had been to series two. Millions of people remembered their transformative journey across Latin America in 2020 and we hold that memory in our hearts as we fondly recall Jo’s passion for life, her kindness, her strength, and above all her utter devotion to Sam and her family.
“At the time of filming, Sam described his mum as amazing – and that is how we will always remember her. Jo became the matriarch of the Race Across the World cast family, she leaves a lasting legacy in the many lives that she touched, both through the series and beyond. It was a privilege to share her story and she will be deeply missed.”
summary: Jo Gardiner, a star of the reality television series "Race Across The World," has died at the age of 61 following a battle with cancer. Her passing occurs one year after the death of her son, Sam, with whom she competed on the second season of the BBC show. Family, the BBC, and production company Studio Lambert paid tribute to her memory, strength, and legacy.
key_points: Jo Gardiner passed away at age 61 after a battle with cancer.
She competed alongside her son Sam on season two of "Race Across The World," finishing fourth.
Her death comes one year after her son Sam died in a car crash in 2025.
The BBC and Studio Lambert released a statement honoring her kindness, strength, and devotion to her family.

title: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulls out of 2027 Eurovision Song Contest
author: Paul Glynn
content:
![Spectators wearing raincoats in rainbow colours gather at the fan area in front of the City Hall in Vienna on May 14, 2026, prior to the second semi-final of the Eurovision Song Contest (ESC).](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/c11e/live/6c8b6380-9fb4-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
Dutch public broadcaster Avrotros has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, saying that the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.
In a statement, external released on Monday, the broadcaster said the decision was due to a lack of clarity from organisers - the Eurovision Broadcasting Union (EBU) - over assessing which countries could compete.
Avrotros added: "The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years."
Earlier this month, the EBU updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year. But Avrotros said those changes "do not provide sufficient confidence that âthe â independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored."
The broadcaster's withdrawal from this year's contest in Burgas, Bulgaria, does not necessarily rule out Dutch participation in Eurovision 2027.
Another broadcaster within the Dutch public broadcasting system could potentially take it on as the country has several public broadcasters, unlike the UK.
But the Netherlands boycotted this year's contest in Vienna, Austria, after Israel were allowed to compete.
Only Ireland and Sweden have won Eurovision more than the Netherlands.
Martin Green, director of the contest, said in a statement that the EBU regretted Avrotros's decision but respected its views.
"We will now continue our dialogue with NPO, the umbrella organization for Dutch public service media, regarding the opportunities for another broadcaster to participate. We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest."
'Platform for division'
Taco Zimmerman, director general of Avrotos, said the Eurovision Song Contest "was originally created to bring people and countries together" but was now "a platform for division".
He said: "It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character.
"The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division. As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values."
He added: "They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts. That is painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the contest again next year."
Green, however, stated that the contest "has always been a place to bring people together, celebrate diverse communities, and show that a better world is possible even in the most difficult times."
New rules
The recent amendment to the rules, that mean a country involved in an armed military conflict can't host the next contest if it wins, was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026.
It stated that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".
Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain, Ireland and the Netherlands.
Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.
It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.
Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.
Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.
summary: Dutch public broadcaster Avrotros has withdrawn from the Eurovision Song Contest due to concerns that the event has lost its neutrality amid ongoing military conflicts. The decision follows a lack of clarity from organizers, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), regarding participation rules. Despite Avrotros's exit, another Dutch public broadcaster could potentially participate in the future.
key_points: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulled out of the Eurovision Song Contest citing a loss of neutrality over a participating country's involvement in a military conflict.
The EBU recently updated rules stating a winning country involved in an armed conflict cannot host the following year, but Avrotros deemed this insufficient.
Avrotros stated that the humanitarian suffering in Gaza and restrictions on press freedom have turned the contest into a platform for division.
Another Dutch public broadcaster could potentially take over participation, as the Netherlands has multiple public broadcasters.
The Netherlands previously boycotted the contest in Vienna after Israel was allowed to compete.

title: Hayley Atwell: Agent Carter Death "Complete Disservice" To Character
author: Jake Kanter
content:
![Hayley Atwell](https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Doctor-Strange-in-the-Multiverse-of-Madness-071323-5ca38f34cdb74b6a9c6946bdc943909b-e1787556087643.jpg?w=681&h=383&crop=1) 
Hayley Atwell was disappointed about the demise of Peggy Carter.
In an interview at the For the Love of Fantasy & Sci-Fi convention in London, Atwell told attendees that she was frustrated by Captain Carter’s storyline in 2022’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.
Cameoing in the film as an alternate to Captain America, Carter — an MCU fixture since 2011 — was apparently killed off by Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen) with her own shield.
Atwell said: “If I’m really like brutally honest, I was so disappointed with how they positioned her and what happened to her in that scene. It’s so small, and she gets frisbeed to death.”
The actress said she pleaded with colleagues on set to make changes to the scene. “I tried on set to kind of go, ‘Can I just add? Can I just suggest?’ And they were like, ‘Sure, but no.'”
Watch on Deadline
She continued: “I felt that was like a bum steer and a complete disservice to the character.”
Atwell, who is expected to return as Carter in Avengers: Doomsday later this year, said the character was having “fun” in the Captain Carter guise — and she hopes for more of the same. “I hope maybe one day in the future they’ll give her more in that capacity,” she teased.
It’s not the first time Atwell has discussed her misgivings about Carter’s cameo in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.
In 2023, she told the Happy Sad Confused podcast: “When she was like, ‘I could do this all day’ and then followed by she’s immediately cut in half by a frisbee. And the audience being like, ‘She can’t do it all day. Apparently you can’t, so, egg on your face.’ That doesn’t really serve Peggy very well.”
Earlier in the For the Love of Fantasy & Sci-Fi interview, Atwell revealed that she uses Carter’s line “I know my value” in her contract negotiations with Marvel. “If I’m able to say these lines with conviction, I’ve got to embody them myself,” she added.
summary: Actress Hayley Atwell expressed strong disappointment over Peggy Carter's brief death scene in the 2022 film Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. Atwell felt that having the character killed off quickly with her own shield was a complete disservice and a bum steer. Despite her frustrations with that cameo, Atwell is expected to return as Carter in Avengers: Doomsday.
key_points: Hayley Atwell criticized Peggy Carter's death in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness during a London convention.
Atwell stated that she tried to suggest changes on set, but her ideas were rejected.
She previously voiced similar concerns in a 2023 podcast regarding how the character's famous catchphrase was undermined.
Atwell is expected to reprise her role as the character in Avengers: Doomsday.
She revealed that she uses Carter's line 'I know my value' during her contract negotiations with Marvel.

title: Manchester Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies year after son
author: Georgie Docker
content:
![Jo and Sam pose together in an ornate room. He's wearing dark baseball cap and green top and rucksack and smiling, while Jo has shoulder-length brown hair and wears a white vest. She's also smiling.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/66b5/live/20cfac90-9fa4-11f1-bff6-57f1422ebb0b.jpg)
Jo Gardiner travelled with her son Sam in the 2020 series of the BBC One show
- Published
A former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.
Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.
Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.
Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".
![Woman in blue vest and shorts wearing a grey rucksack](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/e2a1/live/eaa79bc0-9fa1-11f1-a83c-33ebef033ca4.jpg)
Jo Gardiner's family described her as "our joy, our safe place and our absolute treasure"
Gardiner is survived by her son Charlie.
Her son, Sam, who she appeared with on the show, died in June 2025 after his car came off the road and crashed.
The mother and son competed on Race Across The World because Gardiner wanted to experience a travel adventure with Sam, who had ADHD.
They competed against four other pairs of contestants racing from Mexico City down to Ushuaia in Argentina.
'Outrageous spirit'
Gardiner's family said "she had a rare gift for making everyone around her feel more alive".
"She lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves," they added.
"She was blessed with countless friends, drawn to her extraordinary magnetism.
"Somehow, each one felt as though they were among her very best.
"To us, she was more than all of these things.
"She was our family, our joy, our safe place and our absolute treasure."
"We know how deeply Jo was loved, and we take comfort in knowing that her laughter, her courage, her kindness and her wonderfully outrageous spirit will live on in the many people whose lives she touched."
![A woman in a blue shirt and jeans sits on a garden wall with flowers behind her](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/59f8/live/f0d76df0-9fa0-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Jo Gardiner was the "matriarch" of the Race Across The World family, producers say
The family asked for privacy while they grieved, but urged "everyone who knew and loved Jo to do exactly what she would have wanted: tell the funny stories, raise a glass, have an adventure, laugh loudly and live life to the full".
They said she was "one of a kind", adding: "There will never be another her."
A Race Across The World spokesperson said: "On behalf of the Studio Lambert production team, the BBC and the whole Race Across The World cast, we offer our deepest and heartfelt sympathies to Jo's son Charlie, and her wider family and friends.
"Jo became the matriarch of the Race Across The World cast family, she leaves a lasting legacy in the many lives that she touched, both through the series and beyond.
"It was a privilege to share her story and she will be deeply missed."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio Manchester on Sounds and follow BBC Manchester on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230.
summary: Jo Gardiner, a former contestant on the BBC show Race Across the World, has died at the age of 61 following a battle with cancer. Her death comes a year after her son and co-star, Sam, died in a car crash. Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, competed with Sam in the 2020 series of the show, which followed contestants racing across South America.
key_points: Former Race Across the World contestant Jo Gardiner has died at age 61 following a battle with cancer.
Her death occurs one year after the death of her son and co-star, Sam, who died in a car crash.
Jo and Sam appeared on the second series of the BBC show in 2020, traveling from Mexico City to Ushuaia in Argentina.
Show producers and family members paid tribute to her as the matriarch of the show's cast family and a person with an outrageous spirit.

title: Dan Stevens checks into the hospital from hell in this gold-star frightfest
author: Ed Power
content:
![Dan Stevens stars as a musician erroneously committed to a shady asylum](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498343864_17872264059530_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Dan Stevens stars as a musician erroneously committed to a shady asylum](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498343864_17872264059530_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Dan Stevens is a long way from the period splendour of Downton Abbey in The Terror: Devil In Silver (Sky Atlantic), the third instalment of an agreeably grisly ongoing horror anthology in which he plays a down-on-his-luck musician locked away in a haunted mental-health institution.
Horror is hard to do well on TV. With so many hours to fill, jump-scares only go so far and you can’t go all in on the gore the way an 18-rated movie might. But Devil In Silver is satisfyingly unsettling with grotesque imagery that burrows under the skin and an atmosphere of curdled dread that is gut-punchingly effective. Even more impressively, it lives up to its lofty billing as horror that doubles as a critique of healthcare in the United States.
The vibe is One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest meets the Resident Evil video games as Stevens’s character, Pepper, is arrested during a scuffle with the violent ex of his girlfriend (Juani Feliz) and banged up in a shady asylum in a forgotten corner of Queens, New York. As Pepper soon discovers, New Hyde is hell with straitjackets, where patients are guinea pigs who have a habit of dying in violent circumstances – and nobody asks any awkward questions.
![tmg.video.placeholder.alt 4pMW1Jw5wsY](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/4pMW1Jw5wsY/maxresdefault.jpg) 
There are big themes here about how institutions prioritise reputation and prestige over looking out for those in their care. Pepper has been confined on spurious grounds and left to rot – and the staff respond by following orders and ensuring their paperwork is filled out correctly. Devil in Silver – adapted from the novel by Victor LaValle – also explores the subject of unresolved trauma. A dark incident from years previously has left Pepper estranged from his son: the series argues that demons from our past can be just as terrifying as actual monsters.
But these subtexts never overwhelm the scares. And Devil in Silver is a genuinely scary example of the fashionable “analogue horror” craze that recently conquered the box office with the movie Backrooms. The idea behind that film is that nothing is as petrifying as an abandoned office with industrial carpets and flickering lights. That is precisely the ambience evoked by New Hyde, a purgatorial Neverland of locked doors, institutional metal-frame beds and endless grey corridors.
There’s a surprising amount of gore, too, as Pepper realises that his “temporary” stay has turned into an open-ended incarceration and left him at the mercy of Dr Anand (Aasif Mandvi), the sadistically indifferent hospital chief. Plied with drugs, he wakes to see a zombie-like figure dripping blood on him. This is followed by an equally chilling scene in which a cop trying to help Pepper is confronted by a ghost whose face seems to decompose in real time.
![Aasif Mandvi is suitably sinister as the hospital chief presiding over Pepper's nightmare](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/tv/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498343839_17872263726245_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Provocative, spooky and with Stevens mustering a decent New York accent, it ticks every box on the bingo-card for a top-tier chiller. Small-screen horror is often a letdown. But Devil in Silver is a gold-star frightfest where the real monster isn’t the zombie under the bed but the bureaucrat with a clipboard who doesn’t care if you live or die.
The Terror: Devil in Silver is available now on Sky/NOW and on Sky Atlantic at 9pm on Sunday 23 August
summary: Dan Stevens stars in The Terror: Devil In Silver as Pepper, a down-on-his-luck musician erroneously committed to a shady and terrifying mental-health institution in Queens, New York. Adapted from Victor LaValle's novel, the horror series combines unsettling imagery and genuine scares with a critique of the United States healthcare system and institutional bureaucracy. While enduring grotesque encounters with monsters and ghosts under the sadistic hospital chief Dr Anand, Pepper must also confront his own unresolved past trauma.
key_points: Dan Stevens plays Pepper, a musician erroneously locked away in the New Hyde mental-health institution after being arrested in a scuffle.
The series is the third instalment of the horror anthology The Terror, airing on Sky Atlantic and available on Sky/NOW.
The show doubles as a critique of United States healthcare and institutional prioritization of reputation over patient care.
The horror blends supernatural elements like zombies and ghosts with themes of unresolved trauma and oppressive bureaucracy.

title: ‘Ab-sol-utely incredible!’ The blockbuster ballet that says Pandora’s box unleashed AI
author: Lyndsey Winship
content:
Aszure Barton is taking herself back to the creation of Mere Mortals, remembering the creative buzz of the studio at San Francisco Ballet. “Sam was fiddling around making magic in one corner,” she says – that’s Sam Shepherd, AKA electronic musician Floating Points, who plays live in the show. Digital art duo Hamill Industries were there too, designing visuals for giant LED screens. “I was in a corner with the dancers,” says Barton. “Principals and apprentices, everyone working together. It was a really shared experience, which I loved.” In fact, it’s a “curiosity for real collaboration” that drives the Canadian-American choreographer. “If it was just about me,” she says, “the work wouldn’t be as powerful.”
Mere Mortals, which opened in San Francisco in 2024, is finally getting a European premiere, at this year’s Edinburgh international festival. While Barton’s memories of making the show are all about human connection, the subject matter is quite the opposite: artificial intelligence. It’s inspired by the myth of Pandora’s box, but instead of a box unleashing the evils and sorrows of humanity, it is reimagined as a cautionary tale about AI.
The idea came from SF Ballet’s artistic director Tamara Rojo, who took over the company in 2022 after 26 years in the UK, notably as a principal dancer at the Royal Ballet and artistic director of English National Ballet. “She was very hands-off in terms of the work itself,” says Barton, but Rojo assembled a crack international team for her ambitious commission which garnered some rave reviews for the intensity of its scale, score and visual impact.
![Wei Wang and San Francisco Ballet in Mere Mortals.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/be02d8c0c1bf7f2cdce5fb37d6848b4730360753/846_847_3124_2501/master/3124.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Barton had worked with Rojo before, when she choreographed Fantastic Beings for English National Ballet in 2016, a dance full of endlessly inventive, quirky movement. Beyond that, the 50-year-old isn’t well known on this side of the Atlantic (Rojo has called her “completely underrated”), although she’s been choreographing for more than two decades with major companies all over the world, as well as for her own, Aszure Barton & Artists. She was mentored by the great Mikhail Baryshnikov at his Baryshnikov Arts Center in New York. What did she learn from him? “On day one, he said, ‘Never ask me for money’ and ‘I like your willingness to work your ass off.’”
In the making of Mere Mortals, it turns out the richest conversations were not about the perils of AI, but the myth of Pandora, or “a myth that had been misconstrued”, says Barton. “A false story spread throughout history of this powerful being who didn’t have any agency and was toxic.”
There’ll always be different tellings of Greek myths, but Pandora does seem to have had a bad rap. She was the first woman, an Eve-like figure, created from clay and given by Zeus to Epimetheus, unbeknownst to him, as a punishment for his brother Prometheus giving humans fire. “One of the things I was really driven by was the fact that she was an agent of change,” says Barton.
As well as looking to a fictional figure from the past, however, Barton also used what was right in front of her in the present: the dancer in the lead role, Jennifer Stahl. “Ab-sol-utely incredible!” she says of Stahl, wide-eyed. “This stunning, powerful, amazing woman that I was getting to create with made my job very sweet.” Stahl, who has danced with SF Ballet for 20 years, will be returning to the Pandora role, having had a baby in between premieres.
![Aszure Barton.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/30352024a963c7fab600cdc33b4697043052ed8b/0_1514_5152_4122/master/5152.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the same way the inspiration for Pandora was right there in the studio, the show’s theme was all around her in San Francisco, the AI centre of the world. “You’re living the reality,” says Barton, “the systems and the chaos and the beauty, and I was really intuitively responding to that moment.” Barton uses lots of tech in her working life, not so much AI, more video, to endlessly document, analyse and deconstruct her way through the creative process. She calls choreography “the most magical Legoland for me”, but it always comes back to bodies. “I love dance because it’s so human and so beautiful. You can do some cool stuff with technology, but there’s nothing like sharing a space with a dancer.”
She’s not anti-AI. Some choreographers use AI as a tool to interrupt their creative habits and find new ideas. “That’s cool,” says Barton, although her own creativity is sparked by interacting with dancers. “You never have choreographer’s block if you’re open to what’s right there in front of you,” she says. “Dancers are heroes. They don’t get credited enough for their input.”
Barton hopes that all the fizzing creativity that went into making Mere Mortals is tangible to the audience. She wants them to be “showered with energy”. She can’t sit in her chair and watch it, she says. “I have to be in the back, bouncing up and down like I’m at a rave.” Between the dancers and the musicians (from the Royal Scottish National Orchestra) there are 87 performers in the show. “Masses of people sharing themselves, sharing this raw beauty,” says Barton. “It’s delicious.”
- 
  Mere Mortals is at Edinburgh Playhouse, 28-30 August and Sadler’s Wells, London, 9-12 September.
summary: The blockbuster ballet "Mere Mortals," choreographed by Aszure Barton, is preparing for its European premiere at the Edinburgh International Festival after opening in San Francisco in 2024. Commissioned by SF Ballet artistic director Tamara Rojo, the production uses the myth of Pandora's box as a cautionary tale about artificial intelligence. Despite its tech-focused subject matter, the creative process relied heavily on human collaboration, live music by Floating Points, digital visuals by Hamill Industries, and the performances of dancers like Jennifer Stahl.
key_points: "Mere Mortals" is a ballet inspired by the myth of Pandora's box, serving as a cautionary tale about artificial intelligence.
The production was commissioned by San Francisco Ballet artistic director Tamara Rojo and features choreography by Aszure Barton.
The creative team includes electronic musician Floating Points and digital art duo Hamill Industries.
Dancer Jennifer Stahl stars in the lead role of Pandora, returning to the production after having a baby.
The ballet is scheduled for its European premiere at the Edinburgh International Festival before performances in London.

title: Dr. Dre Embraces AI to Create Music, Criticizes Those Who Don’t
author: Travis Bland
content:
Dr. Dre is all in on using AI in creating music.
The hip-hop legend discussed his use of AI to make beats and his criticism of those who don’t embrace the technology in a New York Times interview published Sunday.
Dre likened the utilization of artificial intelligence in music production to past advances in technology that have become commonplace tools today. The rapper and producer told a reporter that he recently had a conversation with people, and “They were against A.I. and I’m like, ‘OK, you sound like the person that would have been against the drum machine when it came out.’ Or synthesizers, right? It’s a new tool for creativity. Some people are afraid of learning new things.”
Dre continued, “I’m embracing it. I can’t wait to see what’s going to happen with this.”
When asked if he was using AI while producing, Dre was forthcoming, saying he’s using it “as a tool to see what it would do with what I just did.”
AI isn’t a technology he sees as a threat, the Compton producer said. “I think the only people that see it as a threat are the people who have trouble creating,” he declared.
Dre’s longtime partner Jimmy Iovine, co-founder of Interscope Records, is also “very pro-A.I. in music creation,” according to the interview. “I don’t see the downside at all,” Iovine said. “There will be some crappy music. There’s crappy music now. In the studio, when gifted people have A.I., they’re going to make better records.”
The opinion of the Beats headphones masterminds is far from unanimous among musicians. Daft Punk’s Thomas Bangalter recently talked about his view that the use of AI to create music is a shortcut that stunts the creative process.
Other musicians and bands, like King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, are also dealing with AI clones of their music that add to the financial distress they face as well as the technology’s ability to create music with little effort that compete for streaming royalties.
summary: In a recent interview, hip-hop producer Dr. Dre expressed strong support for using artificial intelligence in music creation, comparing it to the historical introduction of drum machines and synthesizers. His longtime partner Jimmy Iovine also endorsed the technology, stating that gifted people will use it to make better records. However, other artists hold opposing views, with some arguing that AI stunts the creative process and others concerned about AI clones competing for streaming royalties.
key_points: Dr. Dre uses artificial intelligence to help create music and produces beats with it.
He compared AI adoption to the initial resistance faced by drum machines and synthesizers.
Jimmy Iovine supports AI in music creation, believing it helps talented artists make better records.
Daft Punk's Thomas Bangalter and other musicians view AI as a creative shortcut and a threat to streaming royalties.

title: ‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked away
author: Simon Hattenstone
content:
The electronic gates slide open to reveal a gorgeous Portuguese villa, a swimming pool and a beansprout of a man. “You’ve made me feel very important,” says Russ Abbot with a smile. “Come in!”
It’s more than 30 years since Abbot, aged 78, dominated Saturday night TV with his sketches, songs and impersonations. He appealed to all sorts. Kids, parents and grandparents united around the TV – first for Russ Abbot’s Madhouse, which ran from 1980 to 1985, then The Russ Abbot Show, from 1986 to 1991. He was joined by the inimitable Bella Emberg and a cast of young comics, including Les Dennis, Dustin Gee and Michael Barrymore. But make no mistake, it was Abbot’s show and the 80s was his decade. At his peak, he attracted 18 million viewers an episode.
When TV commissioners tired of his brand of sketch comedy, he did stints in the sitcoms Boomers and Last of the Summer Wine and played it straight in the moving TV drama September Song. There was a run of West End musical smashes – Fagin in Oliver!, Roger de Bris in The Producers, Alfred P Doolittle in My Fair Lady. Then, in 2016, he quietly retired. For the past seven years, he has split his time between Barbados and the Algarve, where I find him today.
![Abbot on an outdoor sofa with his arm around a smiling woman with a silvery bob and floral dress](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9f1479eaa8346527159bbc277d3bd71cd5661167/0_0_7373_4918/master/7373.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Abbot introduces me to his wife, Trish, who has a smart silver bob and a northern accent. How long have you two been married, I ask her. “Sixty years,” she says quietly. “Not even the Train Robbers got that!” Trish, 80, giggles.
We’re standing in a large, airy hall. On a table are figurines of Laurel and Hardy – Abbot’s heroes. Upstairs, I can make out lots of framed photos. He takes me on a tour. There are pics of him with the great entertainers of his era (Brucey, Elton, Tarby, Shaky) and the royals (Philip, Anne, Charles). We pass the silver discs from his brief period as Britain’s unlikeliest pop star (who can forget Atmosphere?). “That’s a certificate acknowledging the biggest box office in summer season history,” he says, like an accountant conducting an audit of his success. “And that’s whatshisname.” He squints at a picture. “Live Aid. Bob Geldof.”
Pride of place is a photo of him dressed as Cooperman, with Tommy Cooper. Cooperman was one of Abbot’s more surreal mashup characters – Superman meets the brilliantly bumbling comic giant, who died on stage in 1984. He adored Cooper. “It was so funny at the funeral. All the faces were there. Max Bygraves, Eric Sykes, me. And when the cortege came in, we’d forgotten he’d got a younger brother who looked just like him. He walked in and we’re like: ‘Oh God! Another Tommy prank.’ When the curtain closed on the coffin, I thought: he’s going to come out in a minute because he was such a practical joker.”
![Russ Abbot with three other men](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e1bc6154177983282ee8d86ec6ee797ea47a1313/0_0_2500_1724/master/2500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
He pauses. Now he sounds emotional. “After the funeral, we were walking out paying our respects to his wife, Gwen, and she said to me: ‘He thought you were the cat’s whiskers!’ I filled up. Amazing.”
More photos. Dennis and Gee, the double act who memorably impersonated Coronation Street’s Mavis Riley and Vera Duckworth on his show. Gee died in 1986, at 43. “So talented. Died too young.” We come to a picture of Abbot dressed as CU Jimmy, the incomprehensible, ranting Scottish stereotype that he’d struggle to get away with today. He says the character was based on his Scottish mother, whose accent got thicker the nearer the family got to Scotland for their holidays. He impersonates her – and she sounds as incoherent as Jimmy.
Abbot’s mother, Elizabeth, was in domestic service to the Duke of Westminster at Eaton Hall in Cheshire when she met his father, Don Roberts, a tanker driver for Pratt’s Oil who went on to become an area manager. Young Russell Roberts was a bright lad who went to Chester Grammar. But he became obsessed with drumming, flunked his O-levels and left school at 16 to join a band called the Black Abbots. He supplemented his income with a job as a stagehand at the Royalty theatre in Chester, where the band had a residency.
They soon became a comedy band, with Abbot dismounting the drums to tell daft jokes. The band won the talent show Opportunity Knocks six weeks in a row, became huge in the working men’s clubs, but never had a hit record. By 1973, Abbot was appearing on the TV standup comedy show The Comedians and his manager, Mike Hughes, didn’t think Russell Roberts had a ring to it. He suggested he become Russ Abbot. “He said: ‘Think about it, if your bill is in alphabetical order, you’ll always be top of the bill.’ He said: ‘Abba could top you, but that’s about it.’ That’s clever, isn’t it?”
![A young Abbot dressed as a boy scout](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1b03f601c23db06876a706d790509d679f4f6a74/0_0_5769_3763/master/5769.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
By the late 1970s, Abbot was well known as a comic and starred in the original Madhouse series with the more famous Freddie Starr. After 17 years as a Black Abbot, he left to go solo. Within months, Russ Abbot’s Madhouse started on ITV (The Russ Abbot Show would move during its run to the BBC) and he was a Saturday night fixture.
We join Trish outside in the shade. She’s made us coffee and piled a plate with digestive biscuits. Did life change when he became a household name? “No.” He looks at her for confirmation. “Just in the sense we moved up the ladder homewise, didn’t we, Trish? So we started in the caravan. Trish’s dad had a win on the pools that paid for the caravan as a wedding present. Then my dad got us a place with £1-a-week rent. Two up, two down. Then we got a £10,000 bungalow and sold it for twice the price.”
“Yep,” says Trish.
‘Then we moved down south, we moved to Wentworth. We looked at this nice house …”
“And that was it, yes,” says Trish.
“We bought it, cash.”
Were loads of women interested in you? “Not really, no,” he says. There’s a glint in his eye. “Oh, I suppose in my drumming days. Early.” The glint vanishes. “Actually, it was more the singers. Because I was just the drummer in the back.” He tells me how he met Trish. “She came to the stage door of the British Legion in Ellesmere Port as I was packing my drums up. We had a bass player in those days called Paul Dodd. He ended up a policeman. Trish says: ‘Is the bass player around?’ I said: ‘No, he’s gone, love.’ She said: ‘Oh, that’s a shame, I wanted to say hello to him.’”
Did you fancy the bass player, I ask Trish.
“Yeah.”
So you got the wrong bloke?
“Yeah, I got him instead.”
“I said: come on, I’ll buy you a drink. Then I said: let me give you a lift home. She said: I only live across the road. I said: you can’t walk alone at this time of night. So I left with a kiss and a cuddle. And it all started from there, didn’t it, Trish?”
Did she find him funny? “Oh no. Very normal. Lovely brothers, lovely mum and dad. Just normal, like the boy next door.” Did she like comedy? “Oh God, no!” Actually, she says, there was one occasion when he really made her laugh. “He opened the garden fete and chopped his nose off instead of cutting the ribbon.”
Genuinely?
“Yes, he was rushed to hospital. That’s what made me laugh.”
“I had stitches all round my nose.”
Trish is in stitches at the memory.
“But that wasn’t intentionally funny,” Abbot protests.
“No,” says Trish, still hooting. “But it was very funny, Russell. And we’ve laughed ever since.”
He must have been stopped a lot over the years by fans. “No, not really,” he says. “It was always a nod and a wink and a smile. There’s one funny story. We went to the opening show of Miss Saigon.” Trish is already giggling. “We go into the VIP area. We sit there and Trish nudges me. All these heads are turning. And I say: ‘It’s all right! The lights will go down in a minute.’ I say: ‘Trish, it’s a compliment.’ And she nudges me again and says: ‘Look who’s sitting next to me!’ And it was Burt Lancaster. She fell about. Lovely story.”
![Bella Emberg dressed like Wonder Woman and Russ Abbot dressed like Superman with a ‘C’ on his costume.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/75f54be55153aeefd60a63bdcebc25e786d8dbab/86_0_2906_1991/master/2906.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Abbot never considered himself a star. “I always think I’m playing that role of Russ Abbot. I go in the stage door as Russ Abbot and come out as Russell Roberts.” And he was too reserved to play the big I am. “I never used to like chatshows, because I was shy and I found them embarrassing. It’s like, now I’m retired, I’m not so shy and I can talk about it because it’s past.”
Trish has always been his biggest fan, he says. Then he corrects himself. “Trish and my mum. She used to do handouts for the WI. I’d sign the autograph and she’d sign the back: ‘Russ’s mum!’ She loved it!” In her 70s, his mother got dementia. She went into a home, but Abbot didn’t realise how bad it had got until he arranged for her to come to a show. “Trish brought her up to the dressing room and Mum walked in and said: ‘What a pleasure to meet you. Thank you so much, I’ve been so entertained. It was absolutely marvellous, and now to meet you in person.’
“I stood there and said: ‘Mum, it’s me,’ and she said: ‘I’ll have to go now, my family’s waiting for me.’ So Trish took her back. I slammed the dressing room door three times. It was terrible. It’s a terrible illness. She died about a year later. She was still a very elegant lady, very smartly dressed. She didn’t act like she had dementia. She just couldn’t remember who I was.”
Abbot worked incredibly hard in his heyday. “In 1984, I worked 363 days.” Meanwhile, Trish was working incredibly hard, too, bringing up their four children. “Trish raised them all. I was always away, summer season tour or pantomime. Pantomimes, gosh! You’d get home Christmas Eve, put the presents under the tree, go to bed, have breakfast, watch the kids open the toys and then go back to do a matinee.”
![Les Dennis dressed in vintage aristocratic clothing with Russ Abbot dressed as a butler](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/76aebb05c1b1039d4bd8f61535200321dd3e418a/0_0_3072_2048/master/3072.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
But, he says, they were great times. He tells me of all the wonderful people he worked with. It sounds like an Oscar acceptance speech. Barry Cryer wrote much of his material, but there was a whole team involved and there is not an actor, producer, writer or manager he misses out.
He was the ideas man, he says, rather than the wordsmith. “I loved it. All the nonsense.” He talks about the silly names they invented for characters. “My favourite was Miss Funnyfanny intead of Miss Moneypenny. I think that was my cousin Russell. I loved Basildon Bond because of the silliness of it.”
Suddenly he’s quoting a 40-year-old monologue from a sketch featuring his James Bond parody. ‘My name’s Bond. Basildon Bond, licence to kill and drive a heavy-goods vehicle. I’d been away on holiday when I was summonsed back to headquarters to see my boss P … ‘Was it a good holiday Bond?’ I said: ‘Yes, thank you, sir, I went away for a bit of peace and quiet. I found a nice little piece. I just hope she keeps quiet.’ He said: ‘Don’t bother me with a silly little thing like that.’ I said: ‘It’s funny, that’s what she said.’”
He quotes the monologue word-perfect, in all its anachronistic glory. For all the inappropriateness, there’s also an innocence to it, as there is to him. I notice he doesn’t swear and I ask if he’s religious. “Oh, I believe in God. I say my prayers every night.”
Abbot fell out of fashion in the 1990s, as did virtually all the standup rooted in working men’s clubs and seaside summer seasons. Did he mind when his TV show got cancelled? “I wasn’t distressed or angry or anything. It came about when the head of entertainment gave an interview and said: ‘The BBC’s going to change. No more of this, no more of that,’ and somebody said: ‘Does that mean Russ Abbot?’ and he said yes, meaning the sketch shows. So then it became ‘BBC sacks Russ Abbot’, but that didn’t bother me. I thought: well, I’ve had a very good run. Also, I’d just cracked the West End, so I was doing everything I wanted to do without the stress of the TV shows.”
Why did he fall out of fashion? “It was when the new wave came in. Alternative comedy. I thought, alternative comedy? What’s it alternative to? If the thing’s funny, it’s funny. Political correctness came in, and you can’t laugh at each other and you can’t laugh at yourself. At the same time, a lot of comedy started going blue and I thought: I’m not going down that road.”
![Russ in a white t-shirt with his hand under his chin looking at the camera](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/48647af1a5d7bb6531ec66319bfcf73e98360792/578_0_6148_4918/master/6148.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
So much of his show’s humour was rooted in stereotyping and many of the jokes were at the expense of his great friend Emberg’s weight. Did he understand why that was no longer acceptable? “Yes. Some of the scripts I used to look at myself and wonder. I’d say: ‘Bella, have you read the script?’ and she’d say: ‘Yeah, I think it’s funny’. I’d say: ‘Are you sure?’ and she’d say: ‘Yeah, why?’ ‘I’m just asking your opinion,’ and she’d say: ‘I think it’s hilarious,’ and I’d say: ‘So do I!’” Did she ever get upset? “No, she never got upset once.” Emberg died in 2018 at 80. Of all the people he’s worked with, he says he misses her most.
I loved it when Emberg as Blunderwoman lifted Abbot over her shoulders and carried him off. Even at his heaviest, he weighed only 12 and a half stone. Not much for a man over six foot tall. These days, Emberg would have had even less trouble. He’s lost two and a half stone. He knows Trish is worried, but he’s had every test going and nothing has been diagnosed. As for Trish, he says, she’s had two strokes in the past year, so they are taking it easy. Which doesn’t mean they’re not up to a round of golf. Abbot is a fine player and used to play off a handicap of 12, but he insists Trish is better than him. To be fair, so does she.
Stories circulated that Abbot retired because he was embittered that comedy had changed and no straight roles were being offered to him. It’s true that he’s not a great fan of today’s comedy, he says, and he was disappointed when Boomers and Last of the Summer Wine were cancelled, but he insists the stories are nonsense. He actually retired because Hughes, his manager, was retiring and he thought it was a good time to call it quits and spend more time with Trish and have a social life.
“I’ve seen something on YouTube saying ‘The tragedy of Russ Abbot’ and ‘He’s run away to Portugal’.” He smiles.
“We just watched it once,” says Trish. “I said, don’t watch it, Russell.”
It doesn’t look much of a tragedy to me, I say, glancing out at the cloudless sky, swimming pool and topiaried bushes.
“Thank you,” Trish says.
“I’ve had a wonderful career,” Abbot says. “Wonderful!”
“He’s always said that,” Trish says.
And now you’re enjoying a richly deserved retirement? “Absolutely,” he says.
How would Trish feel if he decided to go back to work? Her eyes light up. “Happy,” she says. Why? “I’d like him to do something like Last of the Summer Wine. I think he does miss it, I’ve got to say.”
Abbot gives her a look. “Yeah!” he says. “But not desperately, Trish.”
summary: Russ Abbot dominated British Saturday night television in the 1980s with popular sketch shows like Russ Abbot's Madhouse and The Russ Abbot Show, drawing up to 18 million viewers at his peak. After his sketch comedy era faded, he transitioned into sitcoms, dramas, and West End musicals before quietly retiring in 2016. Today, he lives a relaxed retirement in Portugal and Barbados with his wife of 60 years, Trish.
key_points: Russ Abbot was a dominant TV star in the 1980s, known for sketch comedy, music, and impersonations.
He retired in 2016 after a varied career that included television, sitcoms, dramas, and West End stage roles.
He has been married to his wife, Trish, for 60 years, whom he originally met while playing drums in a band.
At the height of his television success in 1984, Abbot famously worked 363 days of the year.

title: ‘I didn’t miss a thing’: How Nick Haymes photographed his sons’ entire lives from verrucas to homemade hamster coffin
author: Tim Jonze
content:
Not many family photo albums open with images of the twin towers on fire. But for Nick Haymes, it made perfect sense. “When 9/11 happened,” he says, “I realised life was very short.” At the time, he was living in New York, trying to forge a career, while his friend, colleague and future wife Lina was dealing with the fallout of her previous marriage. “It made us realise we should probably get together and have a family. It was this huge historical event, but on a very micro level, it also shaped my relationship with my wife and children.”
Chronograph is a photography book that runs from those terrorist attacks to the present day, tracing the journey of Haymes’s two sons, Philipp and Lawrence, as they grow from drooling babies into young men. We are given a ringside seat as arms get broken, beloved pets die and hairs start sprouting from armpits. The mundane side of life – verrucas, messy kitchens, Lina cleaning out an ear with a cotton bud – is captured in the same way as birthday parties and rites of passage.
“Because we lived in this tiny, 800 sq ft apartment in Manhattan, you don’t miss a thing, all the ups and downs, all the mood swings,” says Haymes. “There was no door slamming, because there was nowhere to go!”
![Two boys seated a a table look on as a pile of wooden blocks collapses](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a353b2d99220f081bc1496eefc3ca354c5b83ecb/0_0_3543_2305/master/3543.png?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Indeed, we are not spared from seeing the children at their least flattering: “We used to have a running joke where Lawrence would say: ‘You’re the only parent that would photograph me when I’m crying rather than deal with the issue straight away,’” admits Haymes, “but I like to think I was attentive. It was a funny balance because the camera was always around, but it seemed to work.”
There are also multiple shots of the boys naked – not just running around the house as young children but as they transition into adulthood too. I suspect most teenagers would not be cool with this, but Haymes insists he had their approval. “They don’t have an issue,” he says. “I’ve been lucky enough to have some very nice photographers in my household at various times, so they’re aware of the creative process.” He shrugs: “There are bigger themes in the book than child nudity. That was just a part of our daily life.”
Besides, when Philipp and Lawrence reach their teens – all bleached hair, tattoos and stubble – they work out an ingenious method of rebellion. Instead of sulking or turning away from the camera, Haymes says his kids smiled and put their thumbs up, knowing that the last thing their dad wanted was a posed family portrait. “That was basically their way of telling me to clear out of their lives,” he says.
![Lawrence in the shower stares at the camera as his bleeds](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d1bd1635b6ebf778024dc24f980dad8e1a090a18/0_0_3543_5344/master/3543.png?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Born in Stratford-upon-Avon, Haymes hoped to study art but ended up dropping out. “I took way too many drugs in my 20s and had a bit of a breakdown,” he says. After couch-surfing in London for a bit, he found work in a photo studio, eventually assisting Jürgen Teller. In 1999, he packed two cameras into a bag and decided to try his luck in New York. It was here he met Lina, a Jewish refugee who, as a teenager, had moved to the US with her parents from Ukraine – then part of the Soviet Union. She was working on a magazine and gave him a commission that allowed him to get a visa and stay.
Haymes’s own difficult transition from youth to adulthood is perhaps what draws him to his subjects. Between Dog and Wolf captured his road trips across California and Oklahoma with a group of young skateboarders. Follow-up Gabe TM unfurled over many years hanging out with Gabe Nevins, the teenage star of Gus Van Sant’s Paranoid Park. Unexpectedly, Haymes found himself chronicling Nevins’s homelessness and addiction in the wake of making the movie. Dancing on the Fault Line, published in 2024, was another mammoth excursion, following teenager Love Bailey and her extended queer family right up to her decision to transition in her 30s.
Haymes is still in touch with his previous subjects: he shot Bailey’s wedding; Gabe is living a “normal life” now in Oregon; the skaters have children of their own. Haymes doesn’t intend to foster such deep relationships with his subjects. “I always think, ‘Oh, I’ll just do a nice quick shoot.’ But then I get attached to everybody, they become part of my life. You can become a father figure to them, or a therapist maybe. That’s part of it, and that’s part of the educational process for me, just to be with people and understand them.”
![Two boys on a sofa with 3D glasses](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/25f60d4e6fbaed1b601daa71a798ed8cd7653bbe/0_0_3543_2672/master/3543.png?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It was during Covid that Haymes found the time to go through all his family negatives and work out what to do with them. “It moved me pretty heavily,” he says. “I also had to try to be as impartial as I could because I didn’t want it to be saccharine.”
Did he know, as he took them, that the photos of his children would end up in a published book? “I suppose, as a photographer, yes. But I really did it for personal memory, and as a little self-analysis. To think about how I was as a parent. Also, I shoot on film and at the time, in the early 2000s, digital photography had kicked in so I was finding myself more and more unemployable. I thought, ‘OK, I am becoming a house husband.’ But I wanted to be a photographer still, so the family life around me is what I photographed.”
Besides Lina and the boys, the other key figures in the book are Lina’s parents Nadia and Mikhail. “They were big characters,” says Haymes. “I had to learn how to become a little more emotional and a little more warm and compassionate.”
One striking image is of Mikhail sitting with wrapping paper on his head. He’s in a full tracksuit, giving off a slightly intimidating Paulie Walnuts vibe. “He was a very loving person,” says Haymes, “but yeah, maybe a bit of a rogue. Whereas my mother-in-law had her issues and I think maybe undiagnosed bipolar disorder. She also became a victim of prescription medication in the US, and we had to deal with that. She was certainly a tough mother-in-law, but at some point you fall in love with her anyway.”
There are some portentous images in the book. Scars on Mikhail’s stomach mirror Lina’s caesarean scars, although we can only guess why he’s been cut open. Then there is the pet hamster, who we see being held, adored and then grieved for as it rests in its cardboard coffin.
![The boys grown up on a beach](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5f7fa59134882d9d3a0c1fbf74a3d81e99fd9f90/0_0_3543_2641/master/3543.png?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The book’s closing passages are extremely moving, as we see Nadia and Mikhail in hospital together, their conditions slowly deteriorating. “We were bringing two people to dialysis every day, which was two pretty gruelling years.” At some point, Haymes converted the home art gallery into a hospice.
In the book, it appears as if the couple died at the same time. In reality it was a year apart and the couple had gone through a divorce by that point. “There are things that don’t need to be known,” says Haymes of the story his book tells. “Everybody has a family album, and through those you only remember certain parts.”
Despite their divorce, Nadia and Mikhail were buried together in Los Angeles. “I’m not sure if Lina’s father is enjoying that right now, but that’s what happened,” says Haymes with a smile.
He says he had been asked to make a photography book of his family for 15 years but it was only when the grandparents died that he realised the project was complete. “The book starts with death and ends with death,” he says. “It’s gone full circle.”
Interspersed with beautiful, closeup images of flowers received at the funeral, we see Philipp and Lawrence standing by the graveside with the urn. “For them to be able to communicate those emotions and to speak at a service, for me that felt like, ‘OK, they’re on their own now. They’ve become men.’”
He pauses, then laughs like only a father can. “Having said that,” he adds, “they’re still on my Uber account.”
summary: Photographer Nick Haymes has compiled a book titled Chronograph that documents the lives of his two sons, Philipp and Lawrence, from the events of 9/11 to the present. The book captures the mundane aspects of daily family life alongside major milestones, growing up in a small Manhattan apartment, and the eventual decline and death of his wife's parents. Haymes began the project for personal memory and self-analysis while functioning as a house husband, ultimately realizing the book was complete when the grandparents passed away.
key_points: The photography book Chronograph spans from the 9/11 terrorist attacks to the present day, chronicling the upbringing of Haymes's two sons.
Haymes captured both mundane moments like verrucas and messy kitchens as well as significant rites of passage and family tragedies.
As teenagers, the sons playfully rebelled against the constant photography by smiling and giving thumbs-up to avoid posed portraits.
The book concludes with the deteriorating health, time in a home hospice, and passing of Lina's parents, Nadia and Mikhail.

title: Hayden Panettiere’s mom lashes out at Gayle King over ‘shameful’ attacks on her
author: Tom Murray
content:
Hayden Panettiere’s estranged mother, Lesley Vogel, has hit back at Gayle King after the CBS Mornings host criticized her response to her daughter’s death.
The Heroes star died August 16 after being found in cardiac arrest at a Greenville, South Carolina, apartment. She was 36.
“I was very, very hurt and deeply disappointed in the lack of professionalism, the lack of compassion in slamming someone who’s lost two children, without even a modicum of consideration,” Vogel told the Daily Mail about King’s criticism of her.
“No one reached out to me before,” she added. “It’s shameful. It’s unconscionable to me.”
The Independent has contacted King’s representatives for comment.
![Hayden Panettiere’s mother, Lesley Vogel (center), hit back at Gayle King (right) after the TV host criticized her reaction to Panettiere’s death](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/23/15/14/Hayden-Panettiere-with-her-mom-Lesley-Vogel-and-Gayle-King.jpeg)
After Panettiere’s death, Vogel told NBC News: “I think Hayden was an amazingly talented person in so many departments and I think young people who grow up in the entertainment industry — it is a struggle and it's a very challenging industry and it’s not unusual for them to sadly find the wrong path.
“I think it becomes very difficult to be true to yourself, and I think Hayden sadly lost her way, and I wish it were different,” Vogel continued. “I wish she had stayed true to herself because she had many incredible attributes.”
She concluded: “I just feel that she’s with her brother and they’re at peace.” Panettiere’s younger brother Jansen died from an enlarged heart in 2023 at the age of 28.
On CBS Mornings, King lashed out at Vogel’s statement.
“You know, guys, you read this and all I can think is, ‘Thanks, Mom, for nothing,’” she said during the broadcast.
“It makes me so sad of the opportunity that you have after your daughter’s death that that’s what you choose to leave us with,” King said.
