"It feels like a huge honour," says Lynsey Rendall, who plays Francis's screen wife Maeve.
"The Wicker Man is such a famous film and has such an impact on popular culture so it was amazing to be part of that world."
John Haswell has worked in theatre for a number of years but says his role as the Rev Knox was a highlight of his career.
"He's a sleazy man of the cloth and I had an absolute ball working on it," he says.
"It was an intense six weeks, filming in Voe virtually every day. It wasn't glamorous but that's part of the fun."
Martha Robertson is 17-years-old and was sitting her Highers during filming.
She says the experience helped her launch a career in acting.
"There was one scene we filmed which was meant to be in the pouring rain on a dark gloomy day but it fell on what seemed to be the sunniest day of the year," she says.
"They had to black out all the windows and two crew members were on a wall with a hose and a leaf blower so we could get wind and rain.
"Which seemed really crazy because it rains every day on Shetland, but not the day we needed it to."
![Three people in warm woollies in front of a bay with a viking style longboat in it.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/4d54/live/81154140-9e42-11f1-bb45-576721ee33bb.jpg)
Lynsey Rendall, John Haswell and Martha Robertson are among the locals who joined the cast of Wrath of The Gods
![Justin Hardy, in a pink open-necked shirt, sits at a desk in front of a window. He is smiling over his shoulder and sitting in a director's chair with his name on it.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/466/cpsprodpb/1879/live/3383a1c0-9e46-11f1-bb45-576721ee33bb.jpg)
Director Justin Hardy died just before the film's premiere
Many of the Shetland cast and crew plan to attend the premiere of Wrath of the Gods at the horror festival FrightFest in London on Friday.
But their celebrations have been overshadowed by the sudden death of Justin Hardy last month at the age of 61.
"We all were â still are â looking forward to seeing the finished film," says John.
"But now it's not just a celebration of the film, it's a celebration of Justin and his life. It will be wonderful and sad. A complex mixture of emotions."
For Lynsey, the film is a testament to the late director.
"It was such a massive risk," she says.
"So to get to the end of that process, when it's going to be on a screen, feels a bit miraculous really and it's so vexing that Justin isn't going to be there to see what he so passionately wanted to achieve."
For the Hardy family, it has become a strange tribute to three of their number.
Wrath of The Gods completes Robin Hardy's Wicker trilogy and is dedicated to Justin's mother Caroline, who was a secret uncredited executive producer on the original 1973 film.
She died in 1984, aged 51, without knowing that the film she'd backed would go on to be so loved and admired.
"It will be poignant beyond imagining. A sad but celebratory moment," says Dominic.
"I know that he [Justin] was extremely proud of it being taken by FrightFest.
"Justin's efforts have brought us all together as a family and helped us harness all our energy."
summary: Director Robin Hardy's sons, Justin and Dominic, completed their late father's planned folk horror trilogy after a surprise family archive discovery yielded a script for the final film, Wrath of the Gods. The project draws on Viking and Shetland mythology and recently premiered at London's FrightFest horror festival. However, celebrations were marred by the sudden death of Justin Hardy at age 61 just before the premiere.
key_points: Robin Hardy always intended his 1973 classic The Wicker Man to be the first part of a trilogy.
A long-lost family archive found in an attic included papers, storyboards, and a script for the final film, Wrath of the Gods.
Filming for Wrath of the Gods took place in Shetland using a mix of professional and local actors.
Director Justin Hardy passed away suddenly at the age of 61 just before the film's premiere.

title: The Sussexes’ selfish return spells peril for the Royal family
author: Allison Pearson
content:
![Royal Family](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499017406_17873034341080_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqaRL1kC4G7DT9ZsZm6Pe3Pf4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Royal Family](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499017406_17873034341080_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqaRL1kC4G7DT9ZsZm6Pe3Pf4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
“Please, boys. Don’t make my final years a misery.” The words of the future King Charles III as he pleaded with his two sons to patch things up at their grandfather’s funeral in April 2021 have just acquired a whole new resonance.
The “boys”, better known as Prince William and Prince Harry, never did make up. Indeed, their feud only darkened and deepened as the elder brother fumed at the younger’s treachery towards the Royal family in general, and his wife, in particular. (Outrageously, in her interview with Oprah, Meghan accused unnamed members of the family of racism in relation to her unborn baby’s skin colour.)
The last time Harry and William stood together, just the two of them, was in July 2021 at the unveiling of a bronze statue of their late mother on what would have been her 60th birthday. The pair could barely look at each other. For William, Harry’s deeply personal and spiteful revelations two years later in his biography, Spare, were an unimaginable betrayal by the human being he once trusted best.
![The Duke of Sussex and Prince William](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000307389582_17873063187100_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
A lid could be kept on that seething Shakespearean sibling rivalry, as long as Diana’s beloved boys, now men in their 40s, were separated by an ocean. Harry and Meghan found freedom in California from the stultifying Windsor ways they so publicly scorned. The Waleses were left to steady the ship after the turbulence of “Megxit”. They did so admirably and to universal acclaim despite Princess Catherine’s shocking brush with cancer.
The sudden announcement on Wednesday night that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are returning to the UK later this month – a typical piece of Sussex melodrama, both blithely selfish and utterly ruthless – threatens the uneasy truce between the brothers. It also heralds a moment of intense danger for the monarchy, I think, because almost anything could happen – and very little of it good.
The King has shown immense fortitude during his cancer treatment, and continues to carry out his duties with charm and aplomb, but the 77-year-old Charles is ailing. Understandably, there is speculation that Harry has seized this moment to shore up his family’s position while a fond Papa is still on the throne and able to bail him out.
With a commitment to a slimmed-down monarchy – probably comprised of his own three children, George, Charlotte and Louis, and their immediate heirs – things would look very different under a future King William V. The Duke and Duchess, and Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet (the children’s faces unknown to the British public even though they are sixth and seventh in line to our throne) might well lose their titles and their access to the only thing that they have left to sell, apart from tens of thousands of jars of Meghan’s jam. A sticky position, you have to agree.
Cynics point out that Harry’s newfound enthusiasm for Britain follows a humiliating failure in the US. After the Duchess’s teeth-rottingly glutinous lifestyle show, With Love, Meghan, was panned, Netflix drastically watered down the couple’s lavish deal. When they were dropped by Spotify, allegedly for not creating enough content to earn out their $20m (£14.7m) payment, a furious senior executive called the royal couple “f---ing grifters”.
Americans love success and stampede like startled bison from its opposite. People began to mock Harry and Meghan’s claim to want a low-profile, secluded private life dedicated to “service”. South Park’s “Worldwide Privacy Tour” episode, a hilarious satire on the shy, retiring Sussexes, burst the dam of deference. They became social poison and couldn’t blag an invitation to the Oscars. Even Oprah appeared to distance herself from the pair on whom she lavished such sympathy when they were revealing how ghastly those heartless Royals were while poor Prince Philip was on his deathbed.
![South Park](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000325731778_17873033431320_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The truth is, however cynical you are about Meghan and Harry, it’s not cynical enough. Their jaw-dropping hypocrisy is only exceeded by their lack of self-awareness and contrition. A champion reciter of his own grievances, Harry can be astonishingly obtuse when it comes to appreciating the pain and embarrassment he has caused his own relatives. For Team Sussex, it’s “my truth” that counts.
Only last year, a tearful Harry was telling the BBC: “It’s impossible for me to take my family back to the UK safely. I can’t see a world in which I would be bringing my wife and children back to the UK at this point.”
So what changed? Is the UK no longer so racist that Meghan couldn’t bear to live here? Is she no longer worried about being “silenced” by her terrible in-laws? Has Queen Camilla ceased to be “dangerous”, as Harry claimed in his book? Is their personal safety no longer a priority? Did they get the apology from the royals they loftily demanded as a condition of returning?
Well, they’re coming back anyway. And we don’t want them – we really don’t want them. Thousands of caustic jibes and angry outbursts mushroomed overnight on social media.
“What have we done to deserve this?” wondered one man.
“Maybe they got an offer to appear on Celebrity Traitors,” quipped another.
“Sickening. It’s obvious that this move, like everything else, is purely about what’s in it for them.”
“There must be a problem with Harry’s US visa – who in their right minds would go back to a country they trashed and where they are hated?”
“Never-ending attention seekers, they just want to cause more aggravation for William and Kate.”
“On the lookout for more material for their Diana documentary and next books no doubt.”
“They are coming back to monetise the kids!”
“With luck it will speed up the divorce.”
“The fact they even contemplate coming back shows they haven’t got a shred of contrition or shame. They will forever be a thorn in the side of the Royal family. And us too because we will never be able to escape hearing about them. They don’t want a quiet life.”
“Skint and hoping daddy will bail them out.”
“The whole thing is grotesque because of their disdain for our country and the way they treated the Queen.”
![The Duke and Duchess of Sussex with Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000453992647_17873038905910_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqOnn7q0yBmQvUBscbvRKZNc9luWBnPl6Sn_iGFrIRcxE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The outpouring of hostility and bitterness is overwhelming, with the odd enthusiastic comment heavily outnumbered. (Judging by the remarks, Meghan will be lucky not to be booed should she ever venture into Waitrose.) Has any couple ever burnt through so much goodwill so quickly?
How different it was back in May 2018 when I wrote for The Telegraph about Harry and Meghan’s fairytale wedding in St George’s Chapel at Windsor Castle. It was a glorious day, the Union flag waved and the people cheered for their favourite young royal. Everyone was so happy that Diana’s lost boy – that shell-shocked 12-year-old we had watched as he walked, ghost-pale, beside his mother’s coffin – had finally found a bright and beautiful woman to love him.
Admittedly, alarm bells rang when Meghan commandeered the engagement interview, promising to “hit the ground running”, more like a pushy contestant on The Apprentice than a doting fiancée, but doubts were vanquished by a beautiful ceremony that combined the best of British and American. In his Blues & Royals uniform, Harry looked like the foxiest Salvation Army sergeant ever, but was pensive and nervous.
Seated beside him, William did his best to reassure his brother. We know now that William had grave doubts about the choice of bride and the speed of the courtship, but a besotted Harry wasn’t in the mood for listening or caution. As the bride stared up at her husband with a look of glistening adoration (that look seemed sweet and genuine back then, but fake and irritating now), the late Queen shot Meghan an owlish glare (she disapproved of the American divorcee wearing virginal white). In retrospect, she seems to have been the only one with a clear-eyed view of what was coming.
![Harry and Meghan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000252520041_17873037630500_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Pretty much the entire country fell for the Sussexes that day. It took some serious effort on their part to make us fall out of love with them – they found fault with their handsome historic cottage, renovated to US standards at absurd expense, complained constantly about the (overwhelmingly positive) media coverage and “racism”, and then there were allegations that a high-maintenance Meghan bullied Palace staff.
An absurdly swollen sense of entitlement led to demands that the couple be allowed to set up as Sussex royals in America, enjoying the perks of proximity to the throne without the dreary responsibilities. The late Queen wisely refused – she didn’t want them destroying trust in the Royal family by combining duty and money-making – and so “Megxit” became permanent in 2021.
Harry was stripped of his military titles and royal patronages – things that had given his life ballast and meaning. Widely adored because he was always good for a laugh, Harry became a scowling social justice warrior parroting modish phrases about “unconscious bias” you knew Meghan had taught him.
And then, the coup de grace. The Sussexes both slagged off the Royal family on American television in front of hundreds of millions – all that after they had caused the late Queen so much worry and distress in her final years. To the British people, who had forked out £32m for their wedding, it felt like the vilest ingratitude.
So, it is to that sulphurous national mood that the Sussexes now return. Meghan narrowly avoids being the least popular Royal because the former Prince Andrew is even more detested than the Duchess. Some 65 per cent of Britons hold an unfavourable opinion of Meghan (22 per cent favourable), while 58 per cent dislike Harry (33 per cent positive).
The Duke and Duchess’s status as “not working royals” will be unchanged, we are told, but who seriously believes that Meghan, the self-styled global humanitarian, will be content hanging out with some chickens in the Cotswolds where the family are likely to settle? She may be able to score the odd chai latte with her near-neighbour, Victoria Beckham, although Jeremy Clarkson definitely won’t be inviting the Sussexes over to Diddly Squat Farm for a hog roast. Meghan would have Clarkson cancelled like a shot.
I think it’s likely that, apart from the Spencer side of the family, as well as Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie, Meghan will find herself ostracised, lonely and increasingly frustrated. She never liked Britain, and is clearly jealous of the huge affection here for Kate. Frequent trips back to the US, with or without the children, could put physical distance between her and Harry, and kickstart the process of separation that many have foretold.
On Friday, we learnt that Meghan may have an acting job lined up in the UK. I wasn’t aware the Royal Shakespeare Company was looking for a Lady Macbeth.
Wherever they settle, Harry and Meghan will be a constant distraction from the activities of the working royals – see how their breaking news displaced the lovely story of Camilla talking about her husband’s cancer. There will effectively be two rival courts led by the warring brothers. What happens when Prince George starts at Eton in a few weeks’ time, and photographers are summoned to take the traditional picture? Will the Sussexes drop Archie and Lilibet off quietly at their new school with no snapper present, or will this be an opportunity to get one over on their rivals, the Waleses? The first picture of the faces of the Sussex children would beat George to every front page. Imagine how that would make William and Kate feel. Now imagine what whoop of satisfaction that would give Meghan.
![The Duchess of Sussex and Queen Camilla in 2022](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000332079473_17873035482790_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpnI8Rj06GSL2LQ_GblAqJmxvjMbu5CgRfn_iW6oZ5QA.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
How long do you think it will be before the Sussexes make it known that they think it’s terribly sad that Archie and Lilibet are prevented from seeing their cousins by the cruel, stand-offish William and Kate? Using their children as pawns may not be beyond them.
“It’s horrible,” says Harry’s biographer, Angela Levin. “Kate is gentle, she’s not like Meghan, and Meghan is not going to change one iota. She thinks she knows everything – she always has to win.” Levin worries about the effect the stress could have on Kate’s health.
Senior members of the Royal family are currently enjoying their traditional summer break at Balmoral. I am told the news that Harry and Meghan returning to the UK went down like a sporran full of cold haggis. One senior Royal insider goes so far as to call it “an act of violent aggression. I feel desperately sorry for William and Kate. It’s awful for them”.
The King is a very kind man, and it’s understandable that he wishes to spend more time with Harry and his children, but I’m not sure Charles has thought through what this means for his heir and his family. Are William and Kate to be pressured into forgiving a pair who caused them so much pain and turmoil? Remember how William angrily snapped at a reporter after that infamous Oprah interview: “We are very much NOT a racist family.”
The Waleses are said by a source to “have no interest in engaging with anything Harry and Meghan do or say”. Easier said than done when “Me Again Meghan” has a track record of trying to upstage the couple’s scheduled events with her own appearances.
William and Kate, who have done so much to uphold the family’s reputation during “Megxit” and the disgrace of Andrew, could find themselves undermined by the Sussexes at every turn. William will be furious, and rightly so, if the prodigal son is so easily taken back into the fold by their good-natured father.
What about Christmas? Must the Royal family gather at Sandringham, fake smiles plastered on their faces, with the ever-present fear that Harry and Meghan are taking notes for their next book or documentary on the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death next year? Heaven forbid, Harry, Meghan and the kids are allowed to join the walk from church on Christmas Day – if they do, the frost won’t just be on the ground. It’s a toxic situation because all trust is gone.
What are Harry and Meghan playing at? There was apparently no mention of them moving back to the UK at the tea they had at Highgrove with the King in July. He was blindsided and only told of the plan on Sunday, which, if true, is an extraordinarily rude way to treat the monarch. They must have been plotting this for months by finding a place to live and enrolling the children in a school. The Sussexes are dangerous. “Manipulative to the highest degree,” warns Tom Bower. If they do lots of charity appearances and fun events over the next year, they may gradually hope to win back the public and wangle the half-in, half-out model of monarchy that was specifically ruled out by the late Queen.
Levin points out that, as non-working royals, “they are free to do and say what they want. They can read what the other family members are up to and get there first. They can muscle in on the limelight and champion political causes that embarrass the King. I’m really worried.”
We should all be worried, at least those of us who care about the survival of the monarchy. “Please, boys. Don’t make my final years a misery,” the King pleaded five years ago. His sons are still estranged, and heaven knows it must be terribly painful. But while Charles may privately long for reconciliation, he has to take the hardest of hard lines with the Sussexes (his wife shares William’s views on that pair). It would be unforgivable, I think, to expect his eldest son to forgive so many unforgivable things – his family’s reputation trashed, his wife attacked when she had cancer, his beloved grandparents having to firefight Harry’s treachery while they were dying.
You can forget building bridges. Isambard Kingdom Brunel himself couldn’t build a bridge that would repair what Harry and Meghan have done to the Windsors. There must be no quasi-Royal roles for them, and no undermining of the heir to the throne and his wonderful wife on whom the future of the institution rests. The King should welcome the family home from California as a father and grandfather. Then, as the monarch, he should remove their titles to limit the mischief they can cause.
Just because the American dream went sour for Harry and Meghan, they have no right to come here and cause a nightmare. If there is to be a war of the rival courts, I am Team William and Kate all the way.
summary: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have announced they are returning to the UK later this month, sparking significant public backlash and raising concerns about potential friction with the Royal Family. Following professional setbacks and declining popularity in the United States, their sudden return threatens the uneasy truce established after their departure, known as "Megxit." Commentators and the public remain deeply skeptical of their motives, citing past criticisms of the monarchy and a perceived lack of contrition.
key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have announced plans to return to the UK later this month.
The announcement has generated widespread public hostility and revived tensions regarding their past criticisms of the Royal Family.
The return follows reported professional and media struggles for the couple in the United States.
Polling indicates unfavorable public opinions of both the Duke and Duchess in Britain.

title: ‘So many people say things about my appearance – it’s not normal’: Jorja Smith on burnout, body-shaming and finding freedom
author: Emma Loffhagen
content:
It is a sticky, sweltering July afternoon, and I have accidentally found myself at a wake with Jorja Smith. I’m told that the pub where we have met, in the leafiest part of leafy south-west London, is usually a safe bet for an inconspicuous table. But today, sweaty black suits carrying pints drift between tables, and long queues snake round the bar.
Dressed in a simple tank top, bare-faced with her hair scraped back, Smith is waiting for me when I arrive. “I’ve been waiting for my drink for ages,” she says. “But I feel bad saying anything because, you know …”
The sombre mood doesn’t last long – in large part because Smith is effortlessly funny. When her alcohol-free sparkling wine finally arrives, she takes one sip, pauses for the waitress to disappear, then winces theatrically. “Oh,” she says. “That’s not good.” Every time we dissolve into laughter, I glance around guiltily, like we’re schoolgirls trying not to get caught talking at the back of assembly.
It’s hard to imagine a less appropriate setting in which to discuss an album made for sunburnt block parties and 2am raves. What Are the Odds, the 29-year-old’s third album, released this week, is a certified, old-fashioned ass-shaker. Made with Richard Isong – the London producer better known as P2J, whose credits include Beyoncé, Burna Boy and Tems – and featuring the likes of Wizkid and Devlin, it is a vibrant collage of Black British dance music, weaving together UK garage, funky house, 2-step and Afrobeats, into a 12-track collection that pulsates from top to bottom.
While dance music has always been threaded through Smith’s catalogue, usually in the form of a summer single – On My Mind in 2017, Little Things in 2023 – she is better known for her introspective, soulful R&B, as epitomised by her 2016 breakout single Blue Lights (which NME praised as “a fantastically introspective and clever piece of songwriting”, and had critics declaring her Amy Winehouse’s successor). This is the first time she has committed fully to the dancefloor.
“I just love dancing,” Smith shrugs. “I like going out to listen to music, a lot of my friends are DJs. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m outside.”
The genesis of this album was different to her previous records. Her Mercury prize-nominated debut album, Lost & Found, emerged because she felt it was time to make an album. Its successor, Falling Or Flying, arrived because she felt she “needed” a second one. What Are the Odds was made almost accidentally, which is perhaps why it feels so light on its feet.
After making the effervescent club single Little Things with P2J, the pair initially planned to write a dance EP. But the songs kept coming, and the project outgrew itself. “We went through nine songs in the first two days,” Smith says, her eyes widening again at the memory. “I turned up to the studio and he’d made all this music from our conversations. I left and went straight to my label and said: ‘I think this is an album, not an EP. This is serious.’ I’m so excited about it.”
![A closeup of Jorja Smith](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4ada550b1424d3dab1323c6b79108f2b1eec6e4b/0_74_7060_8820/master/7060.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The album may be created for the dancefloor, but its emotional resonance remains unmistakably Smith. For Life mourns losing a friend to addiction; Young Heart is a love letter to Smith’s younger self; The Way It Was meditates on the end of a friendship. “If you just sang the songs with keys or piano,” she says, “they’d all probably be quite sad.”
It is tempting to read What Are the Odds as a comeback album. In the weeks before its release, various headlines have announced Smith’s “return”. When I begin to ask her about this supposed break, she cuts in incredulously. “People keep saying, ‘Oh, you’re back!’ What do you mean, back? I’ve been on tour since 2017. When people say that, I’m like … [you should] check my calendar! People are likely talking about a ‘comeback’,” she says, “because I’m back on social media. I take breaks, and I’m not always out at events and things.”
It’s an astute observation, and one that cuts to the heart of Smith’s unconventional relationship with celebrity. Since Blue Lights announced her arrival as an 18-year-old in 2016, she has become one of British music’s defining voices: a Mercury and Grammy nominee, double Brit award winner, and a featured artist capable of surfacing everywhere from Drake’s More Life to Burna Boy’s African Giant. Yet, she has never cultivated the kind of omnipresent celebrity that feels almost compulsory in the social media age, where visibility seems synonymous with existence. There are no carefully choreographed glimpses into her morning routine, no sense that her life exists to be consumed. Smith has clearly never been especially interested in that side of the bargain.
“I never wanted to be famous,” she says. “I’ve always been quite private. I just wanted to put music out as a teenager and see what happened. I feel really lucky that I’ve got such an amazing fanbase and people really show me love, but fame was never the goal.”
The tension, of course, is that success increasingly lives or dies by the algorithm. The defining British stars of recent years – PinkPantheress, Raye, Lola Young – have all been, in some part, forged in the fires of TikTok. Does Smith ever feel pressure to play that game? “Yeah definitely,” she says. “But, luckily, I’ve got a sick team, and we come up with ideas that we can do that are still me. I don’t want to be here doing trends – you’re not going to catch me doing TikTok dances or any of that stuff.”
Her inclination to privacy also stems from growing up under an unusually unforgiving spotlight. Smith first found an audience by uploading covers to YouTube, recorded from her bedroom in Walsall. Aged 15, she signed with a manager, and began making regular trips to London for songwriting sessions. After finishing her A-levels, she moved to the capital full-time, working shifts in a cafe while trying to carve out a career in music.
Blue Lights, which hauntingly paired Smith’s mellifluous voice with lyrics about police profiling and urban anxiety, landed on SoundCloud in 2016, instantly establishing her as one of the most compelling new voices in British music. The following year, Drake invited her on to his blockbuster playlist, More Life, exposing her to millions of listeners around the world.
Alongside the acclaim, though, came another kind of attention. Almost overnight, Smith became a symbol of a modern beauty ideal, often uncomfortably sexualised before she had properly entered adulthood. For years, the conversation around Jorja Smith the musician existed alongside another conversation entirely, one that Smith had no control over: that of Jorja Smith the face, Jorja Smith the body. “It’s not normal,” she says, reflecting on that time. “Growing up and having so many people having something to say about your appearance.”
The internet, as it tends to do, eventually turned. In the run-up to the release of Falling Or Flying in 2023, every online photo or video seemed to invite commentary on her weight. At one point, the phrase “Jorja Smith weight gain” trended on X for two days. It is something she brings up without prompting.
![Jorja Smith picking up the Best British female solo artist award at the Brits, 2019.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/968842352eaa6a933e8a28015b154e225ec8881a/0_0_1862_1384/master/1862.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“It was difficult. I’d be reading things like: ‘What happened to her?’ Or, ‘She’s let herself go.’” She trails off. “It really knocks your confidence.”
On one occasion, she couldn’t resist replying. “Some blog page”– she waves away the name – “had put two photos side by side, like a before and after. I just commented: ‘What the hell, guys? I’m literally 18 in that picture. Why are you doing that?’” She shrugs. “People are so quick. They love you, then they hate you.”
after newsletter promotion
What made that period particularly disorientating, she says, was that the public narrative bore almost no resemblance to reality; at the very moment strangers were dissecting her body online, she felt healthier than ever.
“I’d actually started eating properly,” she says. “Before that, I’d be so busy I’d skip meals, wake up late, I was running every day, obsessively. It was the first time I actually felt healthy, and then people wanted to criticise me? It was a proper headfuck because I was thinking: Wait … can I do anything right?”
For a while, she stopped wanting to do photoshoots, or even go outside for fear of being photographed. “I sort of went into myself,” she says. “I felt like no one could really understand what I was going through.” Her coping mechanisms, she says, are to go for a walk or to the gym, though she catches herself revealing how fragile that equilibrium can still be.
Sometimes she’ll still “see comments … and start thinking: Maybe they’re right?” She stops herself mid-thought. “Oh my God,” she says, laughing in disbelief. “Even me saying that now is crazy. Because they’re just random people!
“But I have my days,” she continues. “I was talking to my mum about it the other day, and she was like: ‘At least they’re not saying you sound shit!’”
One of the ways she’s protected herself is by stepping away from those online platforms. She no longer runs her own social media – her team posts on Instagram, and she only keeps the app to message artists and friends. She hasn’t been on X in years, and never goes looking for commentary about herself.
Part of that self-reclamation meant physically removing herself, too. In 2023, after years in London, she moved back to Walsall – an unusual move for an artist at the height of their career. “I just needed a reset,” she says. “I thought: Let me move back home, touch some grass, see some trees.” London, she says, had become tangled up with the pressures of her career. This City, one of the tracks on What Are the Odds, explores her love-hate relationship with the capital. “Anything negative that happened, I kind of put London as the culprit,” she says. “I was like: ‘I hate this place. I need to get out.’” Distance has since softened London’s hard edges, and today, she divides her time between the West Midlands and the capital: “I’m feeling the buzz of what this place has to offer again, instead of feeling as if I have to wear armour all the time.”
She is fiercely protective, too, of the place she comes from. In an industry so often centred on London, she is keen to keep reminding people that remarkable artists also emerge from elsewhere. “People forget I’m not from London,” she laughs. “And I’m not from Birmingham, either!” In September, Smith will return to Walsall for a home town show at Walsall Arena, a school turned community arts space she used to visit as a girl. Part of Spotify’s Hometown Billboard campaign, the bill doubles as a showcase of local talent: childhood friend Wesley Joseph, with whom she released the single July this year, supports, alongside the Blue Lights Choir she founded to create opportunities for young people in the town. “I hope it’s a moment that inspires the next generation to believe that big things really can come from Walsall,” she says.
These days, when she isn’t working, she is trying to build a life that exists beyond music. She walks, cooks and has rediscovered running. “I’ve signed up for the London marathon next year,” she says. “I wanted a goal, and I watched everyone finishing it this year and thought: That’s such a sick thing to do.”
Despite her instinct to retreat from the spotlight, Smith is also consciously trying to step back into the world. Recently, she was on the phone with a friend back home when she mentioned turning down an invitation to a Vogue party. Her friend wouldn’t let it slide. “She was like, ‘Go! Not everyone gets invited to these things. You only live once. If you keep turning everything down, you’re going to be 70 and have zero stories of fun nights out because you never went anywhere!’” she laughs.
Outside, the heat hasn’t lifted. Mourners are still in the beer garden. As she gets up to leave, Smith pulls a cap low over her face and slides on a pair of oversized sunglasses. Until that moment, it has been surprisingly easy to forget that she is famous at all.
“It’s all about finding that balance,” she says, smiling as she stands. “But I’m feeling good. I’m starting to feel like my younger self again.”
What Are the Odds is out now on FAMM. Jorja Smith performs at Walsall Arena on 6 September.
summary: British singer Jorja Smith is releasing her third album, What Are the Odds, a dance-focused record created in collaboration with producer P2J. Despite her massive success since her 2016 breakout, Smith has struggled with the pressures of fame, online body-shaming, and intense media scrutiny regarding her appearance. To protect her mental health, she has stepped back from social media, moved temporarily back to her hometown of Walsall, and learned to prioritize her personal well-being over algorithmic celebrity culture.
key_points: Jorja Smith's third album, What Are the Odds, fully commits to dance music genres like UK garage, funky house, and Afrobeats.
Smith faced intense online body-shaming and weight commentary in 2023, which severely impacted her confidence despite feeling healthier than ever.
To cope with the pressures of fame and the music industry, Smith stepped away from platforms like X and no longer runs her own social media accounts.
She temporarily moved back to her hometown of Walsall for a reset and continues to split her time between the West Midlands and London.

title: Strictly's Giovanni Pernice claims Amanda Abbington's behaviour was "confusing" and exit left him 'depressed'
author: Joe Anderton
content:
This article contains discussion of suicidal ideation that readers might find distressing.
Former Strictly Come Dancing professional Giovanni Pernice has spoken about his time paired with Amanda Abbington on season 21 of the BBC show, which ended when she exited the competition and he didn't return for the following season.
In his new book Gio: Taking the Lead, which has been serialised in the MailOnline (behind a paywall), Pernice explains that he was "instantly impressed" with his celebrity partner's potential and enjoyed their shared sense of dark humour at first.
But he alleges that a pattern of behaviour soon emerged that he found strange. According to Pernice, Abbington would say positive things to his face and about him on social media but would say the opposite to others behind the scenes.
"Another celebrity on the Strictly WhatsApp group new recruits always set up to support one another confided: 'Amanda said in a group chat that she wants to quit because you are too much,'" Pernice writes.
"I was stunned. Why would she send nice, encouraging messages to me but then tell the group chat she wanted to quit?"
He further claims: "Her behaviour was often confusing. We would happily be in the middle of a routine and then, with no prompting, she would pull away and say how awful she was. She told me she had a habit of 'self-sabotaging'.
"I tried to comfort and encourage her, but I am not a therapist and I found it difficult to handle. Despite everything, when she danced that Saturday night, she was really good."
Later, Pernice states that although their rehearsals were physically and mentally demanding, their "numerous WhatsApps to one another felt consistently positive" – with a reported dialogue about wanting to be pushed harder. Meanwhile, Pernice writes that Abbington denied claims of a complaint made to the BBC on social media.
He then claims that after Abbington was taken to hospital due to concerns about lumps, she asked to change partners and departed Strictly after she was told she couldn't.
Although Pernice thought things had ended there, stories in the press started to appear after the season 21 finale. In 2024, an official investigation launched into complaints of bullying made against him meant that Pernice wouldn't return for the next season.
At the time, he released a statement via Instagram, saying that he "reject[s] any suggestion of abusive or threatening behaviour".
In his book, Pernice claims that the situation led him to a deep depression, so much so that he considered suicide.
"Hunched on the sofa of my London flat, I scrolled through my phone as story after story brought bad news, plunging me deeper into depression," an excerpt reads.
"Is it worth it? I asked myself. What would happen if I wasn't here any more? Who would care? Tomorrow, I pledged, I would end it all. My life was over and the emotional pain was becoming unbearable."
Pernice credits his then-girlfriend Molly Brown with helping him get through his darkest time, writing: "There were certainly times I would have killed myself if Molly hadn't been there."
Last week, Abbington was reported to have received "a five-figure settlement" and apology from the BBC after "some but not all" of her complaints were upheld (via The Guardian). She has not responded publicly to Pernice's new claims.
Digital Spy has reached out to Abbington's representatives for comment and will update accordingly.
We encourage anyone who identifies with the topics raised in this article to reach out. Information about how to access support is available via the NHS, and organisations who can offer help include Samaritans on 116 123 or Mind on 0300 123 3393.
Readers in the US are encouraged to visit mentalhealth.gov or the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention.
Joe Anderton is a freelance news writer at Digital Spy, having worked there since 2016. In his time, he's covered a host of live events and interviewed celebrities big and small. A big fan of TV and movies both mainstream and obscure, Joe also enjoys video games and in particular PlayStation. Joe currently does not use Twitter, but he only ever used it to tell people to watch the film Help! I'm a Fish.
summary: Former Strictly Come Dancing professional Giovanni Pernice discusses his time dancing with Amanda Abbington in his new book, describing her behavior as confusing and detailing the toll the resulting controversy took on his mental health. Pernice claims that Abbington sent encouraging messages to him while complaining about him to others and attempting to change partners before leaving the show. The fallout and subsequent investigation led Pernice into a deep depression, which he credits his then-girlfriend Molly Brown with helping him survive.
key_points: Giovanni Pernice claims in his book that Amanda Abbington exhibited confusing behavior during their time on Strictly Come Dancing.
Pernice alleges that Abbington was supportive to his face but complained about him behind the scenes and wanted to quit.
Abbington eventually left the show after an unfulfilled request to change partners, leading to an official investigation into bullying complaints against Pernice.
Pernice states that the media coverage and investigation drove him to severe depression and suicidal ideation, from which his partner Molly Brown helped save him.
The BBC recently issued an apology and a five-figure settlement to Abbington after upholding some of her complaints.

title: Ludwig scores big ratings for the BBC as millions watch season 2 launch
author: Stefania Sarrubba
content:
David Mitchell's Ludwig has returned for a second season at BBC One, seeing nearly 3 million viewers tuning in for the first episode. Created by Mark Brotherhood, the series stars Mitchell in the dual role of reclusive puzzle maker John Taylor aka Ludwig and his twin, DCI James Taylor, who disappears without a trace in the first episode.
Contacted by James's wife Lucy Betts-Taylor, played by Anna Maxwell Martin, John agrees to pose as Jack, ending up solving murder cases thanks to his deductive skills.
Season 2 kicks off following a big twist, with John's ruse being exposed and the police forcing a resignation from 'James' so his cases wouldn't be reopened. In the final scenes, John receives a phone call from his brother, who's still alive and probably well, and is ultimately hired as a police consultant.
The new season debuted with a first episode on 20 August. The season premiere was watched by 2.8 million viewers, making 28.5% of the TV-watching audience at that time (via Broadcast).
Not only did Ludwig season 2 best its closest rival, ITV1's The Chase Around the World, which racked up 1.2 million viewers across the hour, it also surpassed BBC One's slot average of 2.6 million.
The Cambridge-set cosy crime series also saw its viewership increase compared to the first episode of the first season, which had 2.7 million viewers on TV back in 2024.
Season 1 enjoyed an impressive 7.7 million viewers after 28 days of its premiere, so it remains to be seen whether the new season could do better than that.
So far, Ludwig season 2 has nailed a perfect score on Rotten Tomatoes from six reviews, though the 100% rating could go down as more reviews come in. Meanwhile, season 1 is Certified Fresh on the aggregator with a score of 97% from 33 reviews.
At Digital Spy, we argued that the stakes of Ludwig season 2 are "even higher" as the central mystery of James's disappearance "feels much closer to home".
Ludwig season 2 airs on BBC One on Thursdays until 24 September.
The first three episodes of season 2 are currently available on iPlayer, with the remaining three dropping on 10 September.
Season 1 is streaming on the same platform now.

Reporter, Digital Spy
Stefania is a freelance writer specialising in TV and movies. After graduating from City University, London, she covered LGBTQ+ news and pursued a career in entertainment journalism, with her work appearing in outlets including Little White Lies, The Skinny, Radio Times and Digital Spy.
Her beats are horror films and period dramas, especially if fronted by queer women. She can argue why Scream is the best slasher in four languages (and a half).
summary: David Mitchell's BBC One crime series Ludwig returned for its second season, drawing 2.8 million viewers for its August 20 premiere. The Cambridge-set show outperformed its slot average and rival network programs, continuing the strong viewership established in its first season. Season 2 begins with John Taylor's ruse being exposed, followed by a twist involving a phone call from his missing twin brother and John being hired as a police consultant.
key_points: Ludwig season 2 premiered with 2.8 million viewers, capturing 28.5% of the TV-watching audience.
The premiere surpassed BBC One's slot average of 2.6 million and beat ITV1's rival show The Chase Around the World.
Season 2 viewership increased compared to the first season's premiere, which drew 2.7 million viewers in 2024.
The new season debuted with a 100% rating on Rotten Tomatoes from its first six reviews.
Season 2 episodes air on BBC One and are made available on BBC iPlayer.

title: TV tonight: a hit jumpy horror series returns with Dan Stevens
author: Phil Harrison; Hollie Richardson; Graeme Virtue; Hannah Verdier; Simon Wardell
content:
The Terror: Devil in Silver
9pm, Sky Atlantic
“We all got our demons, don’t we?” We certainly do, though it’s rare to see them manifest so vividly in a drama. This third standalone story in The Terror anthology series is set in an understaffed, underfunded and quite possibly cursed psychiatric hospital. Dan Stevens stars as Peter “Pepper” Coffin, who has been wrongfully committed to the institution and is forced to reckon with its tatty malevolence. We meet the patients in their past and present lives and connect them via the sinister Dr Walter (John Benjamin Hickey) who may just be the key to the whole mystery. It doesn’t lack jump-scares but also generates a subtler, more genuinely unsettling ambient hum of horror. Phil Harrison
Violent Earth
6pm, Sky Nature
“It was chewing up everything in its path!” So begins the first episode – about terrifying tornadoes – in an intense new series about the science behind natural disasters. It’s presented by actor Liev Schreiber, for reasons unknown, and features first-hand footage taken across the world, along with eyewitness accounts. Hollie Richardson
Force of Nature
7pm, ITV1
Extreme heat is tackled in this instalment of the series dramatising how the climate crisis affects animals, from increased drought to the rise of wildfires around the globe. That means a wombat in Australia, a leopard in Zambia and a kangaroo rat in Arizona all abruptly find themselves starring in their own mini disaster movies. Graeme Virtue
Mozart at the Proms
8pm, BBC Four
A pair of Wolfie’s crowd-pleasers for your delectation: the Third Horn Concerto, featuring star soloist Felix Klieser; plus his exuberant Symphony No 35, AKA the “Haffner”, whose first movement, Amadeus advised, should be “played with fire”. Also, pieces by Elgar, Britten and, making its Proms debut, Thea Musgrave’s Out of the Darkness concerto for bassoon. Ali Catterall
The Piano
9pm, Channel 4
![The Piano on Channel 4.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/015e300d68061abd18a84a6c906c9c3c90a0d336/767_366_4259_3407/master/4259.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Jamie asked Claudia to sing a few notes, which he then improvised from when he first played in the competition. Will he need her help again in the final? He plays on stage along with Grace, who lost all her fingers after meningitis, Harri, with his song inspired by his grandad, wildcard teen Sophie and “piano-breaker” Gabby. HR
One Dollar
11.20pm, ITV1
“No guns, no body” and a cast of suspects: this acclaimed US drama knows how to set up a tale. And as a dollar bill changes hands in a struggling rust belt town divided by culture and class, secrets emerge, aided by John Carroll Lynch, Leslie Odom Jr, Nathaniel Martello-White and more. Hannah Verdier
Film choice
H Is for Hawk, out now, Netflix
![H Is for Hawk on Netflix.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f01c86d136fa584b83c1d54965fa6bfe11a0b1ae/0_0_2535_1523/master/2535.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Getting up close and personal with animals can be a life-affirming way of feeling at one with nature. It can also be a way of avoiding the messier everyday of being human. For Helen Macdonald (a febrile Claire Foy), in Philippa Lowthorpe’s adaptation of Macdonald’s bestselling memoir, it is the tug between the two that brings her world crashing down. After her beloved father (Brendan Gleeson) dies, Helen decides to train a goshawk (“a perfectly evolved psychopath,” her mentor warns) in memory of their shared love of the great outdoors. But confronting avian life red in tooth and claw isn’t the same as dealing with the complex emotions of grief. An arresting, affecting drama. Simon Wardell
summary: Tonight's television highlights include the return of the horror anthology series The Terror: Devil in Silver on Sky Atlantic, starring Dan Stevens. Other offerings feature a natural disaster series presented by Liev Schreiber, a documentary on climate change impacts on animals, and classical music at the Proms on BBC Four. Additionally, viewers can watch talent competition The Piano on Channel 4, the US drama series One Dollar on ITV1, and the film adaptation of H Is for Hawk on Netflix.
key_points: The Terror: Devil in Silver returns on Sky Atlantic as a standalone story set in a psychiatric hospital starring Dan Stevens.
Violent Earth on Sky Nature explores the science of natural disasters such as tornadoes, presented by Liev Schreiber.
Force of Nature on ITV1 dramatises how extreme climate change affects animals globally, including wombats and leopards.
Mozart at the Proms on BBC Four features performances by horn soloist Felix Klieser and works by Elgar, Britten, and Thea Musgrave.
The film adaptation of H Is for Hawk starring Claire Foy is available on Netflix.

title: A supreme being, the nearly naked show and politics with paws: Edinburgh fringe pick’n’mix
author: Brian Logan; Lyndsey Winship; Arifa Akbar; Kate Wyver; Tim Jonze; Chris Wiegand
content:
Anna Leong Brophy: Born Sexy Yesterday
For new perspective on the strange ways we behave, we all know the thought experiment “if a visitor from space arrived on Earth, what would they think?” In Born Sexy Yesterday, Anna Leong Brophy plays a supreme being implanted into a grown woman’s body to experience life for the first time. Presenting like some sci-fi sex robot with the soul of a naive child, Brophy duly marries a man on the front row and settles down to a life of domestic drudgery. Until she discovers she has other settings, other brands of femininity available for her to try out … Thus begins a potent hour, not always hilarious but undeniably persuasive, protesting against the strictly circumscribed roles that women are allowed to play – particularly in the movies, as Brophy sardonically demonstrates. The supreme-being conceit dilutes a bit – but our host’s righteous indignation and strong performing chops make this a compelling hour. BL
  At Pleasance Courtyard until 30 August
Taiwan Season: Under Mask
Some of the best dancers I have seen at the fringe are from Mailantia Dance Company, led by choreographer Lai Yun-Chi, who has danced with Hofesh Shechter’s junior company in London. It is worth singling out Huang Hsiao-Wen, who moves with incredible flow and compelling presence. Under Mask is a quartet for dancers dressed in steampunk-style masks and painted faces – the theme of identity, masks and the roles we play don’t come through much more meaningfully than that, but the way they move with swagger and mystery is enough. The piece is inspired by Taiwanese temple rituals and has that feel of something ancient, mythical or spiritual, even when the movement recalls commercial pop. It also draws on martial arts, hip-hop and contemporary dance, and you can see hints of Indian classical dance, maybe even flamenco at one point. A choreographer to watch out for. LW
At Assembly @ Dance Base until 30 August
![Lauryn Jenkins in Big Dog.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ae4b8e7b690e7967863830fb530bc930a6412496/878_0_6662_5333/master/6662.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Big Dog
Promising young writer-actor Izzy Radford’s debut play, Seating Plan, was a romcom set at a birthday party. Now she has penned an exuberant satire about a group of true-crime podcasters. Directed by Zoë Templeman-Young, Radford stars alongside Eleanor Cross and Lauryn Jenkins as fellow podcasters, with Tumba Katanda as a journalist and office newbie. There are energetic performances across the board, but it verges on the chaotic at times and is overstuffed with ideas, wavering somewhere between a true-crime parody and a dark comedy in the vein of Severance, for its observations on managerial-level, white-collar tyranny and conformist office behaviour. Great fun to watch, even if it feels underdeveloped in this current state. AA
At Gilded Balloon Patter House until 31 August
Rosalie Minnitt: Clementine 2
“A single baguette is worth 1,000 francs – and a married one far more!” In her smash-hit maiden show, Rosalie Minnitt’s Regency-era alter ego Clementine tried to find a husband. In its follow-up (and in a bid, jokes Minnitt, to pass the Bechdel test), our heroine makes for the big city, to get caught up in a revolution with a distinctly French flavour. And taking to the streets amid popular revolt could scarcely be more disorientating than Clementine 2, an absolute blizzard of character-comedy that confirms Minnitt as a writer/performer in the vanguard. Does it pack quite the punch of its predecessor? Perhaps the satirical bite of Clementine 1.0 is lacking. Is its plot throwaway bordering on incomprehensible? It is. But this adventure in self-realisation for our bumptious, puppyish heroine (befriending Dickensian pickpockets; orchestrating the regicide of the king; flirting shamelessly with the audience) makes up for that abundantly in chaos, silliness, smarts and Minnitt’s full-pelt approach to comic performance. BL
At Pleasance Courtyard until 30 August
![The Palestinian Circus: Step and a Half.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a02cd51a6252b329d7ca916a3e4f5ec37f9b520f/285_0_1350_1080/master/1350.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Palestinian Circus: Step and a Half
“Hope is a daily choice,” says a voice at the opening of the Palestinian Circus’s Step and a Half. “As long as the heart continues to beat, we keep on moving.” The Palestinian Circus has been running for 20 years, teaching children across the region and spawning this collective of artists. Not all the acts are at the technical level you become accustomed to at the fringe, but that’s not to say there isn’t some great work on the trapeze, straps and silks, taking nosedives from the ceiling. There’s a street performer feel, with fire poi and one guy who seems a very average juggler and then turns out to be a demon on the diabolo. It’s all enveloped in a folky, celebratory atmosphere, with traditional dabke dancing, too. “Joy itself is an act of resistance,” they say. It’s an easy show to feel warm towards. LW
  At Underbelly’s Circus Hub on the Meadows until 29 August
Ahir Shah: Golden
“Three hundred people looking one way, and one person looking the other. How do I justify that?” So asks comedian Ahir Shah, and his answer is: honesty, about where he’s at in his life right now. That’s a laudable principle, but the result in Golden suggests honesty isn’t always the best policy – or at least, not in this dosage. The show finds Shah 35 and married, so overworked and anxious about money he develops a severe allergic reaction to his own life. Pile on depression, autism, a fire in his parents’ house and the expounding of his pessimistic view of midlife stasis with no further possibility of personal growth, and you get a show that no amount of decent jokes (of which there aren’t quite enough) can jollify. What’s left is an hour with a man grappling with his own mordant worldview, towards a sunnier conclusion – and probably towards a show striking a better balance as it develops between dark humour and despondency. BL
  At Pleasance Courtyard until 30 August
![Fanny Bleach: The Nearly Naked Show.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b07832d3b0f1f49d5b75dcca8d74f6e86fd599cb/0_411_3307_2646/master/3307.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Fanny Bleach: The Nearly Naked Show
This is what my mum thinks all fringe theatre looks like. A skulking performer dressed as a many-eyed Ikea bag hag emerges from an overflowing bin to lip-sync with toothy aggression, before stripping down several layers and unhinging her jaw to scream into a microphone. From geordie clown Emma Crowley-Bennett, this is an irreverent cabaret “freak show” – but everyone else in the lineup has tapped out, leaving only nervous work experience kid Daniel to man the stage. Crowley-Bennett’s energy is high and her costumes and characters are inventively grotesque, with Ms One-Tit flashing us her single massive nipple, and a Prawn Star pulling out its dark vein to appease Daniel’s fishy fetish. But what might work as a subversive short slot in a more populated cabaret is dragged out, with not enough dramatic muscle to confidently pull us through. A show that’s yet to find its hairy green feet. KW
At Assembly Roxy until 30 August
Rosco McClelland: The Bones
It’s never a great sign when a comedian airs their difficulties deciding what their show should be about. Rosco McClelland settles on “pathological demand avoidance”, his own brand of stubbornness that resists anyone making demands on him. It provides a very tenuous frame for what is, in effect, several club-comedy routines strung together by the Glaswegian. When that’s the case – when your show isn’t really about anything – you’ve got to hit big joke-to-joke, and happily McClelland lands a few comic haymakers here. There’s some palate-cleansing material about Scotland’s World Cup (mis)adventure, and a dopey anecdote about “ladling piss from a dog”. Later, an argument with his wife about a picture posted on Facebook (and this one is about demand avoidance) ends with a very satisfying punchline, and his shaggy-dog story about a supposed cyborg nemesis stacks laugh upon ridiculous laugh. BL
  At Monkey Barrel Comedy (Cabaret Voltaire) until 30 August
![Meet Mayor Max](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/cced99b1a174f09a9262ffa9901c95e3e857093d/291_543_4094_3277/master/4094.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Meet Mayor Max
Firstly: awwwww! If you love puppy pics – and what kind of heartless fringegoer doesn’t? – then Alex Robins will quickly have you eating out of the palm of his paw. When Robins is dressed in dog ears and yapping away, a PowerPoint presentation is always on hand to bring coos of affection. This one-man play tells the true story of Max, a golden retriever who becomes the mayor of the sleepy California town of Idyllwild. So beloved is Max to this community of artists and hippies that, when he dies, a second Max is installed, and then a third (Maximus Mighty-Dog Mueller III currently serves there with a lifetime term). The play is billed as a story of hope but it can feel like you’re trapped inside a novelty news story. Robins is an engaging performer with an unsettlingly messianic edge, but we’re left with too many unanswered questions: what happens after Idyllwild’s citizens start voting for Trump? How exactly did Robins extract himself from scientology? The ending – no doubt like lovely Max himself – needs a sharper bite. TJ
  At Pleasance Courtyard until 31 August
Crush
Hadsan Mohamud’s debut play, longlisted for the 2025 Tony Craze award, oozes charm. It is a kooky kind of meet-cute in a mental health clinic for people with eating disorders where two British Somali teenagers become friends. When Najma (played by Mohamud) spots Zak (Mohamed Hashi), she finds him pretentious. But they are drawn closer, slowly opening up to each other, in Alena Sahota’s production. Although full of painful truths and culture-specific reflections, it plays out haltingly and rather statically. The couple are sweet although the romance seems contrived. But it captures the insidious and insistent nature of eating disorders and we fear for the outcome of these teenagers in their rocky journeys towards healing. AA
At Underbelly, Bristo Square until 30 August
![Alex Hines and Sarah Stafford in Birds](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/620318305ee51d09721869094681b5c259a8eea4/363_475_4427_3541/master/4427.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Birds
Just sit back and enjoy the heat? Richard Tice should try telling that to this pair. House of Oz’s apocalyptic two-hander, created by Alex Hines and Sarah Stafford, opens with two toweringly beehived ladies of leisure, Shayna and Beverley, on deckchairs beneath the punishing sun. As the booze from the cooler slips down, they watch the birds above whose cackling cries and sharp talons they share – along with the instinct to beak into each other’s business. It can feel like a cheeky camp spin on Caryl Churchill’s Escaped Alone and the flights of fancy build in terrible rage until a rat-a-tat finale delivered almost at the pace of Beckett’s Not I. As their skin begins to peel and houses collapse into the ocean, in a luridly painted show that feels a little over-extended, you may need to lie down in a shady spot yourself. CW 
  At Assembly George Square until 30 August
Burger and a Pint: Treats for the Soul
Sketch duo Burger and a Pint (AKA James Trickey and Ted Milligan) won the Leicester Square Sketch Off in 2024 and arrive promising to explore “expectations of masculinity” in their debut fringe show. That promise is not fulfilled by a conventional and fairly slapdash offering with nothing to say about masculinity whatsoever – unless there’s deeper meaning sublimated in that Indiana Jones-alike sketch about having to amputate your penis to enter an ancient temple. That’s blokey par for the course in a show that reaches its nadir with a sketch in which a puppeteer must repeatedly insist that he doesn’t have sex with his puppets. There’s better stuff elsewhere: a choice Mastermind sketch; Dickens’ Fagin on Diary of a CEO. The between-scene banter, and the relationship it reveals, is unsurprising. Even allowing for tech difficulties at the performance I saw, it all feels a little underworked. BL
  At Pleasance Courtyard until 30 August
Jonathan Oldfield: Exquisite Corpse
Oldfield makes his solo debut this year but he’s been an unseen presence in recent hits, including Lorna Rose Treen’s work and Joe Kent-Walters’ debut as Frankie Monroe. This character-comedy effort is a real eye-catcher, similar to Treen’s in its array of apropos-of-nothing oddballs, yet with a flavour entirely its own. It derives from the kids’ doodling game sometimes called exquisite corpse, in which legs, torso and head, all drawn by different people, are united to create unlikely bodies. Oldfield plays it with his audience here, and feeds the results into his gallery of eccentric creations: an allotment gardener with a sideline in erotic dancing; a Blockbuster video clerk pining for a son. The linking narrative about Oldfield breaking his arm seven times, and how that led to an ambivalent relationship with his body, can feel tenuous – but this is a captivating hour on corporeal fragmentation and reassembly. BL
  At Pleasance Courtyard until 30 August

  In the UK, Beat can be contacted on 0808-801-0677. In the US, the National Eating Disorders Association is on 800-931-2237. In Australia, the Butterfly Foundation is at 1800 33 4673. Other international helplines can be found at Eating Disorder Hope.
summary: This article reviews a diverse selection of shows and performances appearing at the Edinburgh Fringe festival. The critiques cover various genres, including solo comedy, character-driven satire, theatrical plays, dance troupes, and circus acts. Reviewers highlight both the strengths and weaknesses of these productions, offering mixed assessments of their creative execution and thematic depth.
key_points: Anna Leong Brophy's 'Born Sexy Yesterday' uses a supreme-being sci-fi conceit to protest strictly circumscribed roles for women.
Taiwan Season's 'Under Mask' blends martial arts, hip-hop, and temple rituals into a visually compelling dance quartet.
Alex Robins presents 'Meet Mayor Max', a one-man play about a golden retriever who becomes the mayor of a California town.
Burger and a Pint's debut sketch show fails to deliver meaningfully on its promise to explore expectations of masculinity.

title: Piano used by Freddie Mercury to be sold at auction
author: Danny Fullbrook
content:
![A black Yamaha grand piano standing in a dark room with grey carpet and black walls.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/c09e/live/78571230-9d76-11f1-a7fd-5fe2fcb0be12.jpg)
The Yamaha C3 Grand Piano was played by Freddie Mercury at Munich's Musicland Studios
- Published
A piano and other items used by Freddie Mercury could be sold for a total of Â£3m at auction.
Hertfordshire-based Propstore is selling 82 lots from the collection of German producer Reinhold Mack, who worked with Queen on several albums in the 1980s.
This includes a Yamaha C3 Grand Piano, used to compose Crazy Little Thing Called Love, and a teddy bear given to Mack's son Freddie Jr, who was also the Queen frontman's only godson.
The auction for the items which include a microphone used by Mercury and handwritten lyrics from his debut solo album, is scheduled to begin on 1 October.
![A stuffed brown bear sitting against a white background](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/6f2c/live/b4dd4da0-9d76-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
The auction includes a bear given by the star to Reinhold Mack's son
Ahead of that date the items will be displayed in a free exhibition at The Cumberland Hotel in London between 23 and 27 September.
The piano, which was also played by Leonard Cohen, Donna Summer and Bryan Ferry, is expected to sell for at least Â£200,000.
Queen used the piano during the recording of The Game, Hot Space and The Works.
An AKG C414 EB microphone, which can be seen in footage of the band recording the song One Vision, could fetch at least Â£40,000.
Mack said: "Freddie was not only a colleague and close friend; in many ways, he was part of our family.
"To us, he was never a celebrity; he was 'Uncle Freddie' - spending time with his godson Freddie Jr.... and celebrating family birthdays with us."
He said he hoped a fan would appreciate the items, but added: "The memories we shared can never be auctioned; they will remain with our family forever."
Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.
summary: An upcoming auction by Propstore will feature 82 items from the collection of German producer Reinhold Mack, expected to fetch around £3 million. The collection includes a Yamaha C3 Grand Piano played by Freddie Mercury at Munich's Musicland Studios, along with handwritten lyrics, a microphone, and a teddy bear given to Mack's son. The items will be displayed at a free exhibition in London from September 23 to 27 before the auction begins on October 1.
key_points: A Yamaha C3 Grand Piano used by Freddie Mercury to compose 'Crazy Little Thing Called Love' is expected to sell for at least £200,000.
The auction features 82 lots from producer Reinhold Mack, whose son was Mercury's godson.
Other items in the auction include a microphone used by Mercury and handwritten lyrics from his debut solo album.
The items will be exhibited for free at The Cumberland Hotel in London between September 23 and 27.

title: School librarian-turned-TV and film actor Bunny Levine dies at 97
author: Jonathan Lloyd; Dennis Broad
content:
![Bunny Levine attends the Los Angeles Premiere of "Thelma" at The Egyptian Theatre Hollywood on June 14, 2024 in Los Angeles, California.](https://media.nbclosangeles.com/2026/08/GettyImages-2157644072.jpg?quality=85&strip=all&resize=320%2C180) 
Bunny Levine attends the Los Angeles Premiere of “Thelma” at The Egyptian Theatre Hollywood on June 14, 2024 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Amanda Edwards/Getty Images)
Television and film actor Bunny Levine, who worked as a librarian for more than two decades before pursuing acting and earning roles in "Gilmore Girls," "Law & Order" and other productions, has died at age 97, according to her representative.
Representative Mike Eisenstadt told NBCLA that Levine died Thursday at her Tarzana home in her sleep.
Levine was interested in acting at a young age, but placed those aspirations on hold after graduating and worked as a librarian to help raise three children, according to her IMDB profile. After retiring, she took acting classes and auditioned for roles in commercials, daytime dramas and films.
She moved from the East Coast to Los Angeles and built an expansive acting resume that included credits in "Law & Order," "Everybody Loves Raymond," "Gilmore Girls" and "New Girl."
Her film credits included "You Don't Mess wit the Zohan," "A Thousand Words," "You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah" and "Thelma."
Levine continued to audition for roles in her 90s, her representative said.
The LAPD responded to Levine's residence Thursday morning after a report of an unresponsive person. The death appeared to be from natural causes, police said.
summary: Bunny Levine, a former school librarian who launched a successful television and film acting career later in life, has died at the age of 97. According to her representative, she passed away in her sleep at her Tarzana home. Police stated that her death appeared to be from natural causes.
key_points: Bunny Levine died at her Tarzana home at the age of 97.
She worked as a librarian for over two decades and raised three children before pursuing acting.
Her television credits included roles in 'Gilmore Girls,' 'Law & Order,' and 'New Girl.'
She also appeared in films such as 'You Don't Mess wit the Zohan' and 'Thelma.'
Her representative noted that she continued auditioning for roles into her 90s.

title: Hiromu Takahashi Debuts On SmackDown - Gets New Name (WWE News)
author: Jamie Kennedy
content:
![Shinsuke Nakamura Kyoki](https://d2thvodm3xyo6j.cloudfront.net/media/2026/08/ef527d2b57734264a073a3e9b355356e.jpg) 
Former 5 time IWGP Junior Heavyweight Champion Hiromu Takahashi debuted on this week's episode of SmackDown as Shinsuke Nakamura's brand new tag-team partner. Nakamura had been warning fresh tag champs MFTs that he'd be bringing in some backup to slow their roll and dominate the doubles division himself.
Takahashi has been renamed Kyoki for the role, but he's still largely playing the out there gimmick fans of NJPW witnessed for years. During his promo, Kyoki pretty much spoke exclusively in Japanese, which means the onus is on Shinsuke to translate some of what he's saying into English.
That's something Naka did with aplomb during Friday's pre-tape. Nothing about the vignette came across as forced or awkward, but it'll be interesting to see how much mic time the pair get inside the ring in front of live crowds. WWE may prefer to let the team's wrestling do the talking for them, which would be fair enough.
Tama Tonga and Talla Tonga defeated Damian Priest and R-Truth to hold onto their newly won prizes on the same episode of SmackDown. That draws a line under that particular story, but it does look for all the world like Priest is about to turn heel on Truth in the near future.
Meanwhile, Kyoki and Shinsuke will go after Haku's boys.
Takahashi/Kyoki hasn't actually wrestled since February. That month, he and partner Taiji Ishimori beat Francesco Akira and Jakob Austin Young in tag action. It shouldn't be too long until he's working under the bright lights of WWE on SmackDown though, hopefully.
summary: Former IWGP Junior Heavyweight Champion Hiromu Takahashi debuted on SmackDown as Shinsuke Nakamura's new tag-team partner under the name Kyoki. Nakamura translated for Kyoki during a promo, and the duo is now targeting tag champions Tama Tonga and Talla Tonga. Meanwhile, Damian Priest appeared poised to turn heel on R-Truth following a tag-team loss on the same episode.
key_points: Hiromu Takahashi made his SmackDown debut as Shinsuke Nakamura's new tag-team partner.
Takahashi has been given the new ring name Kyoki and spoke exclusively in Japanese during his promo.
Kyoki and Nakamura are set to pursue tag champions Tama Tonga and Talla Tonga.
Damian Priest and R-Truth lost their title match, hinting at a future heel turn by Priest.

title: Backstage Update On WWE's Plans For Mysterious John Cena Classic (WWE News)
author: Jamie Kennedy
content:
![WWE Backlash 2026 John Cena](https://d2thvodm3xyo6j.cloudfront.net/media/2026/05/130f8936723f9195093bcd0bd3601bd1.jpg) 
False Finish is reporting that the mysterious John Cena Classic will happen on 12 December. However, a location hasn't been determined, and there's no news on whether or not WWE will stick to the format Cena himself laid out when announcing the idea at Backlash in May.
Yes, May. Back then, John rambled on about a concept that had still be fleshed out. He pitched matches pitting NXT stars against top names on the mainline Raw and SmackDown rosters, but then bizarrely said that fan voting would be more important than wins or losses.
Again, it sounds like WWE has some serious thinking to do about how all of this will play out in execution, but there's still time. Most thought that the John Cena Classic would happen over the summer months, but everything went radio silent on the premise shortly after Backlash in Tampa.
Cena himself hasn't popped back up to add any further context.
So, circle 12 December a possible date for the JCC. False Finish's post on X seems to suggest that it'll be a standalone event, but it's also conceivable that the event could fall under the banner of Saturday Night's Main Event. After all, SNME has great meaning to Cena's career - he retired after tapping out to Gunther at one of the Saturday series on 13 December 2025.
There's no word just yet on who might be involved, or how the fan voting thing will actually work. Please call 'Mean' Gene on the WCW Hotline for more information*.
*please don't!
summary: According to False Finish, WWE's mysterious John Cena Classic is scheduled to take place on December 12, though a location and exact event format have not yet been finalized. title: Anna Paquin calls out practice of child acting in tribute to Hayden Panettiere
author: Louis Chilton
content:
Anna Paquin has shared a tribute to Hayden Panettiere condemning the practice of child acting, following her death at the age of 36.
Panettiere died on 16 August at an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina. Before finding success as an adult in the TV series Heroes and Nashville, Panettiere had been a prolific child actor, with prominent roles in projects including Remember the Titans (2000), Ally McBeal (2002), Ice Princess (2005), and Bring It On: All or Nothing (2006).
Paquin is a former child actor herself: in 1993 she became the second-youngest actor to ever win an Oscar, at the age of 11, for her role in the intense romantic drama The Piano.
“It’s not a coincidence that so many former, specifically pre-sexualized female, child ‘stars’ have profoundly sad lives and untimely ends,” Paquin wrote on Instagram. “We were not as protected by the ‘systems’ that look great on paper as we are supposed to be.
She also alluded to Michelle Trachtenberg, the Buffy the Vampire Slayer actor and former child star who died last year at 39, and Daveigh Chase, the child star of Donnie Darko who died in June aged 35.
Paquin continued: “RIP [Hayden Panettiere], [Michelle Trachtenberg], [Daveigh Chase] and too many others. It’s a strange small club we belong to and you are worthy of support no matter how our industry made us feel. Literally DM me. I believe you and I will stand by your side. You aren’t alone. Let’s have each other’s backs. It might make public disclosure less terrifying.”
Rose McGowan, meanwhile, also shared a message about Panettiere criticising the practice of employing children in show business.
“Rest in Power Hayden Panettiere,” she wrote on Instagram. “Don’t put kids in show business. None of this is normal. May her spirit be free of those who orchestrated.”
McGowan appeared in 1996’s Scream, years before Panettiere joined the franchise for Scream 4 (2011) and Scream VI (2023).
While the use of children in show business predates the invention of cinema, the practice has proven increasingly controversial down the years.
In the US, child acting is permitted under labour laws thanks to what is often referred to as the “Shirley Temple Act”, a measure introduced in 1938 during the Roosevelt administration when child labour was being outlawed in other professional sectors.
summary: Following the death of Hayden Panettiere at age 36, fellow former child actor Anna Paquin posted a tribute condemning the practices of the entertainment industry toward child stars. Paquin highlighted the lack of protection for pre-sexualized female child stars and paid tribute to several other late former child actors. Rose McGowan also shared a message criticizing the employment of children in show business.
key_points: Anna Paquin criticized child acting in a tribute following the death of Hayden Panettiere at 36.
Paquin highlighted the untimely ends of multiple former child stars, including Michelle Trachtenberg and Daveigh Chase.
Paquin offered direct support to other former child actors via social media.
Rose McGowan also posted a message condemning the use of children in show business.
Child acting in the US is legally permitted under labor laws established by the Shirley Temple Act of 1938.

title: EastEnders announces Lee and Nancy returns ahead of huge Linda exit story
author: Joe Anderton
content:
EastEnders spoilers follow.
EastEnders has officially announced the return of Nancy and Lee Carter to Albert Square as family matriarch Linda's exit draws near.
Maddy Hill and Danny Hatchard last appeared in a 'what if' episode back in 2024, although they were last in Walford full-time in 2022 and 2020, respectively. But now, they're already on set filming for scenes set to air later this year.
