The soap is keeping tight-lipped about how and why they're returning, but executive producer Ben Wadey has tased that after everything that has happened with the family in the last few years, it isn't going to be the smoothest of reunions.
"We are absolutely thrilled to have Maddy and Danny back in Walford, bringing two much-loved pieces of the Carter family back together. And whilst Linda is delighted to have her children all together again, she's got a lot to catch up on," Wadey said in the announcement.
Meanwhile, Hill shared: "I am SO excited to be returning to 'Enders for a short stint and stepping back into Nancy's shoes (or basketball shorts!). I've missed her! I'm especially looking forward to seeing lots of familiar faces and acting alongside my incredible on-screen family."
Hatchard added: "I'm absolutely over the moon to be returning to EastEnders as Lee Carter. Albert Square has always felt like a home away from home, so I'm proper buzzing to be back grafting with the 'Enders family."

title: Lucy Davis 'grateful' for support after cancer diagnosis
author: Alex Kleiderman
content:
![Lucy Davis, a fair-haired woman in a red top and with red-framed glasses worn on top of her head, is seen sitting down and smiling at the For The Love of Fantasy & Sci-Fi convention at Excel London on Saturday 22 August 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/8045/live/c07a3d60-9e68-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Davis was at the convention to speak about her role in Shaun of the Dead
- Published
Actress Lucy Davis has told fans she is "grateful" for their support as she made an appearance at a London sci-fi convention, following the recent revelation she has incurable breast cancer.
The 53-year-old star was appearing at the For The Love of Fantasy & Sci-Fi convention at Excel London on Saturday, less than two weeks after announcing her diagnosis in a post on Instagram., external
Davis, who was on a panel to talk about her role in the 2004 zombie-comedy Shaun of the Dead, told an audience of hundreds of people about the interactions she had enjoyed with the film's fans during the event.
"It's like this whole second family you never knew you had, everyone is like a community, friendly, supportive of not only us but you guys and each other," she said. "We need a bit more niceness in the world, so I'm grateful."
It was the first time Davis had appeared at a public event since announcing on 11 August that she has stage four breast cancer.
She said in that announcement that it had "metastasised" to her bones following a diagnosis a year-and-half-ago, meaning it was "too late" for chemotherapy.
Davis signed autographs and posed for photographs before appearing on Saturday's panel.
Some fans posing questions told the actress "I love you so much", but she was not asked directly about her health.
The Shaun of the Dead director, Edgar Wright, and Simon Pegg, who played the film's lead role were also on the panel. Davis played Dianne, an aspiring actress who was one of the core group of survivors of the zombie apocalypse, in the cult British movie and helps Pegg's character Shaun fight off the legions of the undead.
Her favourite memories of filming, she said, were "when we all pretended to be zombies and walked across the square; it was like being naughty schoolkids.
"It was a fun time, we went a bit mad."
The actress, who played receptionist Dawn Tinsley in the BBC sitcom The Office and whose father is comedian Jasper Carrott, was also applauded when asked for advice about getting into the film industry.
She said: "We all grow up with a different life with a different world telling us we all have limitations.
"None of us do, our only limitations are things that we think are limiting. We can do anything, or be anybody, and don't apologise for that."
David had thanked fans for their "kindness and support" in another post two days after revealing she had cancer.
"OK, so the last two days have been utterly overwhelming, in that I had zero idea my cancer post would have the attention it did," she said.
"Truly, I am in shock. That said, thank you to everyone for the tremendous amount of kindness and support you have sent me. Good grief it was emotional."
summary: Actress Lucy Davis expressed gratitude for the overwhelming support from fans during her first public appearance at a London convention since revealing her stage four breast cancer diagnosis. The 53-year-old star spoke on a panel about her role in the film Shaun of the Dead alongside director Edgar Wright and co-star Simon Pegg. Davis also shared fond memories of filming and offered advice to aspiring actors during the event.
key_points: Lucy Davis made her first public appearance at the Excel London sci-fi convention since announcing she has incurable stage four breast cancer.
She thanked fans for their overwhelming kindness and support following her diagnosis announcement on Instagram.
Davis appeared on a panel discussing Shaun of the Dead alongside director Edgar Wright and co-star Simon Pegg.
She shared favorite filming memories and advised fans not to let perceived limitations hold them back.

title: Meghan’s casting in The Gentlemen reportedly withdrawn
author: Nadeem Badshah
content:
The Duchess of Sussex’s reported casting in Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen has been withdrawn, it was reported.
Tina Brown, the former editor-in-chief of Vanity Fair and the New Yorker, wrote on Saturday: “I learned this morning that the casting of Meghan Markle in season 3 of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series The Gentlemen has been withdrawn. The backlash in the UK was so intense, it became untenable to go forward.”
The development comes a day after reports that the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to make her acting return in The Gentlemen.
According to Variety, Meghan was in discussions to join the third season, which has yet to receive an official greenlight.
The Gentlemen series is a spin-off from the 2019 crime comedy film of the same name, which starred Matthew McConaughey and Charlie Hunnam, with Guy Ritchie acting as creator of both.
The duchess made her name in the legal drama Suits, in which she played the character Rachel Zane for seven seasons.
Her other small-screen appearances include CSI: NY and 90210, while film roles have included a small part in the comedy Horrible Bosses and 2015’s crime thriller Anti-Social. She also led two Hallmark movies: When Sparks Fly and Dater’s Handbook.
She recently filmed a cameo playing herself in the Amazon comedy Close Personal Friends alongside Brie Larson and Jack Quaid.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are planning to return to live in Britain this month, six years after leaving for the US, it is understood.
The couple and their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are expected to relocate to a property believed to be outside London.
King Charles was reportedly informed last Sunday that his son and daughter-in-law would return to Britain.
Last year the Duke and Duchess of Sussex signed a fresh multi-year film and television deal with Netflix.
Harry and Meghan struck the original five-year deal in 2020, reportedly worth $100m (£78m), which resulted in a number of projects.
Meghan’s main release with the streamer was the lifestyle series With Love, Meghan. The show received negative reviews from many critics, with the Guardian’s Chitra Ramaswamy calling it “toe-curling stuff” in a one-star review.
summary: The reported casting of the Duchess of Sussex in the third season of Netflix's The Gentlemen has reportedly been withdrawn following intense backlash in the UK. This development follows recent reports that Meghan was in discussions to join the upcoming season of Guy Ritchie's series. Meanwhile, it is understood that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex plan to return to live in Britain this month with their two children.
key_points: Meghan Markle's reported casting in season 3 of Netflix's The Gentlemen has been withdrawn.
Tina Brown reported that the UK backlash made moving forward untenable.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are reportedly planning to return to live in Britain this month.
Meghan previously starred in the legal drama Suits and recently filmed a cameo in an Amazon comedy.

title: Meghan’s Netflix acting role ‘in doubt’
author: India McTaggart; Hannah Furness
content:
![Meghan Markle as Rachel Zane](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000147763210_17874207741800_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqevv0ZVCe4bK6Dl-1FPOqSR47t-TZCXN1P25xtk1z6Ss.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Meghan Markle as Rachel Zane](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000147763210_17874207741800_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqevv0ZVCe4bK6Dl-1FPOqSR47t-TZCXN1P25xtk1z6Ss.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Duchess of Sussex’s acting role in Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series has been thrown into doubt, The Telegraph understands.
In an about turn less than 24 hours after the news was revealed, the Duchess’s role in the third series of The Gentlemen is reportedly uncertain following a public backlash.
On Friday, it was revealed that she was in advanced discussions to star in the UK-based production after her relocation to Britain with Prince Harry and their two children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, at the end of this month.
But Tina Brown, a former editor of Vanity Fair, reported the offer “has been withdrawn due to a public backlash”.
The Telegraph also understands the deal could collapse after public reaction to the revelation, which would have marked a return to acting for the Duchess after 10 years.
It is understood that the cold feet are not coming from the team behind The Gentlemen, who anticipated a large public response to the news, but from either Netflix – which declined to comment – or the Sussexes, who have not yet commented.
![Guy Ritchie, the director of the The Gentlemen](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499083874_17874208971080_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Sources said the offer of the role, which was only made recently, formed part of the decision-making process in the family relocating to the UK but was not the sole reason.
After having lived in the US for more than six years, the couple intend to relocate to a private, non-royal residence, thought to be outside London, later this month. The Duke and Duchess’s status as non-working royals and private individuals will remain unchanged.
In Ritchie’s action series, Theo James, the lead actor, “transitions from Duke to drug baron” after inheriting his family’s estate and discovering it is home to an underground cannabis empire. The action-comedy originally aired in 2024, and was Ritchie’s first TV show.
![Theo James in The Gentlemen](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000498328769_17874209163200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The Duchess worked as an actress before meeting Prince Harry, and was best known for her role as lawyer Rachel Zane in seven seasons of the US legal drama Suits. She went on an acting hiatus in 2017 and told the BBC she viewed her career break as “a new chapter” after meeting the Duke the year before.
However, she recently returned to the profession with a cameo as herself in forthcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, starring Lily Collins and Brie Larson.
![The Duchess as Rachel Zane on the legal drama series Suits](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000158944191_17874207854440_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
On Friday, it was understood that the Duchess was poised to accept the role in The Gentlemen, although it remained unclear how many episodes she would be appearing in the unannounced third series.
A part was believed to be being written for her specifically to enter the series, which starts its second season next month.
If she were to take on a role in the series, it would mark the latest project in long-standing ties between the Duchess and Netflix.
The streaming giant was a commercial partner for her US-based lifestyle brand As Ever, which she plans to continue running from the UK, and was the host of the unscripted show promoting the brand called With Love, Meghan.
![The Duchess's reality show With Love, Meghan](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000414894261_17874210231540_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqNJjoeBT78QIaYdkJdEY4CnGTJFJS74MYhNY6w3GNbO8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
After stepping down as working royals in 2020, the Duke and Duchess initially had a five-year deal with Netflix, worth a reported $100m (£74m).
However, the deal collapsed last year amid reports published in Variety that the relationship between key executives in the company and the couple had soured.
During their initial deal, the couple produced a six-part documentary on their life after leaving the Royal family, titled Harry & Meghan, and a polo documentary as well as the Duchess’s lifestyle show, which was critically panned and failed to make the top 1,000 most-watched programmes on the streaming platform.
Their production company, Archewell Productions, now maintains a “first look” deal with the streaming giant, and in April the Duchess was pictured holding hands with the wife of Ted Sarandos at a party hosted by the Netflix boss.
Representatives of the Duchess have been contacted for comment.
summary: The Duchess of Sussex's potential acting role in the third series of Guy Ritchie's Netflix show The Gentlemen has been thrown into doubt following a public backlash. Although advanced discussions were recently underway, reports indicate the deal may collapse or has been withdrawn due to the public reaction. The uncertain casting development comes as Prince Harry and the Duchess prepare to relocate back to Britain with their children later this month.
key_points: The Duchess of Sussex's role in the third series of Netflix's The Gentlemen is reportedly uncertain following a public backlash.
Tina Brown reported that the offer had been withdrawn, and sources indicate the deal could collapse due to public reaction.
The role would have marked a return to acting for the Duchess after a 10-year hiatus following her time on the US drama Suits.
The potential casting news coincided with plans for the Duke and Duchess to relocate from the US to the UK later this month.

title: The first reactions to Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars say it's "emotional," and one of the director's most "human" films
author: Steve Seigh
content:
On August 20 in London, at Odeon Luxe Leicester Square, Ridley Scott‘s post-apocalyptic epic The Dog Stars had its world premiere. With the film’s director and many of its stars dressed in their red carpet finery, including Jacob Elordi’s canine co-star, Rak Jasper, the movie, based on the novel by Peter Heller, quickly became the talk of the town. As the first reactions to The Dog Stars roll in, we want to collect several of the comments from fans and critics and share them with you now.
Looking For a Connection
The film tells the story of Hig (Jacob Elordi), a young pilot who, together with a military survivalist, Bangley (Josh Brolin), has carved out an efficient but isolated homestead in a brutal post-apocalyptic world. But when Hig receives a mysterious radio transmission, he ventures into the unknown in search of the hope and humanity he still believes exist.
The rest of the cast includes Margaret Qualley, Allison Janney, Benedict Wong, and Guy Pearce. It will be released in theaters, IMAX, and premium large formats on August 28.
Is The Dog Stars One of Scott’s Best Movies?
Scott has said that The Dog Stars might be his best movie. But if you recall, Scott made a similar claim about Gladiator II, calling it “one of the best things I’ve ever made.”
“The one I just finished, The Dog Stars, [shot for just 34 days],” Scott said in 2024, during the lead-up to Gladiator II. “It’s the speed of a TV show, but maybe my best movie. Every movie is a discovery of who you are, and making choices about actors. Before I speak to anybody, I look at everything they’ve done. I cast Jacob Elordi, Margaret Qualley, Guy Pearce, and Josh Brolin. Frequently, the biggest thing I’m good at is casting. If they’re available, normally I get them.”

title: The Five Heartbeats star Michael Wright dies aged 70
author: Tom Murray
content:
Michael Wright, the actor best known for his powerful performance as Eddie King Jr. in the cult classic 1991 musical drama The Five Heartbeats, has died at age 70.
In a statement sent to TMZ, Wright’s family said he died in Los Angeles Wednesday after suffering heart failure coupled with complications of a rare degenerative neurological disease called Marchiafava-Bignami.
The news was announced by his wife, Susan, on Instagram on Friday.
“It is with profound sadness and an unimaginable heaviness in my heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Michael Wright,” Susan wrote in a statement shared by TV personality Madina Milana.
“Michael was a husband, a father (Manon Wright, Byron Barr, Brittney Briggs, Brianna Barr, Sir Barr, a grandfather (Yoko), loved one, a friend, and an extraordinary artist whose work touched generations,” she continued.
![Wright died of heart failure coupled with complications of a rare degenerative neurological disease called Marchiafava-Bignami, his family said](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/22/11/30/GettyImages-89510625.jpeg)
“Many knew and loved him through The Five Heartbeats, The Wanderers, V, The Principal, Streamers, and the many other characters he brought to life throughout his remarkable career. His talent, presence, and contributions to film and television will live on, but to those of us who loved him personally, he was so much more than the roles the world knew him for.
“Our family is grieving an enormous and deeply personal loss. We understand how much Michael meant to so many people, and we are grateful for the love, prayers, memories, and condolences already being shared.We respectfully ask the public, members of the media, and those who knew and admired Michael to please allow our family the privacy and grace to grieve during this incredibly difficult time.
“We also ask that people refrain from sharing unconfirmed information or speaking on behalf of our family.In the coming days, when we are ready, we will share additional information regarding Michael’s life, legacy, and how we intend to honor and celebrate him. Michael, your work will live forever, but your love will live even longer in the hearts of those who knew you best. Rest peacefully, my love. You will be missed beyond words.”
![Wright (right) starred alongside Tico Wells, Leon and Robert Townsend in ‘The Five Heartbeats,’ which followed the rise and fall of a fictional 1960s R&B vocal group over three decades](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/22/11/55/GettyImages-117478134.jpeg)
Wright was born in 1956 and raised in New York City. He made his feature-film debut as Clinton, leader of the Del Bombers gang, in Philip Kaufman’s 1979 coming-of-age drama The Wanderers. The film, adapted from Richard Price’s novel and set among rival teenage gangs in 1960s New York, became a cult favourite.
He went on to star in the NBC science fiction miniseries V, the 1984 sequel V: The Final Battle, and V: The Series as Elias Taylor. He also appeared in the Robert Altman film Streamers (1983), for which he won the Volpi Cup for Best Actor.
He is perhaps best known for his role in The Five Heartbeats, which followed the rise and fall of a fictional 1960s R&B vocal group over three decades.
A decade after The Five Heartbeats, he joined HBO’s groundbreaking prison drama Oz, playing Omar White across 22 episodes between 2001 and 2003.
Wright continued to work in film and television throughout the following years, appearing in movies including Sugar Hill, Money Talks, Piñero and The Interpreter. His later credits included the television comedy Rel and the superhero series Black Lightning, in which he played Lazarus Prime.
summary: Actor Michael Wright, best known for his role as Eddie King Jr. in the 1991 film The Five Heartbeats, has died at the age of 70 in Los Angeles. His family stated that he passed away from heart failure combined with complications from a rare degenerative neurological disease called Marchiafava-Bignami. Throughout his extensive career, Wright also starred in projects such as The Wanderers, Streamers, V, and Oz.
key_points: Michael Wright died at age 70 in Los Angeles after suffering heart failure and complications from Marchiafava-Bignami disease.
His death was announced by his wife, Susan, on Instagram and confirmed through a family statement.
He gained widespread recognition for his role as Eddie King Jr. in the 1991 musical drama The Five Heartbeats.
His notable career credits also include The Wanderers, Streamers—for which he won the Volpi Cup for Best Actor—and HBO's Oz.

title: "Ebenezer" Test Screenings Score High
author: Garth Franklin
content:
![ebenezer-test-screenings-score-high](https://cdndark.darkhorizons.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/ebenezer-test-screenings-score-high.jpg)
Last month came the teaser trailer for “Ebenezer,” a new take on Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” from filmmaker Ti West and starring Johnny Depp as Ebenezer Scrooge.
The project is being sold as a ‘return’ of Depp, the trailer going so far as to call him the ‘Master of Misfits’, in what will be his first major studio lead role since 2018.
Paramount also spent serious coin promoting the film at San Diego Comic-Con, with Depp showing up in full costume and makeup while a pop-up store meant to represent Scrooge’s office appeared.
It turns out the studio very much believes it’s onto something. Puck News reports that a test screening of the first cut of the film in New Jersey the other week tested very high – in the 80s (meaning over 80% rated it excellent or very good).
Meanwhile Depp scored an 86 overall, and a 90 among women over 35. For comparison, the normal score on a first-cut test is around 72, and for a lead character is around 67.
The trade says studios are realising that, with his personal/legal issues now over, Depp remains a draw with a high Q Score and strong marketability. The film will be seen as something of a test case for jobs with other studios.
Costing just $40 million to make, the film’s cast also includes Ian McKellen as Jacob Marley, Andrea Riseborough as the Ghost of Christmas Past, Tramell Tillman as the Ghost of Christmas Present and Daisy Ridley as the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come.
Also on board are Rupert Grint as Bob Cratchit, Sam Claflin as Fred, Charlie Murphy and Ellie Bamber as the Fezziwigs, Nicholas Day as a Minister, and Arthur Conti as a young Ebenezer.
The project has a script by Nathaniel Halpern, while Emma Watts is producing. “Ebenezer” is set for a November 13th 2026 theatrical release.
summary: Paramount's upcoming film "Ebenezer," a new adaptation of Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol" directed by Ti West and starring Johnny Depp, has scored very high in recent test screenings in New Jersey. The film marks Depp's first major studio lead role since 2018 and has a modest $40 million budget. It features a star-studded cast including Ian McKellen, Daisy Ridley, and Rupert Grint, and is scheduled for a theatrical release on November 13th, 2026.
key_points: A recent test screening for the first cut of "Ebenezer" in New Jersey scored in the 80s, well above the normal first-cut average of 72.
Johnny Depp received an overall score of 86 and a 90 among women over 35, surpassing the typical lead character average of 67.
The $40 million film is directed by Ti West and stars Johnny Depp as Ebenezer Scrooge alongside Ian McKellen, Daisy Ridley, and Rupert Grint.
"Ebenezer" is set for a theatrical release on November 13th, 2026.

- Actor Michael Wright, best known for playing Eddie King Jr in the 1991 musical drama The Five Heartbeats, has died at the age of 70.
- His family confirmed he died in Los Angeles on Wednesday after suffering heart failure coupled with complications from Marchiafava-Bignami disease, a rare, progressive neurological disorder.
- His wife, Susan, paid tribute to her “beloved” husband on Friday, describing him as “an extraordinary artist whose work touched generations.”
- Wright made his feature film debut in 1979's The Wanderers and went on to win the Volpi Cup for Best Actor for his performance in Streamers in 1983.
- His extensive screen credits also included the sci-fi franchise V, HBO's prison drama Oz, Sugar Hill, and the series Black Lightning.
summary: Actor Michael Wright, best known for his role in The Five Heartbeats, has died in Los Angeles at the age of 70 due to heart failure and complications from a rare neurological disorder. His wife, Susan, paid tribute to him, celebrating his legacy as an extraordinary artist who touched generations. Wright's notable career included acclaimed performances in films like The Wanderers and Streamers, as well as television appearances in series such as Oz and V.
key_points: Actor Michael Wright died at the age of 70 in Los Angeles.
His death was caused by heart failure and complications from Marchiafava-Bignami disease.
He was best known for playing Eddie King Jr in the 1991 film The Five Heartbeats.
Wright won the Volpi Cup for Best Actor for his 1983 film Streamers.
His extensive career included roles in The Wanderers, V, Oz, and Black Lightning.

title: Former Hiromu Takahashi Makes First Appearance On WWE SmackDown, Reveals New Ring Name - Wrestling Inc.
author: Daisy Ruth
content:
Former Hiromu Takahashi Makes First Appearance On WWE SmackDown, Reveals New Ring Name
Former NJPW star Hiromu Takahashi has been rumored to be heading to WWE for months, and on Friday's edition of "WWE SmackDown," he was officially revealed as the new tag team partner of Shinsuke Nakamura. In a pre-recorded video promo, the star also revealed his new ring name is Kyoki.
"The King of Strong Style" has had a few vignettes over the weeks, both on the blue brand and social media, teasing his friend's debut, and they're seemingly headed right toward the WWE Tag Team Champions. Nakamura has been challenging the MFTs, and fellow former NJPW talent, Talla Tonga and Tama Tonga.
Nakamura told the tag team champions he had been warning them for weeks, but they haven't been listening. He said what's been in the dark has finally come to light, and Kyoki appeared. Kyoki said after spending years competing around the world, he finally had come to WWE.
"Champions. Legends. Monsters. I don't care," he said. "The stronger they are, the more fun I have."
Nakamura said that Kyoki doesn't fear chaos, he enjoys it. His new partner said there would be "more fights, more gold, and more madness." Nakamura warned the MFTs that when strong style and madness combined, there would be an explosion.
The video promo didn't reveal an in-ring debut date for Kyoki. Nakamura hasn't been seen in the ring since May, when Talla Tonga defeated him on an episode of "SmackDown."
summary: Former NJPW star Hiromu Takahashi debuted on WWE SmackDown as Shinsuke Nakamura's new tag team partner under the ring name Kyoki. In a pre-recorded promo, Kyoki expressed excitement for competition, while Nakamura warned the WWE Tag Team Champions, Talla Tonga and Tama Tonga. An official in-ring debut date for Kyoki was not announced.
key_points: Hiromu Takahashi debuted on WWE SmackDown and revealed his new ring name is Kyoki.
Kyoki is the new tag team partner of Shinsuke Nakamura.
Nakamura and Kyoki are targeting the WWE Tag Team Champions, Talla Tonga and Tama Tonga.
No in-ring debut date was announced for Kyoki.

title: Mastermind fans blown away by ‘most niche specialism in show history’ from contestant
author: Roisin O'Connor
content:
A Mastermind contestant has wowed viewers with what is being dubbed the “most iconic specialist subject ever”.
Policy researcher Emily Medhurst competed on the BBC quiz show in which contestants must answer a series of general knowledge questions but also a round of questions on a specialised subject of their choosing.
For Medhurst’s specialist subject, she opted for Transport for London moquette, the iconic patterned upholstery seen on London buses and Tube trains – some designs of which have featured local landmarks and history.
Medhurst did well in her round, correctly answering eight questions in two minutes, taking only one pass and getting just three questions wrong. She answered questions about famous moquette designers, iconic patterns, and the London Tube lines that have featured specific designs.
Questions included, “Which design, depicting landmarks such as the dome of St Paul’s and The London Eye, is named after the Publicity Manager who commissioned moquettes for London Transport in the 1930s?”, with the answer being “Barman”. Medhurst was also asked which underground line featured “a branded moquette featuring lines of classification headings from the Yellow Pages telephone directory” in the 1990s – other moquette boffs will know that the answer is the Circle line.
In a viral clip shared by the BBC after the episode aired on 17 August, fans praised Medhurst for choosing what they dubbed the “most niche special subject in Mastermind history”.
![Emily found a fan in the official Transport for London account](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/10/19/Screenshot-2026-08-21-at-11-46-21.png)
“Most iconic specialist subject ever,” the official account for Transport for London gushed.
Others spotted that Medhurst was even wearing a knitted vest based on a moquette design: “Nice touch that she even had a jumper to match the topic,” one fan said.
“Don’t wanna brag but she’s in my knit club,” another viewer commented, while another joked: “Wearing one of the answers is a flex.”
“Intelligence is sexy,” one viewer said, as another fan agreed: “This is so hot.”
![Emily Medhurst impressed Mastermind fans with her specialist subject](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/10/53/Screenshot-2026-08-21-at-11-36-23.png)
As the British Transport Museum website explains, “moquette” comes from the French word for carpet and is produced on looms using the Jacquard weaving technique, with a pile typically blending 85 per cent wool and 15 per cent nylon.
It was chosen for public transport due to its hard-wearing and durable nature, as well as because of its colour and patterns that helped disguise signs of dirt, wear and tear. The first moquette was used in London’s public transport systems in the twenties – a pattern called Lozenge made by Firth Furnishings in 1923.
By the 1930s, moquette had become an iconic design feature, with renowned textile designers including Paul Nash and Enid Marx commissioned by London Transport to produce exclusive designs.
Sadly Medhurst didn’t fare well enough to win the episode, but still did well with a total of 16 points.
The contest was won by customer service advisor Donald Campbell, who chose the films of Paul Newman as his specialist subject.
Mastermind, hosted by Clive Myrie, airs each Monday on BBC Two at 7.30pm.
summary: Policy researcher Emily Medhurst impressed viewers of the BBC quiz show Mastermind by choosing Transport for London moquette upholstery as her specialist subject. She successfully answered eight questions on the topic and wore a knitted vest matching the moquette design. Although she scored 16 points total, the episode was ultimately won by customer service advisor Donald Campbell.
key_points: Emily Medhurst chose Transport for London moquette as her Mastermind specialist subject.
She correctly answered eight questions in two minutes with only one pass.
Viewers and the official Transport for London account praised her niche topic and matching knitted vest.
The episode was won by Donald Campbell, who answered questions on the films of Paul Newman.

title: Hayden Panettiere: On-off boyfriend’s brother shares how they found star unconscious
author: Caitlin Hornik
content:
The brother of Hayden Panettiere’s on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson has spoken out days after the Nashville star’s death.
Panettiere died August 16 at an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, aged 36. A cause of death has not yet been revealed.
Zach Hickerson, 38, spoke Friday on what would have been the Heroes star’s 37th birthday, sharing how he and Brian found Panettiere unconscious. He claimed that the trio had plans to get lunch and go indoor golfing Sunday before tragedy struck.
“When I left church I called and texted both of them. When I didn’t reach Brian or Hayden, I just assumed maybe they fell back asleep so I drove over and went to the Airbnb. When I got there I knew the code to the building but not the door code to the AirBnb,” Zach told TMZ.
“I knocked loudly which apparently woke Brian up from a nap they were both taking on the pull out couch bed in the living room. When we went in and tried to wake Hayden up for lunch, we realized she was unconscious.”
Zach also claimed to the outlet that “Brian gave her Narcan,” the medication commonly administered to offset an opioid overdose.
According to a police incident report viewed by The Independent, Brian and Zach called 911 when they realized Panettiere was unconscious. Officers recorded that Zach was emotional as emergency services worked to save Panettiere’s life, but that Brian only became emotional after she was officially declared dead. The report also stated that Brian turned over a “bag of medication” belonging to Panettiere to investigators. The names of the medications were redacted.
A cause of death has not been revealed, but an autopsy showed no signs of trauma.
Panettiere’s death is being investigated.
One day after police reportedly began probing whether there could be criminal conduct behind Panettiere’s death, Brian broke his silence via his lawyer, saying, in part, “it is important to allow that investigation to proceed.”
That now reportedly involves the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, who joined the investigation into Panettiere’s death on Wednesday, according to a person familiar with the case who spoke to The New York Times.
![Panettiere’s on-off boyfriend’s brother has spoken out about her death](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/19/8/35/GettyImages-1244475550.jpeg)
Panettiere’s death was confirmed in a statement released by her father.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden,” Panettiere’s father, Skip, said Sunday to ABC News. “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”
Known for her roles in the 2000 film Remember the Titans, the 2006 NBC series Heroes, and the 2012 ABC series Nashville, Panettiere was also the face of skincare brand Neutrogena for a decade.
After her death, Panettiere’s comments from earlier this year that Neutrogena “fired” her in 2015 after she spoke about her postpartum depression resurfaced, prompting intense backlash against the brand.
Neutrogena issued a formal public apology Thursday, acknowledging “we made her feel unsupported during a very difficult time.”
![Panettiere was the face of skincare brand Neutrogena for a decade](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/18/12/35/images.jpeg)
Panettiere became a mother in December 2014, when she and former fiancé, Ukrainian heavyweight boxer Wladimir Klitschko, welcomed their daughter, Kaya. Panettiere later gave Klitschko full custody of Kaya in 2018 while she was struggling with addiction and postpartum depression.
She spoke about the decision again in 2022, telling Facebook Watch’s Red Table Talk podcast that signing the papers was “the most heartbreaking thing I’ve ever had to do in my life.”
Klitschko released a statement after Panettiere’s death and another Friday to mark what would have been her 37th birthday.
“You are loved, you are missed, and you will never be forgotten,” he wrote in part.
summary: Hayden Panettiere passed away at the age of 36 at a South Carolina apartment, with her cause of death still unrevealed pending an ongoing investigation. Her on-off boyfriend's brother, Zach Hickerson, publicly described finding the star unconscious and administering Narcan before emergency services arrived. Police and the DEA are currently investigating the circumstances surrounding her death. Meanwhile, tributes have poured in from her family, and Neutrogena recently issued an apology regarding past handling of her postpartum depression.
key_points: Hayden Panettiere died at age 36 in Greenville, South Carolina, and her official cause of death has not yet been released.
Zach Hickerson stated that he and his brother Brian found Panettiere unconscious at an Airbnb after trying to wake her for lunch.
Zach claimed that Brian administered Narcan to Panettiere, and police reports noted that Brian handed investigators a bag of redacted medications.
The DEA has joined the ongoing investigation into Panettiere's death to determine if any criminal conduct was involved.
Neutrogena issued a public apology following backlash over past comments regarding Panettiere being dropped by the brand after speaking about postpartum depression.

title: Dolly Parton Shares Health Update With Fans: 'I'm Still Healin,' I'm Still Workin”
author: Charisma Madarang
content:
![Dolly Parton Shares Health Update With Fans: 'I'm Still Healin,' I’m Still Workin''](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
Dolly Parton shared an update on Friday amid ongoing health issues following the death of her husband, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025.
When speaking to People, Parton said, “I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn’t pay attention to when I was watching over Carl.” “It’s not like I haven’t been through hard times with my health,” she said, noting that in the early 1980s she was “down for several months with female issues.” Parton pointed to today’s “24/7 world with social media” and how it magnifies every incident in “ways it wasn’t years ago.”
In true Parton fashion, she quipped, “I used to joke that I was the Queen of the Tabloids, but now I guess I can say I’m the Queen of Social Media AI!” On a more serious note, she added, “Even though I’m still healin’, I’m still workin’.”
Parton told the outlet that she’s also looking at ways to bring fans new experiences. The singer said that she’s currently working with companies to create “avatar performances” and they are still in the “early stages of development.”
On Thursday, Parton appeared virtually to accept the Poet’s Award at the Academy of Country Music Awards, one of multiple recent events the country legend joined remotely (she was never scheduled to attend the ACM Honors to appear in person).
Parton was also unable to attend the recent opening of her Dollywood theme park’s newest ride, the NightFlight Expedition, in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. Instead, Parton greeted fans virtually via video, wearing a pair of sparkling wings. “Now I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I have had a few little health issues,” Parton said in the clip. “And sometimes I get a little dizzy, and I get dehydrated. And I’m dehydrated. And so my Nashville doctor clipped my wings, saying you ain’t traveling this week.”
Though Parton has been dealing with ongoing health setbacks, she’s still been busy with multiple projects. Her SongTeller Hotel in Nashville — which includes two live music venues, a speakeasy, a cafe, and the Dolly’s Life of Many Colors Museum — is scheduled to open next month. According to the museum’s website, it will be the “largest exhibit celebrating her life anywhere in the world, spanning every dynamic decade from the top of the mountains to the top of the world.”
summary: Dolly Parton shared a health update following ongoing issues that arose after the March 2025 death of her husband, Carl Dean. Although she has experienced dizziness and dehydration, leading her doctor to advise against travel, Parton emphasized that she is still working. Her upcoming projects include new avatar performances, the opening of her SongTeller Hotel in Nashville, and managing her ongoing commitments remotely.
key_points: Dolly Parton provided a health update addressing ongoing issues following the death of her husband, Carl Dean, in March 2025.
She missed recent events like the Dollywood NightFlight Expedition opening and the ACM Honors because her doctor advised against traveling due to dizziness and dehydration.
Parton is currently working on new avatar performances with various companies in the early stages of development.
Her SongTeller Hotel and museum in Nashville are scheduled to open next month.

title: CM Punk Retains WWE Title Over Kevin Owens After Sami Zayn Interferes On SmackDown - Wrestling Inc.
author: Max Everett
content:
CM Punk Retains WWE Title Over Kevin Owens After Sami Zayn Interferes On SmackDown
CM Punk defeated Kevin Owens with an assist from Sami Zayn to retain the WWE Championship in the main event of "WWE SmackDown."
Owens started the match getting the better of an immediate striking exchange, throwing Punk around and then outside of the ring. He continued that dominance back inside of the ring and sought for the Stunner, but Punk telegraphed it and dropped him with a neckbreaker to finally take control.
The challenger once again got the better of the champion and had him in position for a frog splash, but the latter rolled out of the ring to escape.
Owens followed Punk, superkicking him onto the announcer's desk and leaping from the barricade to put him through it. He dispensed Punk into the ring and connected with a Swanton bomb and went for the cover, getting only a near-fall.
Owens sought for a Stunner again but that resulted in a referee bump, ensuring there was no official count when he did finally connect with it and cover Punk. Punk managed to hit GTS but there was no official count made.
He tried to rouse the referee but then Sami Zayn emerged and drove him into the ring post, throwing him into the ring for Owens to connect with a stunner. Zayn threw the referee into the ring to make the count, though Punk still managed to kick out.
Zayn then told Owens to use the title belt to hit Punk, which Owens refused to do. That prompted Zayn to hit Owens with the belt and allow Punk to retain the title. After the match, Zayn continued to attack Punk with the belt himself, before laying out Owens again to stand tall at the end of the show.
summary: CM Punk successfully defended his WWE Championship against Kevin Owens in the main event of SmackDown following outside interference. Sami Zayn initially interfered to help Owens, but ultimately turned on him by hitting him with the title belt after Owens refused to use it. This allowed Punk to retain his title, and Zayn concluded the show by attacking both Punk and Owens.
key_points: CM Punk retained the WWE Championship against Kevin Owens in the main event of SmackDown.
A referee bump occurred preventing a count when Owens connected with a Stunner.
Sami Zayn interfered in the match, initially aiding Owens before telling him to use the title belt.
After Owens refused to use the belt, Zayn struck Owens with it, allowing Punk to secure the win.
Zayn attacked both Punk and Owens with the title belt after the match concluded.

title: Is this the end of Harry and Meghan’s American dream?
author: Michael Savage
content:
Having settled in California in the aftermath of their dramatic decoupling from the royal family in 2020, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced a partnership that appeared to set a clear destination for their new lives outside the House of Windsor.
With every global media stable clamouring for their signature, the couple revealed a deal with Netflix reportedly worth $100m. The ambitions were lofty and broad, including scripted and unscripted projects, shows for all ages and documentaries.
A $20m podcast deal with Spotify appeared to confirm their ambitions; the Sussexes were reinventing themselves in the competitive world of content creation, a media powerhouse in the booming universe of streaming and podcasting.
As the couple now prepare to return to the UK, they do so with those mega-deals either pared back or expired, and their media plans less clear. It raises the question: is this the end of their American dream?
As with all things Harry and Meghan-related, their various media forays have spawned copious amounts of reactionary content and commentary. Each appearance, commission and production has been dissected: there have been blockbuster hits, much-publicised misses and some brutal reviews along the way.
![Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, being interviewed on a patio by Oprah Winfrey](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/39e484b95e19012167c9c1a9fc0532eb347b7a20/0_0_3500_2509/master/3500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
For Harry, the pull of returning to the UK, if perhaps not permanently, has been clear for a while.
He says he loves his country, and in an interview with the Guardian last year, he admitted he hankered for home.
“I have always loved the UK and I always will love the UK. It’s been good to reconnect with the causes I am passionate about. I have been able to spend some time with people that I have known for so long. It is hard to do it from far away.”
Perhaps more so recently because his father, King Charles, has been ill. And on the work front, it hasn’t been easy either.
Six years in the content game offers a case study in how difficult it can be to negotiate the shifting sands of a transformed media landscape, so difficult that even a Hollywood actor and a British prince are not guaranteed to succeed.
Those years have proved there is one bankable aspect of the Sussex brand: their relationship with the royal family continues to be devoured on an industrial scale. However, launching lifestyle brands and philanthropic pursuits that rely purely on name recognition – even with a packed contacts book of A-list friends to help – cannot guarantee reliable success in the cut-throat era of the attention economy.
“The Sussexes have kind of got caught up in the media’s awkward teenage transition,” said Evan Shapiro, a former US media executive turned leading analyst of the creator economy. “Just being famous is no longer enough … The last time Meghan Markle worked in show business [starring in the US legal drama Suits], it was a different era. It was top down: ‘We push it out, you watch it.’ That’s just how it worked.
“That era has passed. It’s fucking hard [now] … the competition is literally every human on earth. Eight billion people with phones who are all competing with Meghan Markle.”
The Sussexes could scarcely have had better timing for their eye-catching 2020 Netflix deal, via their Archewell Productions organisation – global streamers were scrambling for big names to lure subscribers.
The pair were in demand, talking with the likes of Disney and Apple before the Netflix deal was signed. Spotify was also pursuing big-name deals when it secured the Sussexes.
While the Netflix announcement talked of a raft of potential projects, the greatest prize was always the story of the Sussexes’ relationship with the royal family. The subsequent 2022 documentary series, Harry & Meghan, duly delivered, setting record viewing figures for a documentary debut and ranking as one of its most successful docuseries ever.
Other Netflix projects featuring the couple followed, including the Live to Lead interview series, Harry’s Polo documentary and two series of the cooking and lifestyle show With Love, Meghan.
Unsurprisingly, content without the royal intrigue could not hit the heights of Harry & Meghan. Polo failed to make Netflix’s top 10 lists around the world, while ratings for the second series of With Love, Meghan dropped off. It was the 1,217th most watched title on Netflix over the second half of last year. A mooted animated children’s series, Pearl, was cancelled.
Netflix also ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, after seven months. The company said handing full control to Meghan was always the plan. However, the relationship endures. Netflix renewed its partnership with the Sussexes, but slimmed it down to a “first look” deal.
As for podcasting, the Spotify deal was ended by mutual consent in 2023, having only produced Meghan’s 12-episode podcast Archetypes, featuring interviews with people such as the former tennis champion Serena Williams and pop star Mariah Carey.
![Meghan stirs a drink in a cocktail glass on a kitchen island while talking to Mindy Kaling](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9afa41960213980602ba460fe0892244f1cfc38e/0_0_3000_2000/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Meghan subsequently launched another podcast series, Confessions of a Female Founder, in 2025, with Lemonada Media. Only nine episodes were made. She revealed last year that there would be no second series, saying she was focusing on As Ever.
In line with all of Harry and Meghan’s exploits, there have been some acerbic assessments of their media production efforts. Most notably, the Spotify executive Bill Simmons called them “fucking grifters” after the company’s deal with the couple ended.
Less incendiary industry analysts point to the significant timing. The Sussexes’ narrowed Netflix deal and split with Spotify coincided with content providers cutting back on their big celebrity bets, and the chaos being wrought by the rapid rise of the creator economy.
“This isn’t a story about nobody being interested in [the Sussexes],” said Matt Navarra, a social media consultant who has worked with broadcasters. “It’s quite the opposite. They can generate attention almost on demand. The harder thing is converting attention into a repeatable media proposition.
“Harry and Meghan arrived in Hollywood with almost every advantage imaginable, but audiences now effectively have infinite choice. They don’t care about how expensive the deal was, or how famous the person is.
“I think that’s one of the brutal lessons of the new media world: that fame can buy you the first click, but only the content earns the second … Their original Harry & Meghan series was pretty much a blockbuster. What they’ve struggled with is repeatability.”
Several industry insiders noted the comparisons with the Obamas, whose Higher Ground production company’s multi-year deal with Netflix narrowed to a “first look” deal in 2024. Their Spotify deal also ended in 2022.
Shapiro said the Sussexes had not yet proved they could draw big audiences beyond content directly related to their dealings with the royal family. “By no fault of their own, the Sussexes were not prepared for the current moment,” he said. “It turns out, other than marrying a prince, Meghan Markle just isn’t that special. Other than being born into royalty, Harry’s just not that interesting.”
Navarra said: “Enormous curiosity exists around them, but curiosity about a person isn’t necessarily the same as demand for everything that person produces. Celebrity is a distribution advantage, but it isn’t a content strategy.
“Harry and Meghan show that you can inherit enormous attention and still have to earn the audience every single time. To me, that is the really interesting shift.”
![Meghan, as Rachel Zane, with Patrick J Adams, as Michael Ross, sitting on a sofa in a living room](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b180be50e1b93d2548263f5d8ef11148344457c9/0_0_3000_2000/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It is perhaps understandable, then, that Meghan is reportedly returning to a bankable acting career that she put on ice after her marriage to Harry. Initial reports from Australia of a UK-based role for Meghan were backed up by Tina Brown, the former Vanity Fair editor and founding editor of the Daily Beast.
Brown said it had been fuelled by Meghan’s positive experience as a celebrity judge on MasterChef Australia last month. “She finally realised how much easier – and more fun – it is to perform in a hit baked by someone else,” Brown wrote.
“She was back on the market, and it did not take long for Hollywood’s mega-deal machine, WME, the talent agency that still represents her, to get her a role.”
Sources close to the Sussexes have not denied the reports.
On Friday night it was reported that Meghan was in talks to return to acting in Netflix’s series The Gentlemen. According to Variety, she was in discussions to join the third season of the Guy Ritchie-created series.
However, the couple are not out of the media production game. Archewell has evolved into a more traditional production company. Its forthcoming Netflix projects include a polo drama and a film adaptation of the romantic novel Meet Me at the Lake. Several sources familiar with the company said there were also projects in the works beyond Netflix.
In practical terms, the move back to the UK creates few issues for their media ambitions. It is not unusual for major production companies to sit outside Hollywood and make shows away from the US, and the UK remains a major production hub.
As for Harry, he – or anyone else – will struggle to replicate the runaway media success of his memoir, Spare. He is focusing on his Invictus Games coming to Birmingham next year. Meanwhile, Meghan has suggested any return as a business podcaster may depend on the progress of her lifestyle brand.
“I would love to bring the show back when I am at a different end of my founder journey,” she said last summer, explaining why she had put her Confessions of a Female Founder podcast on hold. “I think a different time will be so exciting to compare and contrast.”
summary: Since relocating to California in 2020, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have faced a challenging media landscape, resulting in pared-back or expired mega-deals with companies like Netflix and Spotify. While projects centered on their royal connections achieved massive success, their non-royal content struggled to maintain large audiences. As they prepare to return to the UK, the couple continues to adjust their media strategies, with Meghan reportedly in talks to return to acting.
key_points: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex signed major multi-million-dollar deals with Netflix and Spotify after moving to the US in 2020.
Their 2022 Netflix docuseries about their royal exit broke viewing records, but subsequent non-royal content failed to match that success.
Their Spotify partnership ended in 2023, and their Netflix deal was later narrowed to a 'first look' agreement.
Industry analysts noted that while the couple can easily generate initial attention, converting that fame into repeatable media content has proven difficult.
Meghan Markle is reportedly in talks to return to acting in the third season of Netflix's The Gentlemen.

title: From Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumn
author: Guardian staff reporter
content:
Fiction
The Disappearers by Marlon James
Hamish Hamilton, 3 September
  After a detour into mythic fantasy, the author of the Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings returns to Jamaica. This account of a brutal homophobic attack on a group of gay actors in 1980s Kingston has already been longlisted for this year’s prize.
The Bridge by Colm Tóibín
Picador, 3 September
  Twenty years on, this short novel is a sequel to Tóibín’s exquisite story A Long Winter, set around a family tragedy in the isolated Pyrenees. Now the building of a bridge brings modernity, possibility and threat to a father and son, in a spare chronicle of longing and grief.
![The Golden Hours by Louisa Young](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d3eb1c4e41dbf00c09751edbd6691db086f6ea14/0_0_328_500/master/328.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Golden Hours by Louisa Young
Mantle, 3 September
  Young continues her aunt Elizabeth Jane Howard’s much-loved Cazalet Chronicles, bringing her story of a sprawling upper-middle-class English family into the swinging 60s.
Switzy by Emma Cline
Chatto & Windus, 10 September
  With dementia making him increasingly confused, David is on his way to a clinic in Zurich to end his life while he still has the capacity to make a choice. Longlisted for the Booker prize, this is a bravura portrait of a failing mind, told from the inside.
The Rouse by China Miéville
Picador, 17 September
  A leading light of the New Weird, Miéville has been working on this stonking 1,000-page supernatural fantasy for two decades. Political intrigue, continent-hopping global conspiracy and uncanny mysteries unfold.
![The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a521faa44289f9e3848975b665a50b9253af0daf/0_0_650_1000/master/650.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain
Chatto & Windus, 17 September
  An origin story for Daphne du Maurier’s enduring bestseller Rebecca is told from the perspective of the novelist’s secret lover Danni, housekeeper in a Cornish mansion, who is outraged to find herself recast on the page as the malevolent Mrs Danvers.
Stations by Louise Kennedy
Bloomsbury, 24 September
  The author of bestselling 2022 debut novel Trespasses, a Troubles-set love story recently adapted into a C4 drama starring Gillian Anderson, returns with a tale of friendship and loss. Róisín and Red meet in small-town Ireland in the 1980s and reconnect in a London squat, before Red is caught up in a cycle of poverty and addiction.
Doom Painting by AK Blakemore
Granta, 24 September
  One of our most exciting historical novelists takes on the peasants’ revolt, in a blow-by-blow account of unlikely leader Wat Tyler and the 16 days in 1381 that turned England upside down. With cinematic action and a relish for medieval vocabulary, it’s a punky successor to Hilary Mantel.
![Barbara Kingsolver, Marlon James, Bonnie Garmus, Jonathan Coe, Yiyun Li and Emma Cline.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6943583990f4f30cf64771d2834c425571368eba/0_0_2953_2362/master/2953.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee
   4th Estate, 29 September
  The hagwon or cram school is a symbol of Korea’s stress on education. This new saga from the Pachinko author follows a middle-class family, their life in ruins after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, who move to Sydney and then California in search of a better future for their children.
![Partita by Barbara Kingsolver](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f692476d5c7a4deb4a5a1f953fa7ea21a7266cb9/0_0_325_500/master/325.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Partita by Barbara Kingsolver
Faber, 6 October
  After the Pulitzer-winning Demon Copperhead, a retelling of David Copperfield set in Appalachia, Kingsolver returns with a quieter tale of midlife longing and regret. A gifted pianist, Livia used music to escape the sadness of her family life in rural Tennessee, but having married and resettled in her home town, an unexpected call from a former lover drags her back into the past.
Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger
Jonathan Cape, 13 October
  Set a quarter of a century on, this long-awaited sequel focuses on the daughter of the couple in The Time Traveler’s Wife. Alba has inherited her father’s extraordinary condition, jumping unpredictably across the decades, from a United States in turmoil to a dystopian future London. She’s torn between two lovers – one anchored in the present, and one a time traveller like herself.
Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus
Manilla, 13 October
  In the follow-up to global bestseller Lessons in Chemistry, it’s 1982 New York and young Batter Gray lands a job at the eponymous poetry periodical, run by feuding twin brothers. Expect charm, quirk and literary rabbit holes.
![In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/aa9c8b59d38fbc5ee5aadd7d396c897348f135dd/0_0_654_1000/master/654.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak
Viking, 15 October
  From the Booker and Women’s prize-shortlisted author, a study of French writer Gustave Flaubert refracted through the lives of the women around him, including his most iconic creation: Madame Bovary.
Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li
   4th Estate, 22 October
  Set at the end of the 18th century, against a background of global tumult, the Pulitzer winner’s historical epic is inspired by the lives of two musicians: Adelaide Percheron, born in French India, and the Irish John Field, the inventor of the nocturne, who will be brought together by love and talent.
Lessons in Harmony by Jonathan Coe
Viking, 12 November
  Music is in the air this autumn: Coe’s latest follows the friendship between French dandy Maurice Ravel and English traditionalist Ralph Vaughan Williams, exploring creativity and national identity against the encroaching shadow of the first world war.
Crime and thrillers
Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple and George Smiley return
![CrimeColumnBooks](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0c9f6a7fccd74b0a5f1ef0b9263c39959ec19904/0_0_2953_2362/master/2953.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Autumn is back-to-school season for series authors, with William Boyd on the third of his cold war espionage novels starring travel writer Gabriel Dax. In Cold Sunset (Viking, 3 September) our reluctant spy is on his way to Russia, to tussle with the KGB. Richard Osman serves up number two in his We Solve Murders franchise: We Chase Shadows (Viking, 10 September) sees Steve, Amy and Rosie – retired cop, private security officer and bestselling crime author respectively – investigate after a body is found in the Italian hills. Five years on, Janice Hallett publishes a sequel to her hit am-dram debut The Appeal, as the Fairway Players’ new production of Agatha Christie leads to murder in The Silent Appeal (Viper, 3 September). The vigorous afterlife of the queen of crime continues elsewhere, with the first official new outing for Miss Marple, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, 22 September). A varied cast list, death on the mountaintop and plenty of suspects are guaranteed.
Ian Rankin, known for his grumpy Edinburgh detective John Rebus, takes a new direction in The Heights (Orion, 8 October), a standalone thriller set in a luxurious central London high-rise. And there’s a return to the world of John le Carré’s Circus in the latest from his son Nick Harkaway: in The Taper Man (Viking, 5 November), George Smiley finds himself navigating the unlikely terrain of 1960s LA in search of a communist sleeper agent.
Finally, a festive treat: 10 new adventures for the world’s most famous detective in short story anthology Sherlock (Simon & Schuster, 5 November), with contributors including Sarah Perry, Joe Hill, Abir Mukherjee and Kate Mosse.
Nonfiction
Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer 
Penguin Michael Joseph, 22 September
  Thirty years after Princess Diana was killed in a car crash, her brother – whose euology at her funeral echoed around the world – tells the story of their upbringing and recounts the devastating week of her death.
The Castle by Jon Ronson 
Viking, 20 August
  A concerning late-night call from his teenage son marks the start of a strange journey into modern masculinity for the journalist and author of The Psychopath Test and So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed.
The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown
Simon & Schuster, 1 September
  The former PM tries to join the dots between two seemingly disparate political phenomena: the erosion of the international rules-based order, exacerbated by war and climate breakdown, and the fragmentation of the tight-knit communities that keep us connected at a local level.
![The Great Dictator- A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6146e00e5791a57a87d37684bd1af5d43d8b0286/0_0_650_1000/master/650.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet 
Hodder & Stoughton, 10 September
  The queen of romance novels wrote a scarcely believable 723 of them during her career – with a little help from an amanuensis or two. Historian Sweet tells the extraordinary story of a woman born into an upper‑middle-class family fallen on hard times, who navigated scandal and opprobrium to become one of the bestselling writers of the 20th century.
Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History by Lucy Worsley 
Hodder & Stoughton, 3 September 
  The historian and chief curator of royal palaces brings a personal touch to some of British history’s pivotal moments, focusing on the places in which they unfolded, and in which Worsley herself has worked: Hampton Court, Kensington Palace and the Tower of London.
All the Wrong Moves by Anthony Scaramucci 
Bodley Head, 17 September
  Not many political figures are able to give Liz Truss a run for her money in the shortest-ever-tenure stakes, but Scaramucci, Trump’s press secretary for just 10 days, is one of them. Since then he’s reinvented himself as one of the administration’s sharpest critics. His first book is an attempt to chart how the US went from stable postwar consensus to today’s “shitshow politics”.
![End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/36d469ed614e95ebf35f912d81fb225b2bbce37d/0_0_311_500/master/311.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor 
Allen Lane, 15 September
  Thinkers and activists Klein and Taylor have identified a distinctive strand of rightwing nihilism: the kind that seeks to reshape the world in its image, even as it devours the natural resources on which our survival depends (certain tech barons and authoritarian leaders may feel particularly seen). Here they offer both a diagnosis and a plan for resistance.
Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Make a Difference? by Jared Diamond 
Mariner, 22 September
  The author of Guns, Germs and Steel, known for his analyses of the grand, impersonal forces that shape human destiny, returns with a timely book on the role of prominent individuals. What difference does a sports coach, a CEO or an erratic president really make to the fortunes of teams, companies and global civilisation?
An Unexpected Life: A Memoir by Gloria Steinem 
Ebury, 22 September
  A totemic figure in American feminism, Steinem sought to carry the momentum of the civil rights era into what became known as the women’s liberation movement. Here she writes about her childhood and political awakening, and reflects from the present moment on nearly 60 years of activism.
![(Left to right) Joe Biden, Colin Kaepernick, Naomi Klein, Malcolm Gladwell and Judi Dench.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/127920214e53fe6dbe162065caebb3402f4d84c1/0_0_2953_2362/master/2953.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Hawking: His Life and Work by Graham Farmelo
John Murray, 24 September
  In the first authorised biography of Stephen Hawking, Farmelo paints an intimate portrait of the acclaimed physicist based on unique access to his diaries and letters, as well as interviews with family and close associates.
The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic by Malcolm Gladwell
Abacus, 29 September
  The author of The Tipping Point asks why the United States has ended up being so much more violent than comparable countries around the world. From a Chicago ER to a 17th-century court case, he explores stories that may hold the key to what he describes as “the most pressing of all American social problems”.
![Blockers- Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8ea59f705d04f749d86b543d39ba8c5fa2aa46ef/0_0_650_1000/master/650.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis 
Allen Lane, 6 October
  Lewis’s pacy, high-stakes nonfiction has been drawing readers since 1989’s Liar’s Poker, an account of his time on Wall Street in the 1980s. Here he deploys his powers of narration to tell the story of how the US Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) sought to dismantle the state – though his real subject is the principled civil servants who stood in the way of Elon Musk’s campaign of vandalism.
Requiem for Gaza by Joe Sacco and Chris Hedges 
Jonathan Cape, 8 October 
  The master of graphic reportage and author of Palestine teams up with veteran war correspondent Hedges to document the devastating Israeli war on Gaza and its human impact. Interviewing 29 displaced Palestinian families, Sacco and Hedges tell stories of death, destruction and resilience.
The Perilous Fight by Colin Kaepernick
Grand Central Publishing, 8 October
  The NFL quarterback made history in 2016 when he knelt for the US national anthem, rather than standing. Since that time, “taking the knee” has become an emblem of the fight for racial justice, in the US and beyond. In his memoir, Kaepernick traces the relationships and experiences that culminated in a pivotal sporting and political moment.
![Promise Me, America by Joe Biden](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ebce8ea91d21a81b06b674d4ffbd2cb49e58eca9/0_0_265_400/master/265.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Promise Me, America by Joe Biden
John Murray, 17 November
  A year on from 107 Days, in which former vice-president Kamala Harris detailed her boss’s failure to get out of the way, Joe Biden tells his side of the story in a book which promises to reveal “the deeply agonising calculation behind his decision … to step aside from the presidential race”.
Pay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg
Corsair, 5 November 
  The former BBC political editor’s first book reflects on 20 years of upheaval in British politics, and what the broadcaster perceives as being at the root of it all: a failure by the political class to really listen to what people have actually been saying.
Holding Lightning: The Life, Loves and Art of Whitney Houston by Emily Lordi
White Rabbit, 1 October
  English professor Lordi treats the career of one of pop’s greatest stars with the seriousness it deserves, but with emotional intelligence too, tracing the arc of Houston’s life from global success to personal tragedy.
Memoir
From Hollywood hijinks to political scandal – life stories to look out for
![MemoirsColumnBooks](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bd677922fcab1aa95e8ce6ee874d3ce13fcc6d7f/0_0_2953_2362/master/2953.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It’s another bumper autumn for Hollywood stars with plenty of tales to tell – though this year skews male. Michael Douglas’s One Helluva Ride (Headline, 6 October) includes details of “affairs with some of the most celebrated actresses in Hollywood” and the “serious drug addiction that threatened to destroy his first marriage and career”. If you’re still in the mood for testosterone-laced hijinks after that, there’s Sylvester Stallone’s The Steps (Seven Dials, 29 September), which charts the Rocky star’s 1970s journey from homelessness to the Oscars. For a more multilayered take on acting and fame, try Fictional Selves by Kyle MacLachlan (Century, 29 September), whose talent in picking idiosyncratic roles such as such as Agent Cooper in Twin Peaks has earned him a cult following. And then there’s screen icon Dustin Hoffman, whose first memoir Look at Me (Gallery, 10 November), published as he prepares to enter his 10th decade, covers the pressures of being dubbed the “voice of a generation” after The Graduate, and his many acting roles since that extraordinary breakthrough. It would make a neat pairing with Watergate reporter Bob Woodward’s memoir Secrets (Simon & Schuster, 24 November): that era-defining scoop was dramatised in All the President’s Men, with Hoffman playing Woodward’s partner, Carl Bernstein.
On the other side of the Atlantic, Judi Dench reminisces about a 70-year career in Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? (Michael Joseph, 22 October). In Vigilauntie (W&N, 3 September) actor and co-creator of the groundbreaking sketch show Goodness Gracious Me, Meera Syal, writes about family, frustration and making it as an Asian woman on TV, while another veteran of the small screen, Russell T Davies, charts a writing career that has spanned Coronation Street and Doctor Who in The Queerest of Folk (Bantam, 8 October). Everyone’s favourite communist standup Alexei Sayle gets political in How I’ve Tried to Change the World (W&N, 3 September), a memoir of protest through the decades, while actual politician and scourge of the BNP in her Barking constituency, Margaret Hodge, shares the lessons of a life on the frontlines in Battle Axe (William Collins, 10 September).
summary: The upcoming autumn publishing season features a diverse array of new fiction, crime thrillers, and nonfiction releases. Notable works include fiction by acclaimed authors like Marlon James, Colm Tóibín, and Min Jin Lee, alongside highly anticipated crime sequels and anthologies. Nonfiction highlights range from Charles Spencer's memoir of Princess Diana to political and historical analyses by prominent writers.
key_points: Several acclaimed novelists return with major new fiction, including Marlon James, Colm Tóibín, and Barbara Kingsolver.
The crime and thriller genre features returning characters such as Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple, and George Smiley.
Nonfiction releases include Charles Spencer's personal book about his sister, Princess Diana, and memoirs from figures like Gloria Steinem.
Political and historical commentary features heavily in the autumn nonfiction lineup, with works by Gordon Brown, Naomi Klein, and Lucy Worsley.

title: Gillian Anderson on sex, death and saying no to Weinstein
author: Adam White
content:
Every week in the 1990s, Gillian Anderson would throw on a sensible, well-pressed pantsuit and face off against a parade of extraterrestrials and boogeymen. Being a famous woman of the Nineties, Anderson also found herself somewhat inevitably facing off against the era’s IRL boogeymen, such as Harvey Weinstein, the huffing, puffing uber-producer who shaped the film industry back then. He’d always want her to star in “scary things” for him, she once recalled, as if TV’s most prolific monster magnet would want nothing more than to replicate her day job on the big screen, too.
“I mean, he’d try to get me to do his films, period,” Anderson, 58, says today, with the cool, husky drawl of a Wild West gunslinger. She’s famously bidialectal, due to her upbringing between London and Grand Rapids, Michigan, and today is on a video call from France – a neutral ground, maybe, but one she’s chosen to speak with an American accent in. Anyway, she remembers her interactions with Weinstein always involving “a kind of bribery” with an element of quid pro quo. “He’d say, ‘if you do this for me, I’ll do that for you.’ That kind of thing.” She leans her head to her right, before firing off a very Dana Scully-coded roll of the eye. “I didn’t buy into that at all.”
Weinstein is invoked early in Anderson’s new erotic thriller, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, a glowy, sultry celebration of the slasher movie, which also doubles as a bit of a meta commentary on Anderson herself. Playing Billy Presley, a horror icon famed for a starring role in a B-movie film franchise, Anderson tells the prodigious young filmmaker (the actor and comedian Hannah Einbinder, of the acclaimed Hacks) hoping to work with her that she doesn’t scare easily – after all, Billy says, she auditioned for The Burning, a real-life Friday the 13th knock-off that served as Weinstein’s first producer credit.
Anderson’s casting in Camp Miasma is in tribute to writer and director Jane Schoenbrun’s early love of The X-Files. “That show took up probably 50 per cent of my imagination as a kid,” Schoenbrun tells me. “Gillian was always in my life back then, so there was this ephemeral feeling while working with her of having always known them, even though I’d just met them.”
Financiers want to hear a sob story. They always want a minority filmmaker to talk about how their life has been hard, and why they’re dysfunctional
Plus there’s the sex of it all. Camp Miasma is about horror, but it’s also about orgasms. The earliest thoughts of sexual longing felt by Kris, Einbinder’s character, came as she watched archetypal horror heroines flee from masked men – usually while dressed in their underwear, occasionally right before they were horribly butchered. It’s the kind of fantasy that would make Freud’s eye twitch, but also not trouble Anderson in the slightest. She’s about to publish her second collection of erotic fantasies, crowdsourced online. One woman wrote to her about wanting to be tied down by her own dentist; another admitted she craves the sexual freedom that would be instigated by her husband’s demise. In Camp Miasma, it is Billy who grants Kris the freedom to voice, then indulge, those fantasies of hers. It’s as if Anderson took her brilliantly frank sex therapist from Netflix’s Sex Education, drenched her in blood, then sent her overseas to save the world’s libidos one person at a time.
Upon receiving the Camp Miasma script, Anderson began to see the parallels. “It made perfect sense for me to play Billy,” she says, “because of how many layers of the role aligned with what I’ve been talking about quite avidly over the last years.” She gleefully stepped into what she terms “the meta world” of the film. “How bizarre that this would come into my life at this very moment,” she adds. “I felt like I had to do it.”
![Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson in ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/15/36/CampMiasma_Still_6_MUBI.jpeg)
It is May, and we’re speaking a few hours before Camp Miasma’s Cannes Film Festival premiere – where it would go on to earn raves, and ultimately take home the event’s Queer Palm award. Next to a glamorously coiffed Anderson is a groggy Einbinder, 31, who is valiantly persevering through a press junket despite being struck down with flu. Like Anderson, she saw herself in Camp Miasma. She identifies as bisexual, with Kris’s “emotional journey” mirroring hers as a young woman. “You start with discomfort, then shame, then liberation,” she says. “I related to it enormously.”
Kris, too, shares parallels with Jane Schoenbrun, who at 39 is the most exciting millennial filmmaker working today. They specialise in work that is spooky and nerdy and lightly otherworldly, rooted in pop culture ephemera and body horror both literal and supernatural. Their commercial breakthrough was 2024’s breathtaking I Saw the TV Glow, about two outcast teenagers drawn together by their shared love of a fictional supernatural drama called The Pink Opaque, which starts to bleed into reality.
Like Schoenbrun and their dysphoric 2021 thriller We’re All Going to the World’s Fair, Kris’s character in Camp Miasma debuted with a tiny independent film that was warmly received at the Sundance Film Festival – a remake of Psycho told from the perspective of the shower curtain. Also like Schoenbrun, who was sought out to direct a reboot of the flagging Leprechaun franchise (the 1993 original saw a terribly bewigged Warwick Davis chase around a pre-fame Jennifer Aniston), Kris is asked to take the reins of the long-dormant Camp Miasma movies (think an even grimier version of the Friday the 13th series). But unlike Schoenbrun, Kris accepts the movie offer, sending her down a rabbit hole with Billy that unlocks her own psychosexual malaise.
![Jane Schoenbrun, Anderson and Einbinder attend the LA premiere of ‘Camp Miasma’ in July](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/15/06/GettyImages-2288229038.jpeg)
Making Camp Miasma, Schoenbrun experienced a similar blossoming.
