They grew up watching horror movies that cast genderqueer or trans characters as sickos and deviants: think Psycho, The Silence of the Lambs, or the fascinatingly offensive Friday the 13th copy-paste Sleepaway Camp. “I knew that if I was to develop a more positive relationship to sex and to my own body, I had to return to those Buffalo Bills or Norman Bateses, who I loved as a young person but who also probably f***ed me up.”
Today, Schoenbrun stands alone in the Hollywood ecosystem, as the only out trans filmmaker commanding high budgets (relatively speaking, anyway) and major studio backing. It’s no exaggeration – even with The Matrix and Bound as her calling cards, Lilly Wachowski said this month that no one is willing to fund her $10m new indie. It’s a fact that Schoenbrun finds daunting. “The thing I’ve learnt is that financiers want to hear a sob story,” they explain. “They always want a minority filmmaker to talk about how their life has been hard, and why they’re dysfunctional.”
You basically have to fake it until you make it, Schoenbrun explains. “I’ve kind of mastered the language of the pitch meeting. I wouldn’t be sitting here if I hadn’t.” So in those rooms selling Camp Miasma, they leant into the critical acclaim they’d received for TV Glow, the fact that they’re a Sundance Film Festival fave, and that general audiences would love the big, attention-hogging idea of Gillian Anderson and Hannah Einbinder as lovers covered in blood. “It’s a process of making your work understandable to the world of capital, and that’s a very different process to actually making the thing,” they say. “They’re not going to care that much about gender transgression in the history of the horror film…”
![Ian Foreman in Jane Schoenbrun’s star-making 2024 movie ‘I Saw the TV Glow’](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/15/45/TV-GLOW_04.jpeg)
It explains why Camp Miasma is two films in one – the first is an easier-to-sell slasher satire with severed heads and impalings, the second is a tender, sexy love story flush with queer existentialism. Schoenbrun Trojan-horses us, essentially. “It’s a story of queer liberation,” they say, directly inspired by their own gender journey. I Saw the TV Glow was conceived in a period of trauma at the very beginning of their transition, which explains its occasional fatalism. Camp Miasma, comparatively, is the product of a period of joy. “I often compare transition to getting on an antidepressant,” they joke. “You deal with all of the s****y side effects first, and it takes a couple months before the good stuff starts. This movie was made from a place of full enjoyment with the good stuff – the joy, sex and euphoria of becoming myself.”
Schoenbrun cast Anderson because of The X-Files, and Einbinder because of the physicality she saw in her stand-up specials (“she commits her whole body to performance and not only performance but, like, weird performance”). But there’s also a cool, understated muscle to both actors that makes them evenly matched on-screen, as evidenced by Anderson’s run of steely, impervious women (she’s played everything from Margaret Thatcher in The Crown to A Streetcar Named Desire’s Blanche DuBois at the Young Vic), and in Einbinder’s off-camera activism. Einbinder is currently one of the most high-profile Jewish anti-Zionists working in Hollywood, with her continued advocacy for Palestine – as well as her leftist politics generally – earning her repeated drubbings from conservatives. She says that the industry is set up in a way that makes it consistently difficult to navigate ethically.
![Anderson and Einbinder in ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/21/15/20/CampMiasma_Still_5_MUBI.jpeg)
“Life under capitalism implicates an individual in systems that are evil,” Einbinder says. “End of story, you know what I mean? It’s something that torments me on a daily basis.” How does she get through it? “The way I make sense of it is just to continue to act in a way that is in line with my morals. So I do speak to those things and put action behind them. But it’s not straightforward, and it does eat me up.”
For Anderson, she doesn’t think her own story has involved any real fighting, even when I suggest it probably wasn’t easy to use her X-Files clout to make something like her dazzling adaptation of Edith Wharton’s The House of Mirth, and not whatever Weinstein had in mind for her.
“I’ve never allowed anyone to force me into anything that I didn’t want to do,” she says. “It’s more been about choosing to step away for a period of time, or do theatre, or do an indie film, as opposed to whatever your trajectory is meant to be.” As she says this though, she starts to have second thoughts... “It’s funny, only sometimes in retrospect does one realise there might have been a divine plan all along. I think I’ve always stayed on a path that makes sense for me at any given time. And ultimately you get to a point where you feel like, yes – this does represent who I am.”
“This”, at the moment at least, being Camp Miasma – a bloody, profound and sapphic love story soaked in weirdness and joy. It just feels right that Dana Scully found a home there, doesn’t it?
‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ is in cinemas
summary: Gillian Anderson stars alongside Hannah Einbinder in the erotic slasher thriller "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma," directed by Jane Schoenbrun. The film explores themes of horror, sexual liberation, and queer existentialism, paralleling aspects of the actors' and director's real lives. Anderson reflects on her past encounters with Harvey Weinstein, noting she consistently refused his quid pro quo advances and chose her own career path.
key_points: Gillian Anderson stars as horror icon Billy Presley in Jane Schoenbrun's erotic thriller "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma."
Anderson recounted that her past interactions with Harvey Weinstein involved bribery and quid pro quo attempts, which she firmly rejected.
Director Jane Schoenbrun conceived the film as a story of queer liberation and a joyful exploration of gender transition.
Hannah Einbinder stars alongside Anderson, drawing parallels between her own bisexual journey and her character's emotional arc.

title: FND: I was being treated for dehydration - when suddenly I couldn't move
author: Elaine McGee
content:
![Carmel is looking at the camera and is leaning against her hand. She is in a hospital setting and wires and tubes can be seen beside her. She is wearing a red top with white stripes and has short grey hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/0484/live/a5b39820-9d49-11f1-a3dc-c3f8cfe34ff8.jpg)
Carmel McConnellogue said she could not speak or feel her face and "everything was numb"
- Published
Carmel McConnellogue was in hospital, being treated by medical staff for dehydration, when she suddenly felt she could no longer move her body.
She said she could not speak or feel her face and "everything was numb".
Initial symptoms suggested McConnellogue might have had a stroke - but an MRI scan confirmed that she had Functional Neurological Disorder (FND), meaning there was was a problem with how her brain received and sent information to the rest of her body.
She said she never expected to be diagnosed with a condition she had never heard of.
"I could not believe it," she told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
"It was explained to me by a doctor that your brain is perfect but it's like a computer and it has too many tabs open.
"My brain went offline, and the body crashed."
McConnellogue, who was being treated at Altnagelvin Hospital in County Londonderry, was told that the condition was brought on by stress and trauma.
"I felt paralysed, trapped and I couldn't stop thinking â I can't move, what is going to happen to me?"
What is FND?
FND is estimated to affect 50,000-100,000 people in the UK.
It limits the brain and nervous system's ability to send and receive signals., external
Its underlying cause is not known, but some experts think it could be linked to stress, trauma or a response to a virus or other inflammatory condition.
Symptoms can vary from person to person, but can include limb weakness, paralysis, seizures, walking difficulties, spasms, sensory issues and cognitive problems.
Some people may experience short-lived symptoms, while other can have them for many years.
Most treatment options come in the form of rehabilitation therapy, according to NHS Inform.
This can include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, and psychological therapy.
![A woman using a zimmer frame to walk. She is wearing a navy vest top and has short grey hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/c230/live/d1dcfbd0-9d49-11f1-813f-d5ac18465183.jpg)
McConnellogue was told that the condition was brought on by stress and trauma
McConnellogue had no power in the left side of her body, and her speech was seriously impacted.
In the initial stages, she could not lift her legs or wiggle her toes.
She stayed in hospital for five weeks while therapists helped her regain her ability to move independently.
The road to recovery has been challenging for the life-long Derry City supporter.
Before her diagnosis, McConnellogue described herself as a "non-stop Duracell bunny, on the go 24/7".
"The physical part is very tough; I walk with a zimmer frame or a crutch and I have to be helped up the stairs, my husband has to physically put me to bed," she added.
She said the diagnosis had "floored" her and she had relied on counselling services to keep her going.
"My independence is gone. I cannot drive, I can't go to the shop on my own - all those things I took for granted," she said.
Country music singer Lisa McHugh spoke publicly last year about being diagnosed with FND.
According to the NHS, there is no cure for FND but it is treatable providing you adapt your life as much as possible to manage it.
McConnellogue has been sharing her recovery journey on social media.
"I do believe FND is misunderstood and I want people to know they are not alone," she said.
"It is a very real neurological condition, and I want to show others you can recover."
'Postcode lottery'
![A woman wearing a pink top looking at the camera. She is wearing a gold necklace and green glasses. She has red hair and earrings. There are red curtains behind her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a62f/live/0a6a36b0-9d55-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Helen Dickson was diagnosed with FND in 2022
FND Matters NI is the only FND charity in Northern Ireland.
The charity estimates there around 5,000 people living with FND in Northern Ireland but they have struggled to obtain specific figures as Northern Ireland's health trusts do not record FND as a primary condition.
Trustee Helen Dickson was diagnosed with the condition in 2022.
"Treatment for FND can be a postcode lottery," she said.
"More awareness and changes in attitudes are needed, and we need FND specific services.
"There can be a misconception that FND symptoms are imagined or 'all in someone's head' but it's very real."
She said healthcare professionals have asked the charity for advice.
![A woman smiling with her hands int he air wearing a red and white zipped up jacket. She has glasses and short brown hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/58b1/live/0bd97f20-9d4a-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
McConnellogue is a supporter of Derry City Football Club
The Department of Health has previously said in response to a question put forward at Stormont that precise numbers of patients with a diagnosis of FND are not currently captured due to limitations in coding and data systems.
The department estimates there are several thousand people in Northern Ireland with FND.
For Carmel McConnellogue, her next recovery goal is to be able to go to watch a football game.
"I am working towards being at Derry City's next home game, I have come through a lot in life and I will overcome FND," she vowed.
"I know my brain computer is going to come back online, and I will be at the Brandywell again."
summary: While being treated for dehydration in a hospital, Carmel McConnellogue suddenly lost the ability to move and speak, with initial symptoms pointing toward a stroke. An MRI confirmed she had Functional Neurological Disorder (FND), a condition where the brain struggles to properly send and receive signals. McConnellogue spent five weeks in the hospital undergoing rehabilitation and now relies on a zimmer frame and assistance from her husband. She is sharing her journey to raise awareness and hopes to overcome the condition.
key_points: Carmel McConnellogue was diagnosed with Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) after suddenly losing movement and speech while hospitalized for dehydration.
FND is a real neurological condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals, often compared to a computer with too many tabs open.
McConnellogue spent five weeks in the hospital and now requires mobility aids and assistance from her husband for daily tasks.
There is no cure for FND, but it can be treated through rehabilitation therapies and lifestyle adaptations.
Charities and patients in Northern Ireland highlight that FND treatment is a postcode lottery and that health trusts do not record FND as a primary condition.

title: Gillian Anderson wants you to have good sex – and her new film could help
author: Tori Brazier
content:
![This image released by Mubi shows Gillian Anderson, left, and Hannah Einbinder in a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442454-bcb4-e1787130307671.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Gillian Anderson is stepping into brand new territory with her latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, marking her first foray into horror.
And it’s far from your bog-standard fright flick, as a tongue-in-cheek homage to slashers combined with a bracingly bold take on female sexuality.
Just seconds in, there’s a fountain of vibrantly crimson blood shooting several feet in the air after a body is stabbed in a murderous frenzy.
‘It does, it feels that way,’ Anderson – who we’ve seen play roles as varied as Margaret Thatcher, a sex therapist and, of course, FBI Special Agent Dana Scully in The X-Files – tells Metro of her new direction with the movie.
‘It feels new and unique but I’m very proud of it, and proud to be a part of it. I just can’t wait for it to properly come out because I think people are really going to like it.’
Many already have since Cannes Film Festival in May, where it premiered, with five-star review raves from critics for the film dubbed a ‘bizarre pop-cultural black mass of fiercely believed-in trash and kink’ and a ‘Miasma-sterpiece’.
From I Saw the TV Glow’s Jane Schoenbrun, Camp Miasma’s premise sees intellectual young filmmaker Kris (Hannah Einbinder) hired to direct a rebooted instalment of a previously popular but now problematic ‘80s slasher franchise.
After becoming obsessed with casting the reclusive actress who played the original ‘final girl’ in the first film (Anderson) – and after tracking her down to the abandoned campground where the series used to film, and where she now lives – the two descend into sexual and psychological chaos together.
It won the Queer Palm and has steadily been building word of mouth buzz before reaching British shores this week.
‘When we were making it, we were really excited about the stuff we were getting and how it was looking and feeling. So to see that recognised feels really validating,’ shares Einbinder of the meta-slasher film’s reception so far.
But Camp Miasma isn’t just about gory spurting blood (although they both end up covered in it) and murder (although there is a lot of that), it’s also a lot about sex – and specifically women learning to revel in the pleasure of it.
![This image released by Mubi shows Hannah Einbinder in a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442311-6dfb.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
![This image released by Mubi shows a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442841-c267.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
This is a familiar topic for Anderson, who edited a collection of anonymous female sexual fantasies – including one of her own – for 2024 bestseller Want, with an ‘even more daring’ follow-up, fittingly titled More, being published next month. But pushing against the more squeamish boundaries placed on female sexuality and how it’s usually depicted isn’t why she signed up for the film, although she understands the surface-level connection.
‘I guess given that I’ve spent the last couple of years talking about fantasy and women’s sexuality and pleasure, it made a lot of sense as to why I would do it or be the one that was asked to do it. It felt ‘of a piece’,’ she accepts.
Camp Miasma’s focus on sex and death together, two things so intrinsically linked in slasher films, is something that Schoenbrun heavily leans into, calling the franchise’s ghostly recurring villain who lurks at the bottom of the lake ‘Little Death’. Meanwhile, Kris reveals that she can only shoot for an orgasm if she fantasises that she’s the sexualised ‘final girl’, a kink she developed from a formative childhood attachment to the first film starring Anderson’s Billy Presley – and which Billy suggests they explore together.
‘I think it’s important, what Jane is saying through this film. I know they [Schoenbrun] talk light-heartedly about just wanting it to lead to people having good sex – which of course is true and great! – but it’s so much deeper than that,’ adds Anderson. ‘And the depth and the narrative feels similar to what I hear from women through the book and conversations that I’ve had around it, in terms of women and sexuality and pleasure, and the complexities and shame.’
![Still from Mubi film Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma Starring Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson Unit Day 04: A Bad Day At Camp Tivoli](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308319978-404e.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Anderson and Einbinder share a very vulnerable and raw connection onscreen, which becomes at points almost mortifying to watch in its intimacy, as if the audience is intruding on something not meant for public consumption. But the actresses are both ten toes down with this, as the kids say.
‘It’s hard to build chemistry. I think you just have it or you don’t,’ says Einbinder. ‘Gillian and I also did such extensive preparation that when we came to start rehearsing the scenes, we both had a lot to offer. We had in-depth conversations about why we were doing what we were doing, and how we were doing it and why it was important for it to feel a certain way.’
Anderson also points out that, as there’s so much of the film that is ‘outside of the realms of reality’ in its meta murderous fantasy scenes, the elements of human intimacy ‘needed to feel as real and intimate as possible in order to balance out the rest of it’.
‘It felt important to get that aspect of it right. But it’s also a bit of a breath of relief, in a sense. Human relief, somehow,’ she adds.
Anderson makes a memorable entrance as glamorous faded star Billy, speaking with a Dolly Parton-esque drawl and exuding Sunset Boulevard vibes. I haven’t read a single review that doesn’t compare her to Norma Desmond.
‘I was trying to steer her away from Sunset Boulevard because that felt too obvious, almost – and I know that we made a choice of a turban at one point,’ admits Anderson. ‘But the accent was important to me from early on. That was a real gateway into her, it felt like it tied me to ‘final girl’ vibes in a way because the particular Southern [accent] has a lot of strength but a lot of vulnerability in it.’
![This image released by Mubi shows Gillian Anderson in a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442273-8bd6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
![This image released by Mubi shows Hannah Einbinder, left, and Gillian Anderson from the film "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442186-9369.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
But she speaks about ‘piecing together’ Billy in an extremely open and collaborative approach that also understands restrictions like budget. There’s no sense of Anderson’s bursting portfolio or awards pedigree (an Emmy and two Golden Globes, among others) giving her an attitude that she’s got this acting malarkey figured out enough to simply punch in and punch out every time.
‘Sometimes one has an idea in one’s head of what the personality is, what the wardrobe might be, all these different things – and then you show up and you are introduced to a wardrobe person, and they can only get what they can get.’
Anderson suggested the dramatic Twiggy-inspired eye make-up, while Schoenbrun prompted Billy’s deep, back-of-the-throat cackle, which the actress ably (and slightly alarmingly) demonstrates again.
‘That says so much about who she is and her spirit and her personality, and not in a million years would I imagine that she might have done that!’ laughs Anderson. ‘But the fact that, all of a sudden, that was entered into the collection of character traits takes you on a whole other journey in terms of her.’
Anderson is also working alongside Einbinder, who – despite her own Emmy success with hit comedy series Hacks – is remarkably only taking on her second-ever acting role here, after the HBO show, having previously worked as a stand-up comic.
![This image released by Mubi shows Hannah Einbinder in a scene from "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma." (Ryan Plummer/Mubi via AP)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307442253-f210.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Einbinder, quick to giggle at her co-star and quietly deferential as they sit together, learned a lot about character work from her.
‘Gillian has such a clear process. She wants to really understand her physical choreography and motivations. Just watching her craft Billy, I feel it gave me permission to really dive into wanting Kris to feel even more real and to make distinct choices,’ Einbinder recalls. ‘Approaching this was so different because Ava in Hacks and I have more crossover, especially in her physical affect, so this was definitely a new process for me to just really, really feel unlike my actual self.’
- 
	![Jacob Elordi as Hig and Jasper in 20th Century Studios' THE DOG STARS. Photo by Fabio Lovino. ?? 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved (Picture: Fabio Lovino)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309021192-0ff4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=493px%2C396px%2C1621px%2C913px&resize=646%2C363)
- Holly Willoughby just wants to see 'normal fannies' in porn
- BBC DJ Trevor Nelson reveals brain tumour diagnosis in update after stepping down
- Pop singer dies aged 30 after freak accident in bathroom
This year has been a stellar one for horror, with Einbinder acknowledging an even more appreciative public appetite for it, thanks to the huge success of Backrooms and Obsession.
Cannes also gave a major platform to The Substance the year prior to Camp Miasma, and it ended up a five-time Oscar nominee. Anderson brings up Get Out too, when we discuss the genre’s resurgence and the sense of a shift in the industry towards taking it more seriously as well.
‘I do absolutely feel that way,’ says Einbinder, before adding with a laugh: ‘Hopefully we’re contributing!’
Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma releases in UK cinemas on Friday, August 21.
![Film](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Film-Chris-Hemsworth-448b.png?quality=90&strip=true)
summary: Gillian Anderson stars alongside Hannah Einbinder in Jane Schoenbrun's new meta-slasher horror film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. The movie combines a tongue-in-cheek homage to '80s horror franchises with a bold exploration of female sexuality, pleasure, and the complexities of shame. After premiering and receiving critical acclaim at the Cannes Film Festival, where it won the Queer Palm, the film is set for its UK theatrical release.
key_points: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma marks Gillian Anderson's first foray into the horror genre.
The meta-slasher film was directed by Jane Schoenbrun and co-stars Hannah Einbinder.
The movie explores the intersection of sex and death while focusing on women learning to revel in sexual pleasure.
The film received rave reviews and won the Queer Palm following its premiere at the Cannes Film Festival.

title: Brandon Flowers Goes Country But Gets a Little Lost on the Back Roads
author: Jon Dolan
content:
![Brandon Flowers](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
Ever since Bob Dylan cut Nashville Skyline in 1969, rockers have been going to Music City to refresh their sounds, kick it with the world’s best session pros, and drink deep the rejuvenating well of local realness. For his third solo album, Killers frontman Brandon Flowers has gone all-in with a full-fledged country record. He says the music harkens back to his Utah youth listening to Waylon Jennings and Johnny Cash (music his dad called “country Western”), and he’s hired some A-list hands to help out, including guitarist David Rawlings — who’s made excellent records alongside Gillian Welch — and octogenarian harmonica great Charlie McCoy, who literally played on Nashville Skyline. As a neo-New Wave guy with a heartland jones and drama-king chops, Flowers isn’t bad cosplaying his heroes, even if his brawny rock-opera vocal approach is a bit short on the conversational warmth that makes for truly memorable country singing.
As with the Killers, he blasts away as over-the-top as ever, drunk on sweeping Americana imagery and marveling at the sound of his voice booming across those sweet Nashville studios. He tries his luck with some rollicking cosmic philosophizing on “Does It Ever Cross Your Mind” and “One of Us,” and it more or less works. Backed by strings, spacious twang, and mariachi horns, the sweet highlight “Red Ground” beautifully argues for a more traditionally economic notion of his historical reenactment. And he flips back into straight-up rock on “Tiger’s Blood,” a gentle vignette about life in a Podunk town that turns into a big, hungry-hearted Killers-style anthem.
But the mystery train starts veering off the rails as Flowers wanders away from enjoyable rhinestone reinvention and defaults to the heavy-handed Springsteenian realism that’s sometimes been both his Rosetta stone and his Achilles’ heel. On “Miss America” he plays a rural beauty aging into her harsh consignment in the methy underbelly of the American mythscape — “You used to call me Miss America/ Before you got hooked on speed.” On the wind-swept epic “Angel” we’re gifted wisdom along the lines of “Some fit the mold like a book on a shelf/Some are hard-wired for something else.” He officially loses the plot on the closer, “An American Dream,” wandering the lonely lost highway piling up clichéd rambling-man reckonings until he bumps into Elvis himself, driving a Tesla Model X for some reason. “He laughed when I asked him if it was all worth it/And he cried when he asked me about Lisa Marie.” And there’s the issue: These songs aren’t quite strong enough to be this epically melodramatic, but they’re not self-aware enough to be as funny as you hope they might be.
summary: The Killers frontman Brandon Flowers ventures into country music for his third solo album, collaborating with notable session musicians like David Rawlings and Charlie McCoy. While tracks like "Red Ground" and "Tiger's Blood" showcase strong moments, the album ultimately falters when it leans too heavily into melodrama and heavy-handed realism. As it progresses, the record loses its direction with clichéd lyrics and bizarre narratives, lacking both the strength to be truly epic and the self-awareness to be funny.
key_points: Brandon Flowers released a full-fledged country solo album inspired by his Utah youth and artists like Waylon Jennings and Johnny Cash.
The album features contributions from A-list musicians, including guitarist David Rawlings and harmonica player Charlie McCoy.
Highlights include the sweet track "Red Ground" and the rock-infused "Tiger's Blood."
The record struggles when Flowers relies on heavy-handed Springsteenian realism and over-the-top melodrama.
The album's closer features an eccentric narrative encounter with Elvis driving a Tesla Model X.

title: Jimmy Cricket’s Catholic priest son jokes at funeral it’s ‘not the first time I’ve see him die’
author: Casey Cooper-Fiske; Press Association Senior Entertainment Reporter
content:
Comedian Jimmy Cricket’s son has joked it “isn’t the first time I’ve seen him die” as he led his funeral service.
The joke came as his funeral requiem mass began at Salford Cathedral on Friday, following the Northern Irish comic, born James Mulgrew’s death on August 3 at the age of 80 following his battle with a short illness.
The ceremony was attended by comedy veterans such as Syd Little, Tommy Cannon and Roy Walker and led by Cricket’s youngest son Father Frankie Mulgrew, who once worked as his road manager but is now a Catholic priest.
During the service Father Frankie said: “I just want to say this, this isn’t the first time I’ve seen him die, and rise again, comedy metaphor, it’s a comedy metaphor.
![Roy Walker arrives for the funeral of stand-up comedian Jimmy Cricket](https://www.irishnews.com/resizer/v2/QQIGMCAYNNNRTOWF2GJ5L7L4JQ.jpg?auth=67c11d171b098693eac350923d9490d170171f17ede21f5642f4ae7296715a04&width=800&height=1200)
“Friends, about 20 years ago, my dad said, ‘I will sacrifice grandchildren, you go into the priesthood’.”
Cookstown born Cricket, who was known for his signature bowler hat and catchphrase “And there’s more”, became a TV staple in the 80s, appearing in programmes such as The Good Old Days as well as the Royal Variety Performance.
![Tommy Cannon arrives for the funeral of stand-up comedian Jimmy Cricket](https://www.irishnews.com/resizer/v2/EQ5ECB46T5J7NDMDA6WQI4YNY4.jpg?auth=f6f7e74b6a278db205a34da2aa8e78ac30a8fdc42d2d13f906bc2c14a3b1572c&width=800&height=1147)
The star left school at 16 and spent his summers working as Redcoat camp host at Butlins holiday camps.
He went on to work the comedy club scene throughout the 1970s and 1980s, going on to win LWT’s Search For A Star talent contest before getting his own ITV show, And There’s More, which ran for four seasons.
He later fronted his own programme on BBC Radio 2 before appearing on the Royal Variety Show in the 80s and performing in a number of pantomimes.
summary: Comedian Jimmy Cricket's funeral took place at Salford Cathedral following his death at the age of 80. The service was led by his youngest son, Catholic priest Father Frankie Mulgrew, who humorously remarked during the mass about seeing his father 'die and rise again' as a comedy metaphor. The funeral was attended by numerous comedy veterans, celebrating the life of the Northern Irish comic known for his signature bowler hat and catchphrase.
key_points: Comedian Jimmy Cricket died at age 80 following a short illness.
His funeral requiem mass was held at Salford Cathedral and led by his son, Father Frankie Mulgrew.
Father Frankie joked during the service that it was not the first time he had seen his father 'die' in a comedy metaphor.
Comedy veterans including Syd Little, Tommy Cannon, and Roy Walker attended the ceremony.
Jimmy Cricket was a prominent TV and comedy star in the 1970s and 1980s, known for his signature bowler hat and catchphrase.

title: Edward Bluemel Is Agatha Christie’s Hercule Poirot in BBC, BritBox First-Look Image for ‘Hercule’
author: Georg Szalai
content:
![](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-hollywoodreporter-2021/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
![Edward Bluemel as a young Hercule Poirot in 'Hercule'](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Hercule-Mammoth-Screen-H-2026.jpg?w=2000&h=1126&crop=1) 
Hercule Poirot is here. Well, not quite yet — but a first look at him is.
The BBC and BritBox revealed first-look images of Edward Bluemel (My Lady Jane, Killing Eve, Sex Education, A Discovery of Witches) as a young Hercule Poirot in the upcoming six-part series Hercule from Mammoth Screen and Agatha Christie Ltd. on Friday. Check them out in the main image of this article and a shot from a bit more of a distance below.
The series, which has started filming in Liverpool, is described as “an intimate study of Hercule Poirot, the man, and an epic portrait of Britain between the wars.” Hercule will center around three of Christie’s early stories of the Belgian detective, while also introducing the famous sleuth to future friends and allies and, according to a synopsis, “one particular nemesis …”
Related Stories
![Prince Harry arrives at court on Jan. 21.](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-hollywoodreporter-2021/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
![Prince Harry and Meghan Markle](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-hollywoodreporter-2021/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
Previously unveiled to join Bluemel in the cast of the new series were Henry Ashton (A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, A Good Girl’s Guide to Murder), James D’Arcy (Oppenheimer, Constellations), Calvin Demba (Supacell, Life), Phil Dunning (Smoggie Queens, Am I Being Unreasonable?), Jack Gleeson (House of Guinness, In the Land of the Saints and Sinners), Tamsin Greig (Riot Women, Friday Night Dinner), James Nesbitt (Cold Feet, Run Away), Guy Remmers (The Buccaneers, Lessons), Rebecca Rittenhouse (His & Hers, Maggie) and Mawaan Rizwan (Juice, The Split Up).
Christie’s Poirot novels have sold more than 750 million copies. Hercule is produced by Mammoth Screen, part of ITV Studios, and Agatha Christie Ltd. for BBC iPlayer and BBC One in the U.K., as well as BritBox in North America in 2027.
Written by Benji Walters (Code of Silence, The Leopard, Obsession), the first two episodes are being directed by Jonny Campbell (Am I Being Unreasonable?, In the Flesh), with Chanya Button (Code of Silence, Doctor Who) and Alrick Riley (Bridgerton, How to Get Away With Murder) directing the middle two and final two episodes, respectively. Charlie Palmer (A Woman of Substance, Extraordinary) serves as series producer.
![](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-hollywoodreporter-2021/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
The executive producers are Walters and Campbell, James Prichard for Agatha Christie Ltd., Rebecca Durbin and Damien Timmer for Mammoth Screen, Nick Lambon for the BBC and Robert Schildhouse, Jon Farrar and Stephen Nye for BritBox.
Fifth Season is handling global distribution for Hercule.

title: Harry was always going to return to UK – with or without Meghan, ex-butler says
author: Lucy Leeson
content:
Prince Harry’s shock return to the UK has always been on the cards, a former royal butler has claimed, pointing to the Duke’s close bond to his father, King Charles, during his childhood.
Speaking exclusively to The Independent, Grant Harrold said Harry was a “daddy’s boy” in his youth and it was only a matter of time before he returned to rebuild his relationship with his father after the rift caused when he and Meghan dramatically quit royal life six years ago.
But he cautioned that the Duchess of Sussex would likely struggle with her return to the UK, and suggested her husband could have given her “an ultimatum” on coming back to Britain.
And he warned that Prince William would likely be “furious” with his brother’s return after their public fallout, following Harry’s barrage of accusations against him, Kate, the King and Queen Camilla in his memoir, Spare.
Mr Harrold, who worked closely with William and Harry until 2011, said: “Harry was always going to return to the UK to be near his father. When you have a loved one going through different things to do with health and all sorts of other things, it makes you wonder if he [Harry] just wants to be closer.
“Everyone goes on about the close bond between the King and William but Harry was always a daddy’s boy. He was very much a daddy’s boy when I was there. He had an extraordinary relationship with his dad.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/20/9/48/GettyImages-1129888236.jpeg)
The former royal butler believes the King will be pleased to have his son back in the UK, giving him more opportunities to spend time with his grandchildren, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, although he suggests Charles will also remain wary.
“There’s again rumours of TV shows and all sorts going on. Does that mean Harry will speak to his father and then they [Harry and Meghan] will sit down and have a conversation about it? That is the reality and what they will be thinking,” says Mr Harrold.
But the news of Harry and Meghan’s return to the UK is unlikely to have gone down well with the Prince of Wales, Mr Harrold said, who pointed to the Duke’s previous press interviews and claims in Spare that his brother physically attacked him during a row.
“William will be furious,” he said. “Harry has said some extraordinary things about the family.
“William is somebody that when you break trust and you go beyond a certain point, there's no going back. Before, William would have said 'he's 5,000/6,000 miles away and it's not my problem, he's in another country'. But now he's suddenly back on the doorstep. I just don't think he's going to be happy about the situation at all."
![Grant Harrold, also known as The Royal Butler, worked for the King and Queen Camilla, as well as Prince William, Princess Kate and Prince Harry up until 2011.](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/21/12/10/S30Z3DWZ_400x400-(5).jpeg>)
News broke on Wednesday that Prince Harry and Meghan were returning to the UK within weeks after six years across the pond to make their home in a non-royal residence outside London. It is understood the couple have already enrolled their children in British schools.
According to reports on Friday, the Duchess of Sussex could also make a return to acting.
But Mr Harrold, speaking on behalf of OLBG, believes Meghan will struggle to resettle in the UK after finding her time here as a working royal tough with intense media scrutiny.
He said: “I think she will hate it, because from what we understand and the way it’s come across she didn’t like it here,” Mr Harrold says. “I am not saying she doesn’t like visiting here, but this is another story. She’s close to her mother back home, so I think it is going to be a really difficult move for Meghan.
![Harry and William have been estranged since Harry levelled a barrage of claims against the royal family](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/20/13/12dfee705e9f61452db70ce54fa9b5a1Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MzE0NjUz-2.68747482.jpg)
“I’m wondering if Harry gave her an ultimatum after reading reports of that he wants to be closer to his father given what is going on in his life. Maybe Harry woke up one morning and thought ‘I need to be with my dad in this part of his life’. He could have turned around to Meghan and gave her the ultimatum and said ‘come with me or stay’. I don’t think Harry was going to stay in the US, it could be as simple as that.”
Despite the reported fallout between William and Harry, Mr Harrold believes there is still hope of a reconciliation, saying "time is a healer" and relationships can be repaired.
He believes the Princess of Wales can play a key role as a peacemaker, helping to heal relations between the family.
“I think Catherine will be concerned by the situation, but she’s a very diplomatic lady and what she will be trying to do is be the peacemaker and trying to look at the positives of the situation, and I am guessing she will also be trying to reassure William,” he said.
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan are reportedly returning to the UK to make their home outside London after spending six years in the US, according to former royal butler Grant Harrold. Harrold claims Harry's strong childhood bond with King Charles motivated his desire to be closer to his father, while noting that Meghan may struggle with the move and Prince William will likely be furious due to past public fallouts. However, Harrold suggests that Princess Kate could potentially act as a peacemaker to help repair family relations over time.
key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan are returning to live in the UK after six years in the US, with their children already enrolled in British schools.
Former royal butler Grant Harrold states that Harry was a 'daddy's boy' and wanted to return to be closer to King Charles.
Prince William is expected to be furious about Harry's return following past public accusations made against the royal family.
Grant Harrold suggests Meghan may struggle with resettling in the UK due to previous intense media scrutiny.
Princess Kate could potentially act as a diplomatic peacemaker to help heal the rift within the royal family.

title: Why child stars like Hayden Panettiere fall into addiction
author: Madeline Halpert
content:
![Hayden Panettiere](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/21ae/live/441fda80-9a77-11f1-b68f-817a5a696299.jpg)
- Published
Hayden Panettiere was 16 when drugs first arrived in her life in Hollywood.
Ahead of a red carpet event for the hit series Heroes, she has said someone on her team handed her a pill to help amp up her energy. The hit sci-fi NBC series had catapulted the teen into a household name - and that brought with it intense pressure and exhaustion she says felt overwhelming.
"Within minutes, a wave of energy washed over me, like I'd just woken up from the most refreshing night's sleep of my life," Panettiere wrote about that pill in her memoir, which was released just months before her death.
She called it "the gateway drug that ushered me toward the good of pharmaceuticals and the downfall of addiction".
The star's sudden death at the age of 36 has placed a renewed focus on her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, and re-ignited a discussion about the pressures of Hollywood on child stars.
The coroner's office in Greenville, South Carolina said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma".
No cause of death has been released, though additional tests are yet to be completed.
Audio from police dispatchers and crews who responded to the address said they were responding to a "cardiac arrest" and detailed their efforts to resuscitate the woman after a possible "overdose". Panettiere's ex boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack, were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report.
There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on their part, according to police.
It is not known if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, but the US Drug Enforcement Agency is joining an investigation into her death, according to US media reports.
Panettiere is one of many actors who has openly struggled with addiction after exposure to fame at an early age, which addiction experts told the BBC can put people at risk for mental health and substance abuse issues.
It can sometimes seem to the rest of the world that child actors have "everything" at their fingertips - like fame and money, said Lucas Trautman, the medical director of Oxford Treatment Center, an addiction treatment centre in Mississippi.
"But it's important to remember that they were also exposed during a developmental time to many adult aspects of life that the rest of us weren't - including traumatic experiences - and so that gives them unique risk factors for addiction," Trautman said.
Panettiere's death comes after she published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction, her postpartum depression and the loss of her 28-year-old brother.
Panettiere's decision to publicly share her struggles is worthy of respect, said William Moyers, the vice-president of public affairs for Hazelden Betty Ford, the largest nonprofit addiction treatment provider in the US. But he said the constant public scrutiny she faced may not have allowed her room to address her mental health in private.
"Her entire life from the beginning was centred in the intense public spotlight, and this didn't give Hayden much in the way of a respite," said Moyers, who has been in recovery from an addiction since 1989.
Trautman - who has treated child stars - said they often have "adult access" to drugs and alcohol without adult protection.
"We aren't equipped at a young age to be able to say no to it, to manage it, to correctly stay away from it altogether," he said.
Other child stars have talked about being exposed to drugs at an early age, including Drew Barrymore, who went to rehab at 12, and Demi Lovato, a Disney Channel star.
"I got into a car accident and they prescribed me opiates. My mum didn't think she would have to lock up the opiates from her 13-year-old daughter, but I was already drinking at that point," the singer told podcast Call Her Daddy in 2022.
Actress Michelle Rodriguez, who once hosted the World Music Awards with Panettiere, said this week that the number of child actors who had passed away at a young age was strange.
"I just can't stand how many young people are leaving us lately. It's disheartening, and it's making me think, 'What's going on?' It's not normal," she told Variety.
Panettiere's death comes just a year after the death of Michelle Trachtenberg and months after Daveigh Chase, two child stars who both struggled with drugs and alcohol.
In an essay she wrote after Panettiere's death, former Disney star Christy Carlson Romano compared early fame to a traumatic brain disease.
"[W]e have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood," she wrote.
Watch: Hayden Panettiere on her career and growing up in the spotlight
And when a child actor's career changes or comes to an end, they are left without the dopamine of fame and money that came with their identity as an actor, cautioned Trautman.
"At the same time many of them self medicated... so their brain is still reliant on that, and it's really really hard to to stop using," he said.
Many child stars also have professional relationships with their parents, which can blur boundaries and leave them vulnerable, Trautman said.
In her book and in the media, Panettiere has discussed the pressure her mother placed on her to excel as an actress from an early age. She appeared in her first commercial when she was just 11-months-old.
"You always want to think the best of your parents and see them in the brightest light," the actress told the New York Times in May. "But there were a lot of things done with an approach that was not about my mental health or what was emotionally or mentally safe for me to do."
Substance abuse also puts people at risk for a host of medical conditions, including heart disease and liver and other organ damage.
Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition, and Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother was using heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.
But after he died, the actress told People Magazine in 2024 she was committed to staying sober, telling the outlet her addiction was "in the rear view mirror".
She said in her book that at one point a doctor told her that if she did not stop drinking, she would be "dead within five years".
For Moyers and other substance abuse experts, addiction is a chronic illness, meaning that relapses still happen even while treatment saves lives.
"Living in recovery means doing the best we can, but doing it imperfectly," he said.
summary: Hayden Panettiere has died at the age of 36, reigniting discussions about the immense pressures and substance abuse challenges faced by child stars in Hollywood. Her sudden death followed a published memoir detailing her struggles with addiction, which she traced back to being handed a pill on a red carpet team at age 16. Emergency services responded to a cardiac arrest at the scene, and while no cause of death has been released yet, the DEA has joined the investigation.
key_points: Hayden Panettiere passed away at the age of 36, with emergency responders treating her for cardiac arrest.
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency joined an investigation into her death, though the official cause of death has not yet been released.
Panettiere previously wrote in her memoir that her substance abuse began at age 16 when someone on her team gave her a pill to boost her energy.
Addiction experts note that child stars are uniquely vulnerable to mental health and substance abuse issues due to early exposure to fame, trauma, and adult environments without adequate protection.

title: Jason Statham goes full Die Hard at sea - Splash247
author: Sam Chambers
content:
![](https://splash247.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/MutinyPosterFinal-780x470.jpg) 
Jason Statham’s latest action movie, Mutiny, puts the British hardman aboard a containership packed with mercenaries, with much of the maritime action filmed not on a studio set but aboard an actual 30-year-old feeder.
Statham plays Cole Reed, a former special forces operative and cop turned private security contractor who is framed for the murder of his billionaire shipping tycoon boss. His escape route is one of the company’s containerships, where things rapidly deteriorate into the sort of confined-space mayhem Statham has made a career out of.
The floating film set was the 1,042 teu Sky Light, a 149 m boxship built at Szczecin in Poland in 1996.
Transport Malta issued notices to mariners ahead of filming in October and November 2024, confirming that shooting would take place aboard the ship at Malta Freeport, Valletta and offshore on Malta’s east coast. Other vessels were instructed to give Sky Light and its support craft room during filming.
The ship has had a rather more eventful career than the average Hollywood prop.
Now Vanuatu-flagged, Sky Light is 12,380 dwt and has traded under a string of names including CGM Jean Laborde, MSC Biscay and Mekong Spirit.
It was under the latter name that the vessel once appeared on the US sanctions list in connection with Iran-linked Hafiz Darya Shipping Company. Washington removed IMO 9118513 from its Specially Designated Nationals list in November 2011.
Mutiny, directed by Jean-François Richet, the man behind Plane, runs for 95 minutes and reaches US cinemas today.
Reviews have inevitably reached for comparisons with the great enclosed-location action movies, with The Times describing its finale as heading into “Die Hard-style” territory.
John McClane got Nakatomi Plaza. Jason Statham gets a 1,042 teu feeder.
summary: Jason Statham stars as a framed security contractor in the action movie Mutiny, which is largely set aboard an actual containership. The film, directed by Jean-François Richet, was shot on location in Malta using a 30-year-old vessel named Sky Light. Reviewers have compared the confined-space action and finale of the 95-minute movie to classic enclosed-location films like Die Hard.
key_points: Jason Statham plays Cole Reed, a former special forces operative framed for murdering his billionaire shipping tycoon boss.
Much of the maritime action was filmed aboard the actual 30-year-old feeder containership Sky Light in Malta.
Transport Malta issued notices to mariners ahead of filming in late 2024.
The 1,042 teu vessel has previously traded under names such as CGM Jean Laborde, MSC Biscay, and Mekong Spirit.
The 95-minute movie is directed by Jean-François Richet and features a Die Hard-style finale.

title: Meghan reportedly in talks to join Guy Ritchie’s TV series The Gentlemen
author: Benjamin Lee
content:
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to make her acting return in Netflix’s hit series The Gentlemen.
According to Variety, Meghan is in discussions to join the third season, which has yet to receive an official greenlight. The Gentlemen is a spin-off from the 2019 crime comedy of the same name with Guy Ritchie acting as creator of both.
Meghan’s role in the show is as-yet-unknown, with a contract reportedly still not in place and no official announcement.
Reports have emerged quickly after news that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex would relocate to the UK from the US, where they have lived for six years. It is believed that they will return in September, with early rumours suggesting it was related to Meghan’s return to acting.
Meghan’s best-known acting role was in the legal drama Suits, in which she played the character Rachel Zane for seven seasons. Her other small-screen appearances include CSI: NY and 90210, while film roles have included a small part in the comedy Horrible Bosses and 2015’s crime thriller Anti-Social. She also led two Hallmark movies: When Sparks Fly and Dater’s Handbook.
She recently filmed a cameo playing herself in the Amazon comedy Close Personal Friends alongside Brie Larson and Jack Quaid.
Harry and Meghan had previously signed a deal with Netflix in 2020 worth a reported $100m. It was renewed last year.
Meghan’s main release with the streamer was lifestyle series With Love, Meghan. The show received negative reviews from many critics, with the Guardian’s Chitra Ramaswamy calling it “toe-curling stuff” in a one-star review.
In a 2022 interview, Meghan claimed a return to acting was unlikely. “I’m done,” she said. “I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not.”
The first season of The Gentlemen proved to be a hit with both critics and audiences for Netflix. The second season will premiere in September with returning cast members Theo James and Kaya Scodelario joined by Love Island host Maya Jama.
summary: The Duchess of Sussex is reportedly in discussions to join the third season of Netflix's hit series The Gentlemen, created by Guy Ritchie. Her potential role remains unknown, and a contract is not yet in place as the upcoming season has not received an official greenlight. This news follows reports that the Duke and Duchess are planning to relocate back to the UK from the US.
key_points: Meghan is in talks to appear in the third season of Netflix's The Gentlemen.
The third season has not yet received an official greenlight and no contract is in place.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are reportedly planning to relocate to the UK from the US.
Meghan's best-known acting role was playing Rachel Zane in the legal drama Suits.

title: Jacob Elordi Ducks James Bond Question at London World Premiere of Ridley Scott’s ‘The Dog Stars’ When Asked if He’s Been Auditioning: ‘I’m Here on Holiday’
author: Alex Ritman
content:
Jacob Elordi was the star guest in London on Thursday night as he touched down for the world premiere of Ridley Scott‘s latest feature “The Dog Stars.”
The actor’s arrival in Leicester Square was immediately soundtracked by the noise of screams from fans, including from a group of girls leaning out of nearby window, who dramatically upped both their volume and pitch when the actor turned to wave at them. The actor also sparked swoons when he walked and posed on the carpet with Rak Jasper, one of three acting dogs who appear in the movie.
Alongside Elordi, “The Dog Stars'” other cast — including Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley and Guy Pearce — were in attendance at the Odeon Luxe cinema, together with the legendary director himself (who premiered his last movie, “Gladiator 2,” in the same spot less than two years ago).
Popular on Variety
Speaking to Variety, Elordi described Scott as “the king of movies,” saying that working with him was “such a treat — a dream come true.”
He added: “I don’t think I’ll ever have an experience like that. Yeah. He’s one of a kind and he’s a pioneer of of modern cinema.”
With the casting for James Bond now very much underway and Elordi continuing to have a strong presence among the favorites for the coveted role, Variety also managed to sneak in a question about whether he’d been involved in the auditions. It was a query he, clearly with some experience now under his belt, expertly ducked. “I’m here on holiday,” he said with a smile.
![](https://variety.com/wp-content/themes/pmc-variety-2020/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) 
“The Dog Stars,” from Disney’s 20th Century Studios, is a post-apocalyptic sci-fi, directed by Scott from a screenplay by Mark L. Smith and based on Peter Heller’s 2012 novel of the same name. The film is set in the aftermath of a devastating flu pandemic that has almost eradicated humanity, and follows a former civilian pilot and hardened ex Marine as they confront outside threats and hold onto the possibility of a better life.
Ironically, Scott had originally eyed his “Gladiator 2” leading man Paul Mescal for the main role, but he had to drop out due to scheduling conflicts with the Beatles’ biopics, and Elordi stepped in.
Speaking to Empire Magazine before the premiere, Brolin said that he almost quit “The Dog Stars” after just one day due to Scott’s intense filmmaking process. “It bugged me out, and I got really scared,” he said, adding that he called his agent to say “I want out. Something’s really wrong and I’ve got to get the f— out of here.”
However, he said things settled eventually down enough for him to continue, describing Scott’s approach as “stratospherically creative and stratospherically dangerous.”
“The Dog Stars” will release in theaters on Aug. 28.
summary: Actor Jacob Elordi attended the London world premiere of Ridley Scott's post-apocalyptic sci-fi film "The Dog Stars," alongside co-stars Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley, and Guy Pearce. On the red carpet, Elordi deflected a question regarding whether he has been auditioning for the role of James Bond, claiming he was simply in town on holiday. The 20th Century Studios film, adapted from Peter Heller's 2012 novel, is scheduled for a theatrical release on August 28.
key_points: Jacob Elordi starred at the London world premiere of Ridley Scott's "The Dog Stars" in Leicester Square.
When asked by Variety if he was auditioning to play James Bond, Elordi smiled and stated he was "here on holiday."
"The Dog Stars" is a post-apocalyptic sci-fi film based on Peter Heller's 2012 novel and is set to release on August 28.
Josh Brolin revealed he nearly quit the film after one day due to Scott's intense filmmaking process before ultimately deciding to stay.
Elordi stepped into the main role after Paul Mescal dropped out due to scheduling conflicts with Beatles biopics.

title: Tupac murder trial: Accused told police in 2008 his nephew fired fatal shots
author: Angus Thompson
content:
![Duane "Keffe D" Davis appears in court for his murder trial in Las Vegas](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/37e6/live/437eb910-9d57-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Duane "Keffe D" Davis is on trial in Las Vegas
- Published
The man accused of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur told police more than a decade later that he handed the gun used in the drive-by shooting to a passenger who then passed it to his nephew who opened fire on the rapper.
Duane "Keffe D" Davis is on trial in Las Vegas, charged with one count of murder with a deadly weapon over the killing of the rap superstar in 1996. On Thursday jurors heard a recording of a police interview with Davis in 2008.
Prosecutors allege that although Davis did not fire the gun that killed Shakur, he ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further criminal conduct for the gang he helped lead.
Davis, 63, has pleaded not guilty.
His lawyer Michael Sanft has argued that what his client had previously said of his involvement cannot be believed.
Shakur's murder is a cold case that has gripped the public's fascination for 30 years.
Prosecutors allege Davis planned the 7 September 1996 shooting after his nephew Orlando Anderson was involved in a fight with Shakur in Las Vegas hours earlier. They argue that Davis believed the attack on his nephew could not "go unanswered".
Central to the case are testimonies by Davis in the formerly secret 2008 police interview and, later, in a 2019 memoir he co-authored called Compton Street Legend.
Prosecutors on Thursday played the 2008 interview Davis conducted with Los Angeles Police detectives Daryn Dupree and Greg Kading, who were investigating the death of another rapper, Chris Wallace aka The Notorious B.I.G.
Davis described the moment the Cadillac he was a passenger in stopped alongside the car Shakur was in.
"Yeah, if we would've been on my side, I would've blasted," Davis said, according to a transcript.
According to the transcript, Davis said in the interview he passed his gun back to Deandre "Big Dre" Smith, but Smith did not want the weapon.
Anderson, who was also in the back seat, took the weapon and started firing, Davis said.
Anderson died a decade before the interview, having denied any involvement in Shakur's murder.
![A 1996 photo of rapper Tupac Shakur (L) and Marion "Suge" Knight is displayed during the Duane Davis murder trial.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/f9f8/live/0d6c23b0-9d63-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
A 1996 photo of rapper Tupac Shakur (L) and Marion "Suge" Knight displayed during the murder trial
One of the detectives, Kading, told Davis in reference to a deal for his information: "Nothing you say today can be used against you."
But prosecutors say any agreement was negated when Davis went public with his version in his memoir several years later.
The prosecutor said the book shows Davis was "mad" after his nephew was involved in a fight with Shakur in a Las Vegas casino, with Davis writing: "Them jumping on my nephew gave us the ultimate green light to do something to their ass."
In the memoir he claimed he was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot, and "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat.
Davis has since distanced himself from the book, saying he did not write all of it and that parts were fictionalised to sell more copies.
In the interview played to court, Davis said he repeatedly spoke with Sean "Diddy" Combs and discussed killing Shakur.
The detectives questioned Davis about meetings with Combs during Bad Boy Records tour stops in San Diego, Anaheim, Irvine and Las Vegas.
"Which of those four is it when you talk to him about murdering Tupac?" Kading asked, according to a transcript shown in court, as reported by Reuters.
"It was really about both of them, yeah, either one of them," Davis responded.
"Tupac and Suge?" Kading asked, referring to Death Row Records founder Marion "Suge" Knight, who was with Shakur in the vehicle during the shooting.
"Yeah," Davis responded.
Representatives for Combs did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.
However, Davis' lawyer Sanft asked jurors earlier in the trial: "What facts do you have to support any of what Keffe D said in any of his interviews or the book?"
"You have to ask yourself the question: If I just say things, is that going to end up being one of those things where I'm going to be handed up for a murder by just repeating that fiction? I keep repeating that? The answer is no. You have to corroborate everything I say in order for it to be true. Otherwise, it's just that."
Sanft has also said prosecution witnesses were unreliable and the police investigation was riddled with issues.
A former Las Vegas homicide detective told the jury earlier this week that no witnesses had been able to identify the shooter.
Later, a former member of Shakur's entourage, James "Mob James" McDonald, gave evidence that even though he was not there to witness the shooting, those who were there that night within Shakur's circle had quickly communicated who was responsible.
"It was a gang war. People were getting hurt. People were being sought," he said. "Orlando (Anderson), him and certain other people were being sought because people wanted to kill them."
  - Published3 days ago
 ![A 1996 photo of rapper Tupac Shakur (L) and Marion "Suge" Knight is displayed during the Duane Davis murder trial, related to the 1996 killing of the rapper, at Clark County District Court at the Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas, Nevada, on August 17, 2026. The trial of the former gang leader accused of orchestrating the murder of rapper Tupac Shakur began on August 10, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unresolved killings. The proceedings, expected to last a month, will likely not make clear who fired the shots that killed the California hip-hop legend on the night of September 7, 1996, while he was in Las Vegas to see a Mike Tyson boxing match.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/c9c2/live/383684b0-9ad3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
  - Published2 days ago
 ![Tupac Shakur is seen wearing all red, including a red ball cap, and a gold chain.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/e351/live/b5761980-9b79-11f1-afeb-4d7c67d79c36.jpg)
summary: During the murder trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis in Las Vegas, jurors heard a 2008 police recording in which Davis claimed his nephew, Orlando Anderson, fired the fatal shots that killed Tupac Shakur in 1996. Prosecutors allege Davis orchestrated the shooting and supplied the weapon following a casino fight involving his nephew, while Davis has pleaded not guilty. His defense argues that his prior statements and memoir accounts cannot be believed and lack corroborating facts.
key_points: Duane "Keffe D" Davis is on trial in Las Vegas, charged with murder with a deadly weapon for allegedly orchestrating the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur.
Prosecutors played a 2008 police interview recording in court where Davis stated he supplied the gun and his nephew, Orlando Anderson, fired the fatal shots.
Prosecutors argue the shooting was planned after Shakur was involved in a fight with Anderson hours earlier in Las Vegas.
Davis's defense lawyer has pleaded not guilty and argued that previous statements made by Davis in interviews and a memoir are fictionalized and lack corroboration.

title: We’ll never be royals: the California town where Prince Harry and Meghan lived says goodbye
author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
content:
The bucolic coastal California town of Montecito was thrust into the limelight six years ago as the backdrop for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s second act following an acrimonious split from Buckingham Palace.
But as the couple plans their return to the United Kingdom, Montecito’s whirlwind stint on the global stage may be coming to an end.
To be clear, the well-to-do enclave near Santa Barbara is unlikely to lose its reputation as a hideout for celebrities – a respite from the paparazzi den that Los Angeles, about 90 miles (145km) south, can be. Oprah, Gwyneth Paltrow and Ellen DeGeneres, among other public figures, have all resided in the exclusive community.
Prince Harry and Meghan, though, were arguably top contenders for Montecito’s most attention-grabbing residents. After news emerged that the couple had bought a $14.7m estate in the area, news helicopters and photographers swarmed in, to the annoyance of some neighbors.
![a gate surrounded by trees](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c83f6014128f98276d59414ff1fc94b3f320f519/0_0_5340_3477/master/5340.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Reporters even clamored for intel on a local Facebook page, prompting a moderator to warn journalists in a 2020 post: “No one will sell out or talk to the press. We don’t care who you are or where you came from, if you are our neighbor and act like a neighbor we support you.”
Santa Barbara tourism officials, meanwhile, embraced the fervor, beckoning future residents or visitors with an online tagline: “Montecito: Fit for Royalty”.
The Sussexes maintained a low profile, blending into everyday life, according to Montecito residents who spoke with the Guardian. As the couple’s next move lands like a bombshell across the pond – a shock even to some royal officials – in Montecito, residents reacted with a range of indifference and understanding.
At lunch hour on Thursday afternoon, shops along a stretch of Coast Village Road roared to life. At the Montecito Country Mart, visitors lingered outside, dining on sandwiches and sipping caffeinated drinks from a slew of nearby bakeries. The bustling area stood in stark contrast to other, quieter parts of town with lavish homes hidden behind tall, well-manicured shrubs.
In a boutique brimming with nautical trinkets, 65-year-old Susanne pondered the prospect of Harry and Meghan reconciling with their family. “I would love to see that,” she said, declining to give her last name.
![a person crossing the street](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/80ebda05bb54dad4826eb29b5d079a5c8eaf7259/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In recent years, the couple have given a wide berth to Buckingham Palace. Meghan, who is biracial, publicly chastised her royal relatives for racist mistreatment and inadequate handling of media intrusion. More recently, the couple was embroiled in a protracted legal dispute over funding for their security protection.
“It’s sad that it’s been divided,” Susanne said.
Erin E Doherty, moderator of a Montecito Facebook page with more than 11,000 members, had no problem with Harry and Meghan living in her area, which she called a “little slice of heaven”.
It was not unusual for billionaires to socialize with people in lower-income brackets, she said, noting that she would run into Harry strolling on the beach with his children “all the time”.
Doherty’s only gripe around the royal ordeal was with overzealous members of the press.
“I think it’s natural to want to raise children around family and let them have relationships with cousins,” she said of their move. “If they didn’t, I’m sure they would regret it.”
![a road](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b30536927c6953f2ceb9490dfea0b716af565eab/0_0_3000_2000/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Karna Hughes, the director of public relations at Visit Santa Barbara, heaped praise on the couple for patronizing local businesses.
Some of the town’s attractions received the Hollywood treatment with screen time on Meghan’s Netflix cooking show, With Love, Meghan.
“We hope they found respite in the beautiful vistas of the mountains and beaches as well as neighborly camaraderie,” Hughes said. “We will warmly welcome them back any time.”
Another area resident, though, held Harry and Meghan in comparatively low regard.
Montecito used to be a “cute small town”, said a man, dining outside Sakana Sushi, who declined to give his name. It always had old money, but from his perspective as a “working-class contractor” who has lived nearby since 1974, he has seen the enclave creep toward being untenably “rich-ified”.
“Good riddance,” he said of the couple’s return across the pond.
Harry and Meghan may not be entirely through with Montecito. They reportedly plan to keep their property.
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan are planning to return to the United Kingdom after spending six years living in the affluent California town of Montecito. Their presence in the community drew swarms of media attention and paparazzi, frustrating some locals while tourism officials embraced the publicity. Local residents reacted to the news of their departure with a mix of indifference, understanding, and occasional relief.
key_points: Prince Harry and Meghan lived in Montecito for six years after splitting from Buckingham Palace.
The couple's arrival brought an influx of news helicopters and photographers that annoyed some neighbors.
Despite media attention, the couple largely maintained a low profile and patronized local businesses.
Residents and local officials expressed a mix of reactions to their departure, ranging from support and understanding to indifference.

title: Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understands
author: Daniela Relph; Paul Gribben
content:
![Duchess of Sussex, head and shoulders pic](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/9235/live/6a8b1d10-7bcd-11f1-b543-9988255dfa81.jpg)
- Published
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, the BBC has learned.
Discussions are in their early stages but this would be Meghan's first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.
Much of the two previous series of The Gentlemen, which was created by Guy Ritchie, have been filmed in the Cotswolds - the area it is rumoured Harry and Meghan will set up home when they return to the UK later this month.
The Gentlemen, starring the actor Theo James, is a comedy series about a duke who becomes a drug baron.
The details of the discussions and any role Meghan might be offered have not yet been revealed.
Actors Hugh Bonneville and Vinnie Jones have appeared in previous series of the show.
Meghan was best known in acting for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode aired in 2018.
The duchess put her career on hold after her marriage to Prince Harry in May 2018. At the time, she told the BBC she did not view quitting acting as giving anything up, but rather as "a new chapter".
She recently returned to acting for the first time in nearly a decade, with a cameo as herself in forthcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, which stars Lily Collins and Brie Larson.
A return to acting could be lucrative for Meghan. The BBC understands that while based in the UK she also hopes to expand the global reach of her US-based lifestyle and cooking brand, As Ever.
News of her possible return to acting comes after it was announced that Prince Harry and Meghan are to move back to the UK.
The BBC understands Prince Harry and Meghan intend to relocate from the US later this month to a private, non-royal residence outside London, as first reported by the Daily Telegraph and the Sun.
The couple's children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
There are no current plans for either Prince Harry or Meghan to resume their roles as working royals.
Their plan to move to the UK follows a visit in July by Prince Harry, Meghan and their children to see King Charles III at his Highgrove home in Gloucestershire.
It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years, and the couple's first visit to the UK together since 2022.
Returning on a longer term basis has reignited questions over the level of the couple's publicly funded security in Britain.
Their UK security was downgraded after they stopped being working royals in 2020 and moved to the US, where they have paid for their own protection.
The Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), an independent body overseen by the Home Office, will now have to make a new decision about security as previous arrangements were based on the Sussexes not living in the UK permanently.
summary: The Duchess of Sussex is reportedly in early discussions for a role in the Netflix series The Gentlemen, marking her first significant acting role since her marriage. This news coincides with plans for Prince Harry, Meghan, and their children to relocate from the US to the UK later this month. The move back to the UK follows a visit to King Charles III in July and has raised questions regarding the couple's publicly funded security arrangements.
key_points: Meghan is in early talks for a role in the Netflix comedy series The Gentlemen.
Prince Harry and Meghan plan to relocate from the US to a private residence in the UK later this month.
The couple's children are enrolled to start at a British school in September.
There are no current plans for the couple to resume their roles as working royals.
The move back to the UK prompts a new review of the couple's publicly funded security by Ravec.
